News.title: What time is Andy Burnham becoming Prime Minister today – and how to watch
News.content:
ANDY BURNHAM is preparing to walk through the famous black door of No10 Downing Street to become the UK’s next Prime Minister.

Following a whirlwind transition, the new Labour leader is taking the reins of government.

What time will Andy Burnham officially be PM?

The keys to Downing Street are being handed over today in a swift, tightly timed sequence of events.



The switchover begins this morning as outgoing Prime Minister Sir Keir Starmer travels to Buckingham Palace to formally tender his resignation to King Charles III.



This is expected to take place at around 11.15am.

Once Starmer departs, Burnham will make his own journey to the Palace..

The exact moment Burnham accepts the King’s invitation to form a new administration, he officially becomes the Prime Minister of the United Kingdom.



Following his audience with the monarch, the new PM will be driven directly to his new home at No10.

If everything runs to schedule, you can expect Burnham to deliver his first official speech to the nation on the steps of Downing Street at around 12.15pm.

Here is a breakdown of today’s expected timeline:

11.15am: Keir Starmer delivers his farewell speech outside No10, then travels to Buckingham Palace to formally resign.

Keir Starmer delivers his farewell speech outside No10, then travels to Buckingham Palace to formally resign. 11.45am: Andy Burnham meets King Charles III at Buckingham Palace to officially become Prime Minister.

Andy Burnham meets King Charles III at Buckingham Palace to officially become Prime Minister. 12.15pm: Burnham arrives at Downing Street and delivers his first speech to the nation.

Burnham arrives at Downing Street and delivers his first speech to the nation. 2.00pm: The official appointment of the new Cabinet begins.

How does Burnham officially become PM?

Britain doesn’t have an official inauguration ceremony or a public swearing-in on a Bible.



Instead, the entire transfer of power happens during a private meeting at Buckingham Palace known as an audience.

During this meeting, King Charles III will formally ask Burnham if he will form a new government. Once Burnham accepts, the deal is done.

But what about the famous “Kissing of the Hands” tradition? Will Burnham actually have to kiss the King’s hands?

While the constitutional ritual is still officially called the Kissing of Hands, the literal act has not been practised for generations.

Today, the incoming Prime Minister simply offers a respectful, formal handshake to the monarch to seal the agreement.



The phrase survives purely as a historic term of loyalty to the Crown.

Once the meeting is over, an official notification is published in the Court Circular, confirming to the public that political power has officially changed hands.

How can I watch it all live?

You won’t have to miss a single second of today’s events as the country welcomes its new leader.

For full live coverage, head over to The Sun’s official YouTube channel.

News.title: Trump ‘planning for return of all out war with Iran’ as US unleashes ninth night of strikes & ships ‘explode’ in Strait
News.content:
THE US has reportedly deployed warplanes to the Middle East as it prepares to escalate the conflict with Iran – after blitzing the rogue nation in a ninth night of strikes.

US President Donald Trump said the latest bombardment “hit them [Iran] very hard” on Sunday night.



The strikes were meant to “swiftly punish” Tehran for the suspected deaths of three American soldiers.

“Iran has been very, very badly damaged. They’ve lost everything almost militarily. They’ve got very little left,” Trump said.



It comes as Air Force F-16 fighter jets from Germany and stealthy F-35 jets from Britain are being sent to the Middle East, officials told the New York Times.

US Central Command (Centcom) said Sunday nights strikes targeted Iranian military assets including coastal surveillance and missile and drone sites.



Explosions were also reported in several Iranian cities, state news reported on Monday morning.

The reeling regime has responded with fury, launching a volley of strikes at US-allies Kuwait, Bahrain, Jordan and a “surprise attack” in Syria.



“The US military is holding Iran accountable at the Commander in Chief’s direction,” Centcom declared in a post on X.

It added that the operation aimed to “diminish Iran’s ability” to attack commercial vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Control of the key waterway has become a focal point of the conflict in recent days.

Iran’s Revolutionary Guard (IRGC) warned the Strait “will ⁠not be safe” for ships carrying “a single drop of oil and gas” as long as “US aggression” persists.

It also said two oil tankers were blitzed after attempting to pass through the strait via an unauthorised route.



“Both vessels exploded and were forced to cease movement”, the IRGC said.

On Saturday the US military said a US soldier was killed by the “controlled detonation of an Iranian drone” in northern Iraq.

It came one day after an attack on a base in Jordan killed two US soldiers with a third missing and presumed dead.



Centcom announced on Sunday it had found “unidentified remains” in the search for a missing soldier.

Several others were wounded in the assault on Muwaffaq Salti Air Base, which has suffered unrelenting attacks from Iran in recent days.

Trump called the American deaths “a shame” but declared the armed forces operation remained essential.

Even before the fatal attacks, the US president signalled plans to escalate military action including targeting key infrastructure including bridges and power plants.

The deaths bring the American toll of the war to 17 – but the two service members confirmed dead on Friday were the first to be killed by direct fire from Iran since the conflict began in February.



And it’s the first time US troops have been killed since the ceasefire collapsed two weeks ago.

An interim agreement to end the war has been left in tatters since July 7, when Iran struck ships in the key waterway and the US responded with air strikes.

Iran then announced the closure of the strait, but Washington reimposed its own blockade of Iranian ports.



The collapse of the deal has left the raging war with no clear end in sight after more than four months of devastating violence.

News.title: Spluttering economy, ballooning welfare, defence blackhole & immigration fury… new PM Burnham faces in-tray from hell
News.content:
ANDY Burnham becomes PM at a precarious time for his party, the country and the wider world.

Awaiting him in Downing Street is an unenviable intray of thorny issues that will require some hard decisions.



Since returning to Parliament the new PM has been tight-lipped about his plans for government except for promising a programme of mass devolution.

Mr Burnham has been criticised for failing to come clean with his agenda and instead largely resorting to “vibes”.



But there are undodgeable decisions hurtling down the tracks that will force him to make tough choices in the coming months and years.

Economy

Mr Burnham inherits a spluttering economy starved of any meaningful growth and hamstrung by eye-watering amounts of debt.

For years Britain has been in a high-tax, high-spend doom loop that is forever squeezing workers for more of their cash.

The national debt currently stands at almost £3trillion, of which the interest alone is costing us £110billion every year.



Mr Burnham has pledged “good growth in every postcode” but is yet to lay out exactly how he plans to achieve that.

He famously said that Britain should not be so “in hock” to the bond markets, in a signal that he could loosen the fiscal rules to allow him to borrow even more.

The PM has vowed to stick to Labour’s election commitment to freeze the rates of income tax, national insurance and VAT.

But he has already said people will have to “pay a little bit more”, suggesting he could raise capital gains tax, inheritance tax and reform council tax bands.

Welfare

By far the largest area of spending that needs cutting is the ballooning welfare budget, which is on course to hit £407billion by the end of the decade.



Mr Burnham has vowed to rein in the benefits bill by driving the army of unemployed Brits back into work.

But he has signalled he will avoid the kind of “crude” cuts to welfare that saw Labour MPs rebel against Sir Keir Starmer.

Despite Labour MP opposition to welfare restraint, the spending is becoming such a drag on the economy that Mr Burnham will find he has no choice but to act.



The PM has already committed to keeping the pensions triple lock, which accounts for around half of all welfare spending.

Immigration

While the Starmer government may have crowed about reducing both legal and illegal migration in recent months, the public is far from satisfied.

Poll after poll shows immigration is among the top concerns for voters, with small boats especially still a major issue.

Mr Burnham has already stressed the need to close migrant hotels and HMOs but that only happens by ramping up deportations.

Removals of Channel crossers have historically been pitifully low.



On legal migration, Mr Burnham has tentatively backed Shabana Mahmood’s crackdown on settled status for foreigners but has opened the door to softening it later.

Labour MPs are already gearing up to water down the plan to double the length of time someone must live here before getting permanent residency from five to 10 years.

Defence

In a fractious world, there is a public clamour to shore up Britain’s defences with increased military firepower.

But Sir Keir has left him with £15billion to find after failing to stump up the funds in his last few weeks as PM.

How Mr Burnham goes about scrabbling together the cash to plug the black hole in the armed forces will be an early test.



Donald Trump

How Mr Burnham deals with Donald Trump will be crucial to Britain’s alliance with the United States.

Sir Keir love-bombed the erratic President but their pair quickly found themselves in conflict over immigration, Net Zero and Iran.

Labour MPs, who loathe Trump, may cheer Mr Burnham for squaring up to him initially but may find themselves with unhappy constituents if the results are more tariffs on goods.

Early election?

Mr Burnham’s biggest weakness is that he lacks a mandate of his own, having swept into No10 coronated by Labour MPs.

Pollsters will be telling him that new PMs never have it as good as their first three months.



Indeed there already seems signs of a “Burnham bounce” as Labour ties level with Reform.

So – despite insisting he will not pull the trigger – Mr Burnham will be seriously considering going to the country.

But he will almost certainly see his majority slashed, and big beasts are almost nailed on to lose their seats on current projections.

Can he really tell Yvette Cooper, John Healey and Ed Miliband they need to be sacrificial lambs just so he can claim his own mandate to govern.

It’ll be one to chew over, for sure.

News.title: Dramatic vids show Moscow blitzed by biggest attack of war with 400 Ukraine drones sent to rain hell on Putin’s doorstep
News.content:
MOSCOW has been blitzed by Ukraine’s biggest attack of the war so far – with dramatic clips showing 400 drones raining hell on Vladimir Putin’s doorstep.

Extraordinary footage showed huge plumes of smoke rising over the Russian capital amid the onslaught – part of Volodymyr Zelensky’s endgame blitz.



A critical oil depot in Podolsk and a key logistics hub called the Yuzhnye Vorota Industrial Park – located near Moscow’s Domodedovo airport – were among the targets.

Footage showed one of Ukraine’s drones crashing into a high-rise tower – reportedly leaving at least six people injured.



In the same clip, another UAV struck a nearby apartment building sparking a huge fire.

Plumes of smoke could be seen rising in the background amid the air assault.

Huge infernos raged around Moscow in the latest drone salvo which is part of Kyiv’s 40-day endgame blitz aimed at ending the war.

Ukraine has been targeting key energy hubs in Russia to cripple Putin’s fuel supplies and suffocate the economy.



Moscow’s governor Andrei Vorobyov said: “Overnight, air defence forces and electronic warfare systems repelled a drone attack on Moscow region.

“The main consequences were recorded in Podolsk, Domodedovo, and the Odintsovo district.”

A sprawling warehouse in Koledino belonging to Russian e-commerce store Wildberries was also evacuated amid the drone onslaught.



The same firm suffered £1.5billion in damages following a wave of attacks last weekend.

There were also reports of a power blackout in Russian-occupied Crimea after hits on power plants.

And a fire ignited at a military airfield in Yeisk, Krasnodar, following drone strikes.



In the early hours of Monday, Ukraine also hit three oil depots and a fuel facility in Russia’s Stavropol region.

Zelensky said three Russian shadow fleet tankers – vessels used by Putin to dodge Western sanctions – were also struck in the Black Sea.

It came after Russia unleashed a barrage of deadly ballistic missiles on Ukraine in one of the most intense blitzes of the war so far.

The ferocious assault on Sunday in Kyiv lasted around 40 minutes as swarms of drones pounded the capital, sparking dozens of fires.

At least one person was killed and 16 others wounded after more than 40 explosions rocked five districts of the capital city.



Zelensky said: “Throughout the night, Russia launched one of the most massive ballistic missile attacks on Kyiv.

“The enemy fired more than 40 missiles of various types, most of them targeting the capital, and 120 attack drones.”

Among the targets were civilian homes, office buildings, a metro station and a key logistics hub linked to Ukraine‘s armed forces.

Elsewhere, Russian strikes hit a warehouse and logistics facility near Bucha.

Missiles also struck a rehabilitation centre for children with disabilities in Sumy.



It comes after The Sun revealed that the British Army has war-gamed strikes on Putin’s home city of St Petersburg with new jet-powered drones.

The UAVs have a range of more than 150 miles and are designed to destroy targets such as oil depots, ammunition dumps and military command posts.

A top Army source told us: “A tank can deny Russia ground, a drone can punish them.”

News.title: Who will be in Andy Burnham’s Cabinet? Expected winners and losers from Ed Miliband to Shabana Mahmood
News.content:
ANDY Burnham is set to unveil his first Cabinet after weeks of feverish Westminster speculation.

The Labour leader is expected to reveal his top team after officially becoming Prime Minister on today.



Here, The Sun looks at the runners and riders for the biggest jobs in government.

Chancellor

Ever since Andy Burnham returned to Westminster, one question has dominated politics: who will get the keys to No11?



For weeks, Ed Miliband looked like the favourite.

The former Labour leader has played a key role in Burnham’s rise and is regarded by allies as one of the Government’s most effective Cabinet ministers.

But his promotion has also alarmed MPs, advisers and market watchers, who see him as too closely associated with Labour’s soft left and worry his commitment to net zero could unsettle investors.

His supporters have insisted he is fiscally disciplined and have been pointing out there is little in his ministerial record to suggest he would embark on a borrowing spree.

However, concerns over market confidence are understood to have persuaded Burnham that Miliband may not be the right person for the Treasury.

Home Secretary Shabana Mahmood is now widely tipped to become Chancellor despite wanting to remain at the Home Office.



Seen as being on the right of the Labour Party, she is viewed as a reassuring choice for the financial markets.

The biggest question mark is her lack of economic experience.

Foreign Secretary

Yvette Cooper has spent weeks fighting to keep hold of the Foreign Office.



During her first year in the role, she has built what allies describe as a strong working relationship with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio.

But if Mr Miliband misses out on the Treasury, Burnham could hand him the Foreign Office as a consolation prize.

His brother David Miliband was also rumoured to be in line for the job – but The Sun reported last week he is actually eyeing the role of US ambassador in Washington.

Former Defence Secretary John Healey, who extraordinarily quit Sir Keir Starmer‘s Government over the defence investment plan, has also been tipped for the job.



Defence Secretary

Dan Jarvis only took over as Defence Secretary a matter of weeks ago after replacing John Healey.

At the time, many in Westminster thought he had inherited a poisoned chalice as ministers scrambled to find billions to fund Labour’s ambitious Defence Investment Plan.

Jarvis managed to secure a little bit extra cash from the Treasury and won praise for getting the DIP off the ground.

The former South Yorkshire Mayor is also seen as politically close to Andy Burnham, with the pair having worked together as metro mayors.



It has made him one of the ministers most likely to survive the reshuffle – although Healey is still seen by some as a contender if Burnham opts for experience.

Who is almost certain to be in the Cabinet?

Louise Haigh has become one of Burnham’s closest allies.

The former Transport Secretary, who was sacked by Sir Keir Starmer, is expected to be appointed Chancellor of the Duchy of Lancaster, making her one of the Prime Minister’s most trusted and powerful ministers.



Angela Rayner is also expected to return to Cabinet. She had wanted the Education brief but is now seen as more likely to return to the Department for Housing, Communities and Local Government.

Lucy Powell, Burnham’s constituency neighbour and another minister dismissed by Starmer, is expected to make a Cabinet comeback. The Labour deputy leader is likely to be rewarded with a senior role.

Heidi Alexander is heavily rumoured to become Chief Whip despite wanting to stay on as Transport Secretary.

Wes Streeting is also seen as a frontrunner for one of the biggest jobs in Burnham’s government.

The Health Secretary was one of Labour’s most high-profile performers under Sir Keir and is viewed as one of the party’s strongest communicators.



Cabinet Casualties

Not everyone is expected to survive the cull.

Several of Sir Keir Starmer’s closest allies are widely expected to be shown the door. Business Secretary Peter Kyle is expected to lose his Cabinet seat.

Technology Secretary Liz Kendall is also widely tipped to be sacked.



Several other junior ministers are also expected to be removed as the new Prime Minister wants to reward loyalists who backed his leadership campaign.

News.title: Football fan, 13, dies after fountain he climbed while celebrating Spain’s World Cup win collapses as two left injured
News.content:
Add us as a preferred source

WORLD CUP HORROR Football fan, 13, dies after fountain he climbed while celebrating Spain’s World Cup win collapses as two left injured

A 13-YEAR-OLD boy has died during Spain’s World Cup celebrations after a fountain he was standing on suddenly collapsed.

The teenager had climbed onto the structure to celebrate Spain‘s triumph when it gave way beneath him, causing him to fall.



Emergency services rushed to the scene in Spain’s western city of Ciudad Rodrigo and desperately tried to remove heavy debris.

After freeing the victim, he was rushed to a nearby hospital and pronounced dead shortly after arrival.



The shocking incident occurred in the early hours of Monday morning.

The historic walled settlement is located in the province of Salamanca near the Spanish border.

City bosses has since declared three days of mourning will be observed.

A statement read: “The City Council of Ciudad Rodrigo expresses its sorrow and condolences over the death of the 13-year-old child.

“The entire city of Ciudad Rodrigo mourns this loss and stands with the child’s family and friends in their grief.

“What should have been a celebration of the Spanish national team’s victory in the World Cup has turned into a tragedy for the entire community of Ciudad Rodrigo.



“The City Council also wishes a speedy recovery to the other people who were affected by the incident.

“As a sign of mourning for this loss, the City Council’s flags will fly at half-mast from July 20 to July 22.”

The fountain where the tragedy occurred stands at a junction known locally in English as the Fat Tree Roundabout.

The name dates back to a century-old elm tree that once dominated the site, until it was felled after succumbing to Dutch elm disease.

Tributes to the young fan have poured in, with one writing: “How unfair life is when tears of joy turn into pain.



“It’s very hard. Strength to the family. Rest in peace.”

“What a great tragedy. Sending hugs and strength to the family,” another added.

“Ciudad Rodrigo is in mourning. Rest in peace, little angel.”

Spain’s exuberant celebrations came after they claimed a second World Cup title with a hard-fought 1-0 extra-time victory over Argentina.

Ferran Torres scored the decisive goal, while Lionel Messi brought the curtain down on his international career in defeat.



RECOMMENDED STORIES

Scenes of jubilation across Spain quickly went viral following the final whistle, as fans celebrated their nation’s historic triumph.

US President Donald Trump presented the trophy after Spain were crowned world champions at MetLife Stadium in New Jersey.

News.content:
Andy Burnham becomes the sixth Prime Minister to walk up Downing Street in a decade later today - after King Charles invites the new Labour leader to form a government

Andy Burnham will today become Prime Minister — and will have an audience with King Charles before he delivers his first speech at Downing Street as leader.

The so-called King of the North will set the tone of his government for years to come, acknowledging a nation weary at the frequent sight of the No10 podium. Crucially though, the address will give Mr Burnham, 56, the chance to vow to give Britain “more breathing space” on the cost of living.

And Labour’s deputy leader, Lucy Powell, insisted on Sunday that Mr Burnham will set out a “bolder more ambitious” vision for fixing Britain’s thorny problems.

Other allies of Mr Burnham said he would argue that political stability must deliver “tangible” improvements along with the “breathing room” on the cost of living he has previously promised.

When Keir Starmer resigned last month, the politician fought back the tears as he admitted Labour MPs did not think he was "best placed" to lead Labour into the next general election.

News.title: 'Why bereaved Hillsborough families like mine believe in Andy Burnham'
News.content:
I had never heard of Andy Burnham until the 20th anniversary of Hillsborough. I had given birth to my second son two days before and was watching the Anfield memorial service from the hospital.

It feels somewhat mean to say this now, but I was so cross that a politician had been allowed to speak at a memorial service. Midway through his speech, he stopped as the people on the Kop shouted "Justice", I felt so empowered and was elated that people were chanting at him.

Then I saw the sincerity in Andy's eyes, and my disgust turned to empathy. My respect for Andy came when the Hillsborough Independent Panel materialised, and when the Panel concluded, Andy earned my trust. In the years that followed, Andy and I became friends.

Andy Burnham live: Labour leader to become PM today and address the nation READ MORE :

View 2 Images Andy Burnham with families of Hillsborough victims outside (Image: Stefan Rousseau/PA Wire)

‌



He has lots of qualities, he's kind, unassuming, understanding, approachable, incredibly loyal, and empathetic, but the quality I admire the most is that he is unbelievably calm. When he asked me to be a part of the "Hillsborough Law Now" launch, I immediately agreed.

There have been countless times during the process of negotiations for the Public Office Accountability Bill where I have felt totally out of my depth, riddled with anxiety and spiralling in the thought of losing all progress completely, he has taken the time to speak with me at length, explain the process and has never faltered on his hope that we would achieve it - "we will get there Charl, on way or another. I promise you that".

Hillsborough Law Now is made up of many different campaigners, from many different injustices. Andy completely understands that within all of these different groups, there are many traumatised people.

It is seeing that distress and the damage that injustice does, which has driven him. He genuinely wants to right the wrongs. He has also never made a commitment that he could not fulfil, where there have been areas out of his remit, he has been honest and never hesitates to provide an explanation why.

‌



I was in the House of Commons for Keir Starmer's final speech on the Public Office Accountability Bill, as I entered the under gallery I was already emotional but as I looked further left I saw Andy's smiley little face amongst all the MPs, that really made me cry.

Watching Andy give his speech on the Bill is right up there with one of the proudest most of my life. Seeing the original Parliamentary Lead, who brought the Bill in to the Commons, now be a part of its final steps was obviously meant to be.

These past few months have been really strange, watching your friend become Prime Minister is so surreal. But he's taken it all in his stride.

Cool, calm Andy. He does come with downsides though. His football banter consists of that typical bluenose nonsense, and when i say he is thrilled to be the first Evertonian Prime Minister, I do not exaggerate!

‌



It was lovely to watch on TV last Friday as he became the Leader of the Labour Party. I have also found it highly amusing to change his name in my phone. If you're reading this, Andy, you've been upgraded, love – Bluenose Burnham is now - "Prime Minister Bluenose”.

On a serious note - I'm so excited for our political future, I wish Andy and his family every success in this new chapter and have no doubt that he will do himself, his family, the Labour Party and our country proud, as he always has.

News.title: People only just learning what Neil Armstrong really said on the Moon as many get it wrong
News.content:
People only just learning what Neil Armstrong really said on the Moon as many get it wrong

People have been left baffled to learn that the iconic quote said by Neil Armstrong as he took the first steps on the Moon is actually commonly misquoted, as many miss out one word

View Image Neil Armstrong took this picture of Buzz Aldrin on the Moon during the Apollo 11 mission (Image: NASA/Heritage Images via Getty Images)

Back in 1969, millions of people around the world gathered around their televisions and radios as Neil Armstrong became the first person in history to set foot on the Moon, uttering an iconic phrase as he did.

‌



Launched from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on July 16, 1969, the Apollo 11 mission made history as NASA astronauts Armstrong, Buzz Aldrin, and Michael Collins set off for the Moon. Four days later, on July 20, Armstrong and Aldrin made history once again as the first people to land on the moon, while Collins remained in lunar orbit

‌



As Armstrong took his first steps, he famously uttered a phrase that would be known as generations to come as the first words uttered by an astronaut when walking on the Moon.

‌



However, one Reddit user has now pointed out that most people actually misquote Armstrong when they mention his historic phrase.

They explained: "As he took his first steps, he uttered words that would be written into history books for generations to come: 'That’s one small step for man. One giant leap for mankind.' Or at least that’s how the media reported his words."

‌



The user went on to explain that Armstrong since has insisted that the media got this phrase wrong, and that he actually said: "That’s one small step for a man."

"In fact, in the official transcript of the Moon landing mission, NASA transcribes the quote as “that’s one small step for (a) man," the user added.

Users quickly took to the comments section to share their thoughts, as many had different thoughts about whether or not they could hear Armstrong say the 'a' in the sentence.

‌



"Have you listened to the recording? No one misheard it. The recording does not have the 'a'," one person said.

Another went on to say: "This is true, but my counterpoint to you is that the iconic nature of his words weren’t what he said, but what the world heard.

"As Neil said, this was a giant leap for mankind, and so I argue the importance of the line is how we, as a species heard it, not how a man in a suit half a million kilometres away heard it."

Article continues below

They added: "We heard 'one small step for man', and that’s how history will remember the line because that’s how we heard it, sitting in our homes, watching humanity make history."

Someone else went on to say: "NASA transcribes it like that because its unclear if the 'a; was said or not with the poor sound quality. People have researched this and its still unclear 50 years later.

"Neil says he said the 'a' but if no one heard it then the quote we all heard is all that matters."

News.title: New Lidl £20 kit that cleans kitchens, bathrooms and blasts mould out this Sunday
News.content:
New Lidl £20 kit that cleans kitchens, bathrooms and blasts mould out this Sunday

Shoppers can clean almost any room in their house with the upcoming SpecialBuy deal

View 3 Images The new SpecialBuy offer is coming out in a few days (Image: Getty)

A new household product is coming out in Lidl stores across the UK in a few days that "cleans, disinfects and degreases". As part of the supermarket's next round of SpecialBuy deals on Sunday, July 26, shoppers can get their hands on a kit that can help kill bacteria and lift mould around the house.

‌



The budget supermarket is launching a range of new cleaning products on Sunday. One item is the Silvercrest Hand-Held Steam Cleaner, which will be on sale for £19.99. In addition to the cleaning gadget, it comes with seven extra accessories: an extension nozzle, an angled nozzle, an upholstery nozzle, a fabric cover, a round brush, an extension hose, and a measuring cup.

‌



A portable steam cleaner typically uses high-pressure hot water vapour to break down grease, remove dirt, and disinfect surfaces without the need for harsh chemicals. It can be useful for tasks such as cleaning tile grout, removing stubborn oven grease, revitalising upholstery, and blasting dirt from narrow window tracks.

‌



A steam cleaner can be handy to use when trying to remove mould from hard, non-porous surfaces. The high temperature, usually above 100°C, kills mould spores, and the pressurised steam forces dirt out of small spaces such as tile grout.

Lidl says the £19.99 steam cleaner "produces a powerful jet of steam for a deep clean" that "uses no chemicals or cleaning agents". It adds how it can remove dirt "thoroughly", even in "hard-to-reach areas". The supermarket also says it is:

For shiny taps, basins, mirrors and tiles.

For refreshing upholstery and textiles.

For all steam-resistant surfaces such as glass, ceramic, masonry, metal and enamel.

‌



View 3 Images The £19.99 Silvercrest Hand-Held Steam Cleaner comes with seven accessories (Image: Lidl)

The steam cleaner has an "extra long" cable for use in a large area without unplugging (4m), as well as a "short" heat-up time of three minutes. It also has indicator lights, a safety lock, and overheat protection.

The "small, handy and easy to store" cleaner has a water tank capacity of 250ml, and the steam pressure is 2.8–3.5 bar. It comes with a three-year warranty, and its total size with the steam nozzle is 28cm wide, 23cm tall and 14cm long.

‌



Steam can clean many things, but the high heat and moisture can harm certain materials. Avoid using a handheld steam cleaner on Unsealed wood or laminate floors, as moisture can cause warping. As well as delicate fabrics that are sensitive to heat, like silk or thin synthetics.

View 3 Images Lidl is releasing several new cleaning items this Sunday (Image: Lidl)

Other things to steer clear of include cold glass, as sudden temperature changes could cause it to shatter. Avoid using it on unpainted drywall or things painted with water-based paint.

Article continues below

Also coming out on Sunday is Lidl's new £7.99 W5 Spray Mop, which the store says is ideal for tiles and all smooth floors. It adds: "With a detergent spray function – easy floor cleaning without a bucket. Ergonomic handle with an integrated lever for spraying detergent with ease."

Fire crews are still battling the blaze that broke out on Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh yesterday evening

Arthur's Seat fire live: Fire crews still at the scene of huge Edinburgh blaze

A large fire broke out on Arthur's Seat in Edinburgh yesterday - and fire crews are still battling the blaze this morning.

The fire, located next to the Palace of Holyrood House, started around 6.30pm on Sunday. Four fire engines from the Scottish Fire and Rescue Service are in attendance.

News.title: 'I ignored weird sounds in my ears for years, but it was a tumour'
News.content:
'I ignored weird sounds in my ears for years, but it was a tumour'

Paige Footner, 31, thought her symptoms were down to stress

'I ignored weird sounds in my ears for years, but it was a tumour'

A paramedic who ignored strange noises in her ear for years was left stunned when doctors discovered a huge brain tumour. Paige Footner had suffered with tinnitus for three years, brushing it off as stress from her busy life as both a medic and circus performer.

‌



But the 31-year-old was left reeling when a scan revealed a 4cm growth on her brain. Now recovering after surgery, she says the experience has completely changed her outlook and even inspired her to go on 50 dates in search of love.

‌



“I had pulsatile tinnitus in one of my ears for three years,” said Paige. “I thought it was maybe stress related but after a year or two it started to get worse and was there all the time. Even though I wasn’t overly stressed about it, I mentioned it to my GP who said it could be a sign of something sinister and referred me to an ENT specialist.

‌



View 8 Images Paige Footner in hospital after surgery.

“But because I go away a lot for the circus, it took me over a year to properly follow up. The specialist said it was probably from a benign cause, maybe an infection or past trauma – and I hit my head a lot doing circus so it made sense. He said to get an MRI just in case, but it would likely be fine.

“I also got some headaches occasionally, but because I work shift work, they’re not uncommon. I was recently diagnosed with ADHD too, which my neurosurgeon said was probably a symptom of the tumour because it was in my frontal lobe. They actually think the tumour was an incidental finding and it wasn’t causing the tinnitus.

‌



“I was just super lucky they found it.”

View 8 Images Paige during her treatment

Paige’s MRI had revealed she had a very significant brain tumour. The radiologist told her it could be cancer and she was referred to a neurosurgeon. She said: “I had a lot of scans done after that – MRIs, CTs, and PET scans – but the tumour was considered to have atypical findings so they couldn’t diagnose it without surgery.

‌



“When I saw the neurosurgeon she gave some hope and said it looked like a meningioma which is often benign but she needed to do another scan to be sure. Unfortunately, that scan did not show the typical features of a benign tumour, it showed some concerning findings that meant it could be a cancerous tumour or lymphoma.”

With the surgery now urgent, Paige had to cancel her trip to Edinburgh Fringe festival and all of her work overseas, which she said was “a huge financial and mental blow”.

View 8 Images Paige Footner as a circus performer.

‌



But after the surgery, she was “immensely blessed” with good news. Paige said: “It ended up being a grade one meningioma which is benign. Unfortunately the tumour does have a high proliferative score, though, which means it can be more aggressive than a grade one and has a higher chance of returning, but they will just monitor it closely and do surgery again rather than radiotherapy.”

Paige said the diagnosis eight months ago forced her to reassess her life. She said: “In the radiology clinic time instantly froze and my life flashed before my eyes like a TV show. As a paramedic, we get a front row seat into other people’s lives and decisions, as well as their regrets before they die.

“This had motivated me to live my life fully, but in that moment I realised I had failed. I was 30 and I’d never experienced love. I’d never had a boyfriend, never even had a fling or a romantic kiss. I was literally a virgin.

‌



View 8 Images Paige at the circus

“The pain of missing out on love was indescribable. I also regretted hustling so much at work, missing my friends’ events and not putting them first. I had money in the bank rather than spending it making memories.

“But I also looked back on my life and smiled. I’d performed in the circus all over the world, achieved what I never thought I could, and made incredible friends that held my heart and became family.

‌



“At the end of the day, all we have are our memories and connections with our loved ones. And I had more than most, what a privilege.”

View 8 Images Paige Footner with Daniel Radcliffe

Paige says she struggled to tell people at first because it was her job to be “brave”. She said: “I couldn’t let my family see this side of me, so I did what I always do in times of crisis – I messaged my boss. I said, ‘Matt, I have a brain tumour, I don’t mean to scare you but I don’t think I’m going to be at work Monday’.

‌



“And I am so glad I told him. It was helpful having someone rational and medical to talk through it with me. My plan was to tell everyone I was injured – that’s why I wouldn’t be at work – and to tell my parents I was going overseas for six months.

“I was going to have brain surgery without them knowing. My boss was adamant that I needed to tell people, though, and even though I argued, he was right. Telling people opened the door for people to show me I was loved, that I was memorable and that I’d made a positive impact in their life.

View 8 Images Paige Footner

‌



“It was crazy. People who I thought didn’t even know who I was, because they were so cool, messaged me. Even my crush messaged me.”

Paige says she wasn’t scared going into brain surgery because she’d reframed vulnerability as a strength. And despite a tough recovery, she’s now determined to live life to the full. She said: “I had surgery to remove the tumour – it was 4cm which is quite big.

“I must admit, the thought of your brain and skull being cut open is rather scary and intimidating. But I was very lucky to have a good experience. I had an all female team and my neurosurgeon was one of the best, kindest and most compassionate people I’ve ever met.

‌



View 8 Images Paige's brain scan

“She really made a difference and helped bring some light to a dark, vulnerable time. I actually got quite sick after the surgery and was in there for three weeks. I couldn’t move my left arm very well, couldn’t walk without falling over and sometimes I couldn’t even lift my head off the pillow or talk.

“My body had always been the door to my dreams and now I was stuck in a bed barely able to even roll over. One of the doctors said, ‘We don’t know if you’re ever going to make it back to acrobatics and paramedics,’ which was a very confronting and not at all helpful thing to say.

‌



“My neurosurgeon thankfully was far more reassuring and turned over every stone to figure out what was causing it. It ended up being a multitude of factors but one of them was seizures, which can happen from the swelling.”

View 8 Images Paige Footner in her paramedic role

‌



Paige has lost her driving license as a result of the seizures and can’t work for a year, which has caused financial stress. She also can’t perform. S he said: “People talk a lot about the difficulties of immediate recovery post major surgeries, but the months after when you go home, and you’re starting to feel better but can’t go back to your normal life, are also incredibly hard to navigate.

“In hospital, your sole purpose is to rest, but at home you start to have energy. You feel as though you have no purpose. I had to learn to find joy in small things and create new purposes. As soon as I could get on a plane, I went overseas to see my friends.

“I’ve made a pact with myself to go on 50 dates in a quest to find love. My neurosurgeon also inspired me so much that I’ve also started studying for the exam to get into medical school. I want to do what she did for me – I want to help make difficult times a little less difficult, lonely and scary.

Article continues below

“My biggest advice would be to chase that dream, do the thing, start the hobby, tell the boy you like him. The pain of dying with regret is far, far, far worse than the pain of any rejection, failure or embarrassment.”

News.title: Tourists slam 'European Maldives' for beaches' 'faecal bacteria' and 'rubbish everywhere'
News.content:
Tourists slam 'European Maldives' for beaches' 'faecal bacteria' and 'rubbish everywhere'

The country has grown in popularity in recent years, as it has drawn comparisons to far-flung beaches such as the Maldives, but a recent study has shown its beaches may be hiding a dirty secret

View 2 Images The beaches failed to meet some holidaymaker's expectations (Image: Florian Gaertner/Photothek via Getty Images)

A major holiday hotspot often dubbed the ‘Maldives of Europe’ has been named the country with the dirtiest seas on the continent.

‌



A study by Which? looked at 22,289 European Environment Agency (EEA) reports on bathing water quality and the number of beaches in each country ranked as either ‘excellent’ or ‘poor’.

‌



While it was good news overall, with 96% of beaches across the European Union (EU) meeting minimum quality standards, one country saw only 16% of its bathing waters rated as ‘excellent’. Despite the country drawing comparisons with the Maldives, and its popularity soaring in recent years due to its enticing white sand beaches, it scored extremely poorly compared to other nations.

‌



View 2 Images Albania has the most beaches with 'poor' water quality in Europe (Image: Armando Babani/ZUMA Press Wire/Shutterstock)

Albania found itself at the bottom of the rankings, with 23% of its beaches showing water of poor quality, meaning “significant levels of faecal bacteria were found” according to Which?. By comparison, in the UK, only 7% were ranked as poor.

The sea can become polluted from sewage overflows or agricultural run-off, which can cause e. coli and intestinal enterococci to enter the water. These contaminants can cause illnesses from skin, ear, and eye infections to diarrhoea and vomiting, and vulnerable people such as children and the elderly can be more susceptible.

‌



Many visitors to Albania have taken to social media to share their experiences on the country’s beaches. TikTokker @paveltrips dubbed Durres the “worst beach in Europe” and showed images of rubbish on the sand, peeling paint on buildings, and houses falling apart.

A TripAdvisor review of the beach area said it had: “Rubbish strewn everywhere and no sign of any cleaning service attending to it. Pavements on the main Rruga Paravesia are broken and (there are) many potholes and open manholes. High-rise buildings are empty, with unpainted and cracked masonry. Beach had rubbish strewn about."

Content cannot be displayed without consent

‌



Another video showed one visitor’s “expectations vs reality” of Ksamil, famous for its photogenic beaches with overwater hammocks and swings, much loved by influencers. However, the video, taken in 2024 shows torn hammocks, broken furniture and overflowing bins.

Ksamil Beach has a dismal 2.7 stars on TripAdvisor, with a review from September 2025 saying: “The beach has been totally privatised and there is no space to go unless you go to a tacky beach bar and pay 10 euros to be on a crowded beach with sun loungers inches apart and covering the whole beach. A place that social media has bigged up but it’s to be avoided.”

A few reviews said it was overcrowded, with another saying: “Big disappointment. I have never seen a beach with so many sunbeds and umbrellas. You could hardly see any sand. Loud boom boom music dominates. It really should be avoided if you want tranquillity, charm and relaxation.”

‌



Content cannot be displayed without consent

Holidaymakers should check the EEA’s interactive map when swimming in Europe, as this shows whether a beach or lake meets EU standards for cleanliness. In the UK, the Safer Seas & Rivers Service app covers over 450 locations, so you can check whether any water quality alerts are in place.

Some areas that have been ranked as having excellent water quality in Albania include Dhërmi, a village with two beaches, as well as Vlorë, the country's third-largest city, which is a popular beach destination.

‌



At the other end of the rankings by Which?, Cyprus came out on top with 100% of its beaches offering waters ranked excellent, followed by Greece at 97.1%.

Albania’s National Tourism Agency (NTA) has been contacted for comment.

News.title: Man fined £1,000 for leaving cardboard box at recycling bin
News.content:
Man fined £1,000 for leaving cardboard box at recycling bin

He has vowed to fight 'all the way' after being fined for taking his rubbish to a bin

View 2 Images Lee Reynolds had left the box on the floor as all four bins were overflowing

A man who was fined £1,000 for fly-tipping after leaving cardboard next to a recycling bin has vowed to fight on after having the penalty reduced. Lee Reynolds had left the box on the floor as all four bins at Tesco, in New Milton, in Hampshire, were overflowing with rubbish

‌



On June 3 he received a penalty for “illegally depositing waste” from New Forest District Council (NDFC) which left him feeling “physically sick”. The authority claimed the facilities were emptied three times a week, but photographs taken at the time of the alleged offence showed that all the bins were full.

‌



Mr Reynolds appealed the notice, arguing the sign warning against leaving waste was obscured by the huge volume of rubbish. NDFC then downgraded his “offence’ from flytipping to a “failure to control household waste” offence, which carries a £300 fine – reduced to £150 if paid by July 3. Mr Reynolds paid up, but is still not happy.

‌



View 2 Images The councl said the bins were 'emptied three times a week'

He said: “I tried several routes of appeal, and basically NFDC did not accept my argument that the signs were obscured. I have tried to meet up with the councillors to discuss it but, again, this didn’t get me anywhere.

‌



“With the deadline looming I felt I had no choice but to pay the £150, so reluctantly that’s what I did. It was really weighing on my mind – as a law-abiding citizen the whole situation was causing me a lot of anguish. I was basically told that the matter was closed and there will be no more discussion. If I didn’t pay the fine, I was facing prosecution.”

Mr Reynolds said he is not backing down and has taken the matter to the district council’s complaints process. If this is unsuccessful, he will lodge a complaint with the the Local Government and Social Care Ombudsman. He said: “The level of waste piled up is a fire hazard. There is just rubbish everywhere and the whole area is a mess. It seems extremely unfair that the council fails to keep the area tidy and I’m the one that ends up with a fine.

Full to overflowing

“The bins were full to overflowing and there was no available capacity for additional cardboard. I did not see any instructions or signage warning against leaving recycling adjacent to full containers; if signage exists, it was not visible due to the volume of waste already present.”

Article continues below

A spokesperson for NFDC said the authority would not comment on individual cases, but added: “While we recognise that many residents are keen to recycle and dispose of their waste responsibly, placing waste next to full containers at the community recycling sites is flytipping.

“Flytipping and failure to control household waste is an offence, and not only unsightly but causes environmental hazards. It can also lead to additional costs for the council, for example, where waste becomes contaminated and cannot be recycled.

“We have seen an increase in fly tipping at this location and have been working to address this through education and awareness. The site was remodelled and additional signage was installed on May 20, prior to this incident.”

News.title: Chris Mason: Burnham is fifth PM in four years - now he'll try to buck the trend
News.content:
By lunchtime today, the UK will have its fifth prime minister in four years.

No other sentence can so pithily summarise the nature of British politics right now than that one.

In the summer of 2022 Boris Johnson was on his way out, but still in office. Since then there has been Liz Truss, Rishi Sunak and Sir Keir Starmer.

Little wonder Andy Burnham will say later, we are told, that he is "acutely conscious" of this churn at the top. His critics, within the Labour Party and beyond it, may allow themselves a wry smile at that, given they would argue he has been agitating for this moment for ages.

In the post-pandemic, post-Brexit 2020s, when for so long so many have felt like life is getting harder, the national mood is impatient and political support is fragmenting.

The consequence of that in recent years has meant those in government have been unpopular.

That is the backdrop to Burnham's arrival in Downing Street, just as it was for Sir Keir Starmer 746 days ago - on another sunny July day, just two years back.

That trend of unpopular governments is the thing Burnham is now trying to buck.

He is determined to hit the ground running and, where possible, to maintain the style of leadership he adopted as the mayor of Greater Manchester.

The rules of the House of Commons and meetings with the King, among others, will probably mean he wears a suit more often than he has in recent years.

But other conventions may be very intentionally ditched. I hear, for instance, that he may not bother with a lectern for his first speech as prime minister, outside 10 Downing Street, on Monday.

I also hear he is keen on question and answer sessions with voters around the country - "People's Question Time" as one ally put it.

Before Burnham's big moment will come Sir Keir's departure.

News.title: Victory for football? Spain beat Argentina to win World Cup
News.content:
Describing a result as a 'victory for football' might seem like a trite cliche - but you won't find many neutrals disagreeing with that description of Spain's win in the 2026 World Cup final.

When Ferran Torres slammed in the extra-time winner, and Rodri lifted the trophy high in New Jersey, it is hard to imagine many will have had sympathy for Argentina.

Spain triumphed in a battle of endurance, for players and spectators, to beat the Argentines and win their second men's World Cup.

On every football metric - and, some would say, morality too - this was the right result.

"There is no doubt that the right team won," former England captain Alan Shearer said on BBC One. "From start to finish, Spain controlled possession. They were the ones looking to play football, create chances and get in behind.

"This is a result for football because of the way that they have played. Spain deserve it."

Spain had 65% possession, an expected goals tally of 1.94 and 20 shots on goal - 11 on target.

At the other end, goalkeeper Unai Simon kept his seventh clean sheet in eight matches as he won the Golden Glove for the tournament's best goalkeeper.

Spain conceded just one goal at the 2026 World Cup - the fewest conceded by any winning team.

News.title: Broadcaster and journalist Edward Stourton dies aged 68
News.content:
Broadcaster and journalist Edward Stourton, whose career spanned more than 40 years including a decade on Radio 4's Today, has died aged 68.

Stourton, who had been diagnosed with prostate cancer in 2014, died on Saturday surrounded by his family, the BBC announced in a statement.

The presenter's friend and former Today co-host James Naughtie praised Stourton's "warm intelligence and wit", adding he was "one of the best colleagues".

Another former Today presenter, Evan Davis, said Stourton was "a very important figure for all of us on the daily news programmes on Radio 4".

"One of those people you're really glad to have around," Davis continued. "All substance, minimum ego, deeply knowledgeable, totally reliable.

"And he was one of the nicest of colleagues as well. He'll be missed."

Mishal Husain remembered Stourton as "a true gentleman and a broadcaster of immense capacity and intellect".

In his 2023 memoir Confessions, Stourton revealed he had been diagnosed with prostate cancer nearly a decade earlier.

He had treatment but was later told it had become incurable and spread. Stourton continued to work until very recently.

News.title: Fire crews battle blaze on Arthur’s Seat in Edinburgh
News.content:
Jon Henderson, SFRS assistant chief officer, said the service had dealt with a number of incidents over the course of the weekend.

"We've had crews at Arthur's Seat since about 15:00 on Sunday afternoon and then overnight," he told BBC Radio Scotland Breakfast.

"At first light we stepped up that response again when the conditions were favourable for that.

"The feeling from the ground there is that we will probably be there for a couple of days continuing to tackle it and dampen out hotspots."

Henderson said it was too early to speculate on the cause of the fire.

"Our focus at the moment is dealing with the fire and the response but there will be a full fire investigation," he said.

"The difficulty we have with open fires is that they can be difficult to assess where they started because of the scale and sometimes these do happen naturally."

News.title: My fitness tracker knew I was pregnant before I did
News.content:
Dr Stuart Lavery, consultant of reproductive medicine at University College Hospital in London, said: "People are understandably using this technology to try to get a greater understanding, and to try and pick up things as early as possible because it has such a profound impact on your life if you're planning a pregnancy."

However, "we might be running before we can walk," he cautioned.

"We probably need a lot more data on the reliability, we need a lot more researchâ¦ otherwise what happens is your levels of anxiety will just skyrocket," he said.

"I have no doubt that more people will be using technology, an app-based approach or a wearable-based approach, to try and pick up these things. But I think it should come with quite a big health warning about how much we can rely on them for accuracy."

When asked about the anxiety women reported feeling early in their pregnancy as a result of checking their ring data, Dr Chris Curry, Oura's clinical director of women's health, told BBC News: "With or without biometric tracking, pregnancy can be an uncertain time where many women, particularly those pregnant for the first time, are in the dark about the range of what's normal."

She added that if women feel overwhelmed, the company "encourages members to take a break from the app experience, whilst Oura Ring continues to collect data and gather insights", adding: "The ring is a support tool, not a replacement for your care team."

Ravika sadly did miscarry. She's hoping to start trying to conceive again soon - and when she does, her experience has made her rethink wearing her tracker again.

"I didn't really see myself as being an anxious person, butâ¦ I think going forward if it came to a point where I had an inkling that I was pregnant and my stats were low, as soon as that positive pregnancy test was there, I do think it would be the best thing for me to take the ring off."

News.title: Trump says US strikes hit Iran in 'honour' of American soldiers killed
News.content:
President Donald Trump says the latest strikes by the US hit Iran "very hard", adding that the attacks were "in honour" of three US soldiers killed in recent days - two in Jordan, one in Iraq.

In the early hours of Monday local time, US Central Command (Centcom) said it had launched a "new wave" of strikes for the ninth consecutive night as explosions were heard across Iran.

The US said it had targeted military sites and communications networks to "further diminish" Tehran's attacks on vessels in the Strait of Hormuz.

Iran said it had responded with a "surprise attack" in Syria and targeted US aircraft at Jordan's Aqaba airport.

Elsewhere in the region, Kuwait's armed forces said they had intercepted Iranian drones.

On the US strikes, Iran's semi-official Tasnim news agency reported that several cities had been hit including Tabriz, Chabahar, Konarak, Bandar Mahshahr and Bandar Imam Khomeini.

There were also Iranian state media reports that two oil tankers had exploded as the vessels tried to cross the strait.

The Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps (IRGC) said the tankers were going through what it called an "unsafe and hazardous southern route" of the strait and "exploded and were brought to a halt". Centcom disputed the claims.

The IRGC added that the strait "will not be safe for the transit of petrochemical products, nor even a single drop of oil and gas" as long as the US strikes continue and that it will respond with a "punitive operation".

Over the weekend, the US confirmed that a service member had been killed after an Iranian attack in northern Iraq on Saturday.

The death came a day after an attack on a base in Jordan where two US soldiers were killed and another was reported missing. The US said "unidentified remains" had been found, with verification of the remains ongoing.

As the strikes continued over the weekend between the US and Iran, US Secretary of State Marco Rubio said that the US "always remains open to a diplomatic solution".

He also said "the world has to decide whether or not it's going to allow an international waterway to be under the control" of Iran, saying Tehran was using the crucial shipping route as leverage.

His comments come as a preliminary deal made in mid-June to stop fighting has unravelled, with negotiations for a permanent peace making little progress after Trump declared the agreement was "over" on 8 July.

News.title: ‘Everyone's afraid to die’: Struggle to recruit soldiers in Ukraine turns violent
News.content:
Vasyl Krupych knows what it is to fight for Ukraine.

He describes terrifying scenes from battles in the eastern Donbas region where, sometimes praying, sometimes crying, the machine gunner somehow survived the onslaught by Russian troops.

But last December, by then serving in the rear, Krupych was attacked by his own countrymen whilst out searching for draft dodgers.

He says two men ignored demands to show their documents and fled. When his patrol gave chase, Krupych was badly beaten with a crowbar. He spent six weeks in hospital.

"He broke my rib, I was lying there and couldn't breathe," the veteran recalled in a recent interview.

"What did we fight for, if soldiers can now get beaten?"

News.title: Thames Water lenders preparing legal challenge in event of Burnham nationalisation
News.content:
The lenders to Thames Water are preparing a legal challenge in case a Burnham-led government attempts to nationalise the UK's biggest water company.

Burnham - who takes over as PM on Monday - has previously said he wants to see "greater public control" of the water and energy sectors and has called for Thames Water to be nationalised.

Thames Water is about Â£20bn in debt.

Its lenders had proposed a deal to write off nearly half of that and inject new cash in return for some leniency from future pollution fines, but this deal has previously been rejected by the government as being "weak" and bad for consumers and the environment.

Sources close to the creditors have told the BBC that in the event of full nationalisation, they would pursue payment in full of the outstanding debts as has happened in previous cases, which could leave the government with a multi-billion-pound bill.

Fears first emerged three years ago that Thames Water could collapse and on Thursday, the firm warned it has enough cash to last until the end of this year.

Creditors insisted on Sunday that they were still working with officials and regulators to reach an agreement to rescue the company.

A spokesperson for the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs said the government was "prepared for any eventuality".

"Thames Water customers have been let down for far too long, with 15 years of under-performance, increasing serious pollution, and customers left to pick up the bill," the spokesperson said.

"The secretary of state has written to Ofwat to outline her early views that she is not convinced Londonâ¯andâ¯Valleyâ¯Water's proposal is good enough for consumers or the environment."

The lenders have offered to write off Â£9.4bn of Thames Water's near Â£20bn debt pile and put Â£3.35bn of cash into the company, but in return they want leniency from future pollution fines in order to turn the firm's fortunes around.

Objecting to the proposal, Emma Reynolds said in June that she did not want a scenario where Thames Water customers had to "pick up the bill for the company's failures".

At the time, she told reporters that the government "stands ready for all eventualities", including temporary nationalisation.

When asked in a Sky News interview on Sunday whether a Burnham government would nationalise Thames Water, Labour's deputy leader Lucy Powell said: "Let's see".

"This has been an ongoing issue and concern in government," she said.

"The government has powers to to bring a distressed water company under special measures, and let's see if the government needs to, wants to use those powers."

Powell added that "the privatisation of water hasn't worked".

"It's not created competition. What you've seen is bills going up and up and up over years and years and years. Investment not being made... and then now these companies are in are in real distress," she said.

There is a halfway house, in which Thames would be placed into a so called "special administration regime", or SAR, which is usually a temporary situation until another private sector buyer can be found.

The existing lenders have made it clear that they would be prepared to join the bidders for Thames in that scenario.

However, comments from the incoming prime minister Andy Burnham that key utilities should be under increased "public control" make it hard to imagine that the government will have much political appetite to find a new set of private sector owners for a company that serves 16 million people which means that a temporary nationalisation might become permanent.

But under either a SAR or full nationalisation, Thames ongoing problems could then leave taxpayers footing the bill for Thames cash shortfalls - a figure that Thames Water management puts at Â£2bn by the end of next year.

Whatever happens, its customers' taps and loos will still function, but the future of Thames Water is a key policy test for the new administration.

News.title: New EU border system tripling time at passport control, airport boss says
News.content:
The EU's new border system has nearly tripled the time it's taking for Brits to get through passport control even after improvements have been made, a boss at Rome's main airport has said.

It comes as Ryanair has warned passengers travelling to Europe this summer to prepare for extended waits.

Border police at Portugal's Faro airport also told the BBC the Entry Exit System technology suffered from bugs, but insisted any queues there would go down quickly.

The European Commission (EC) has said in most EU airports disruption is limited, and added that it will continue to support member states in the system's implementation.

It added: "This support will continue to the fullest extent possible."

The digital Entry Exit System (EES) requires non-EU citizens entering the Schengen area - made up of 29 European countries - to register fingerprints and a photo when they arrive. The information is checked as they leave.

It's often done using standalone, automated machines known as "kiosks" and sometimes with border officers - for example, for children under 12. The new process and machines have been phased in since October.

Some European airports have seen hours-long queues at passport control. Passengers have even reported missing flights home.

This week, Ryanair said "the failed EES rollout" was causing unnecessary delays and long queues.

The airline said UK passengers should "allow extra time for their journey and be prepared for extended waits at passport control."

In Rome, a perennially popular destination for tourists from the UK and around the globe, everyone we spoke to in the Piazza di Spagna had an EES story.

News.title: Residents told to pay £7,000 each to fix water pipe outside their homes
News.content:
Residents say they could face prosecution if they do not pay thousands of pounds to repair a water pipe outside their homes.

The residents of five houses in Pontycymer, Bridgend county, said they were told by Welsh Water that a leak from the shared pipe supplying their homes needs to be repaired at their own cost, which they estimate could cost more than Â£7,000 each.

The Garw Valley locals claim they have been given no evidence of where the leak is which their insurance companies need to cover the cost, causing sleepless nights.

A Welsh Water spokesperson said it does not own or manage the pipe so it's the responsibility of property owners, and residents have 11 days to fix it.

The estimated cost of more than Â£7,000 would go towards replacing the rear water pipe in their back gardens with a new pipe at the front of the terraced row, they said, along with connecting it to each house individually.

Resident Nerys Walters said the dispute had brought her massive amounts of stress over the last two years.

She said they initially thought the cost of repairs could be covered through insurance, but with no evidence of the leak being provided, insurers have said they would not pay out.

Walters said: "It's been a nightmare situation for us that has really caused us all a lot of stress.

"Welsh Water have said they would pay for a new line that runs parallel to the front of the property, but we would then have to fund the cost of it coming in from the gate, and through the house to our rear stopcock.

Walters said she had spoken to "numerous contractors" who quoted the residents more than Â£1,000 a metre for the work.

"This has been going on for about a year and a half now and we've been asking for that evidence ever since but have been given nothing", she said.

"No evidence of the leak, and no reason as to why they adopted other pipes in the street but not ours. All the while the deadline they have given runs down. It's been very difficult and we just want to get it sorted."

News.title: Going with the flow: Renewable energy battery breakthrough
News.content:
A 3D-printed battery developed at Queen's University Belfast could "make a genuine impact" on the road to net zero, say the researchers behind it.

Flow batteries are seen as key to scaling up renewable energy, allowing it to be stored for when the wind is not blowing and the sun is not shining.

But they are expensive and typically use a metallic element - vanadium - that is only produced in a few places round the world.

Now, scientists at QUB have developed one based on iron, which is much easier to source, and have sent it around the world to help standardise research.

It is hoped it will accelerate the renewable energy revolution, making research more reliable and its findings more scalable.

News.title: 'I'm petrified my rapist could be released early'
News.content:
When Jade Belgrove finally saw the jailing of the man who raped her as a child, she thought her fight was over.

After waiting a decade to report the abuse she suffered as a 14-year-old, she believed justice had finally been served when Simon Tyler was jailed for nine years in 2024.

Now, after being told her attacker could be released years early under government plans to ease prison overcrowding, the 30-year-old from Coventry - who spoke to the BBC having waived her right to anonymity - said victims were being "let down all over again".

The Ministry of Justice (MoJ) said it understood "the distress victims will feel" but added prisons could run out of spaces in November "without this action".

That, the MoJ continued, could leave the "justice system unable to jail serious offenders at all".

Belgrove has launched a petition - signed by more than 85,000 people - that calls on ministers to exclude violent sexual offenders from the early release scheme.

News.title: 'No more families should endure this' - parents of student who died from MenB back new vaccine advice
News.content:
The parents of a university student who died from meningitis B (MenB) say new vaccine advice represents a "poignant moment" and will save countless lives.

Helen and Lee Draper from Pontypool, Torfaen, lost their 18-year-old daughter Meg to the disease in October 2025, just weeks after she started at the University of Bournemouth.

Last week, official advice changed, telling governments they should offer a free jab from age 15 - despite previously saying this was not cost effective.

The Welsh government said implementation took time and it must consider affordability, feasibility and the effect on the wider NHS.

News.title: Chinese firm seeks compensation over British Steel nationalisation
News.content:
The former owner of British Steel has said it will pursue the British government for compensation after the loss-making firm was nationalised.

The UK took control of the Scunthorpe steelworks a year ago after China's Jingye Group said it planned to close the site because it was not financially viable, and fully nationalised the plant on Thursday.

In a statement on Sunday, Jingye said it will seek "full compensation through legal means to the very end" over the UK's move.

A government spokesperson said draft compensation regulations due to be released in the autumn will set out a compensation process through which an independent assessor "would determine what, if any, is payable".

Jingye bought the Lincolnshire steel plant in 2020, but in March last year the firm launched a consultation on its closure saying the plant was losing Â£700,000 a day.

The government took control of British Steel operations in April 2025, but until this week it remained under Jingye's ownership which limited the government's ability to shape the firm's future.

On Thursday the UK government said it was taking the firm into public hands in order to safeguard a "vital national capability", giving the government the power to decide the plant's future.

The decision to nationalise British Steel has threatened to strain the relationship between London and Beijing just as Andy Burnham prepares to enter Downing Street as prime minister on Monday.

News.title: Bruno Mars has an unexpected opening before Wembley party starts
News.content:
Bruno Mars appeared determined to lift the nation's mood during the first of his six nights at Wembley Stadium.

His last UK performance came in July 2018, shortly after England had been knocked out of the men's World Cup semi-finals. Eight years later, history had repeated itself.

But wearing an England football scarf, Union Jack bucket hat and clutching a Paddington Bear, the showman energised a 75,000-strong, multi-generational crowd.

After nearly a decade away from UK audiences, Mars proved why fans had snapped up tickets in record numbers, external.
