Sports.title: Argentina players show true colours with response to Spain lifting the World Cup
Sports.content:
Argentina players show true colours with response to Spain lifting the World Cup

Argentina were beaten in the World Cup final and provoked the unsavoury scenes after the full-time whistle with their players refusing to acknowledge Spain's victory

View 2 Images Argentina stood with their back to the World Cup presentation (Image: @Mark_Ogden)

The Argentinean players refused to even watch Spain lift the World Cup as they stood with their backs to the trophy presentation after defeat.

‌



Ferran Torres' goal in extra-time decided the final in New York and saw Spain win their second World Cup and underline their status as the best on the planet following their Euros success two years ago.

‌



Argentina failed to defend the crown they won in 2022 as Lionel Messi missed out on adding another World Cup to his CV. It was an ill-tempered affair that saw Enzo Fernandez sent-off and emotions boil over at the final whistle.

‌



The South Americans have long been known for having an edge about them and didn't take defeat well. They were pictured standing together by the 18-yard box with their back to the Spanish players as they were presented with the World Cup.

Argentina's president Javier Milei declares bank holiday after World Cup loss to Spain READ MORE :

Tottenham star Cristian Romero 'snubs' Trump handshake after World Cup final READ MORE :

Even after losing out, it is normal for the runners-up to at least acknowledge or applaud those who have emerged victorious, but the Argentineans were clearly in no mood for that.

Leandro Paredes, who were perhaps lucky to stay on the pitch until the end, was shown a red card for throwing punches at Spanish stars Eric Garcia and Gavi after the full-time whistle. Spanish players raced onto the pitch to celebrate when Argentinian defender Nahuel Molina appeared to punch Rodri in the stomach.

‌



Messi was left in tears after playing, what could prove to be, his final match for Argentina. He had been crucial in their run to the final but his future is now in doubt at 39, as is that of head coach Lionel Scaloni.

View 2 Images Argentina failed to defend their crown as they were outclassed in the final

He cut an emotional figure and said on his next move: "I will talk to the president. I have an idea of what I would like to do. I will see out my contract and I feel the need, I don't know if something as big can be done. We need to speak this through.

Article continues below

"I am thankful to the president for bringing me this chance of being in this place where I am at the moment. It was a dream place for everyone. We have tried up until the very last minute to give our utmost, the staff and players. I believe it's only fair that I can take this time for myself to think this through."

Sports.title: England's World Cup assessed - by Sky Sports readers
Sports.content:
It's all over - and, once again, it's not coming home.

Thomas Tuchel, who faced heavy criticism after England's late semi-final collapse against Argentina, says the "scars" of 2026 will remain, but his side signed off by beating France 6-4 in a remarkable bronze medal match to secure their best finish for 60 years.

What conclusions can really be drawn from that game? How should England's tournament be viewed overall? Who impressed you and who didn't? And is Tuchel still the right man for Euro 2028?

We asked you for your comments and reflections and you delivered. Here's the verdict on England's World Cup in the words of Sky Sports readers...

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Sky Sports football correspondent Rob Dorsett has been with England every step of the way at the World Cup - he reflects on England's performance at the tournament and what could have been...

Was the France win cause for optimism or frustration?

Brid Deano: "After the showing vs France, you can just imagine the threat we would have posed in the last 30 mins vs Argentina, with either Bukayo Saka or Marcus Rashford on the pitch. Mind-blowing not throwing just even one of them on, rather than four defenders."

Ryan: "Don't read too much into to the first half, it was second XI vs second XI. As soon as France brought on the superstars their quality shone through. Rashford and Saka showed why Tuchel was wrong to drop them, and our defence was more than questionable."

'Frustration inevitable - England left it too late to show it' Sky Sports' Patrick Rowe:



"It is hard not to feel frustration following the dramatic 6-4 win against France. The handbrake was let off and England showed what they are capable of going forward.



"Thomas Tuchel's side carved through world-class opposition with ease. It was thrilling from start to finish and in the final third, they were everything that the nation had been desperate to see throughout.



"Yes, the defensive performance left a lot to be desired. But that could have been fine-tuned, tweaked and addressed.



"Everyone knew this was how England could, and should, stamp their authority on games. They just left it too late to show it."

How should England's campaign be viewed overall?

Gunnerlukey: "I think the one thing we should be worried about is lack of a striker for the next tournament. Kane, although a great goalscorer, is too far back and the other options are lacking. There's a big hole up top for England in years to come."

Sports.title: Bay Bridge's full brother set for first start at Windsor
Sports.content:
All eyes will be on Windsor at 6.50pm when Bay Bridge's brother Castlemont makes his first start in the Godolphin blue for Charlie Appleby.

6.50 Windsor - Bay Bridge's full-brother Castlemont debuts

Charlie Appleby unveils Bay Bridge's full brother Castlemont this evening at Windsor in the Join Fitzdares For A Personal Service Maiden Stakes.

The already-gelded son of New Bay was purchased for 375,000 guineas as a yearling - which is no surprise given the pedigree on show. His brother Bay Bridge was rated 122 at his peak winning and even downed the great Baaeed in his 2022 Champion Stakes swansong. If he is anything like his sibling, we could have another top-class animal on our hands.

Lava Stream's half brother Treble Bass also debuts for Charlie Appleby and could be anything in the second-string Godolphin colours. Ray Dawson takes the ride on this son of Sea The Stars, who - like his stablemate - has been gelded.

Of those with experience, Lord d'Or sets the standard on form, having finished second behind Wood Ditton winner Portcullis at York in May. One that should be monitored in the betting is the Amo Racing-owned Cool Girl. This Pinatubo filly - who cost €100,000, is partnered with the in-form David Egan for Charlie Johnston.

2.28 Vichy - Saint Martin and Lady Mara clash in French feature

Saint Martin and Lady Mara clash in the Listed Prix Frédéric de Lagrange this afternoon at Vichy.

Saint Martin comes here with three wins from seven starts to his name, which have all been notched this year. After two wins at Cagnes-Sur-Mer, Christophe Escuder's colt claimed Listed honours in the Prix Francois, beating Mirik from the Graffard stable.

Graffard's representative here is Lady Mara, who will be ridden by Mickael Barzalona. She comes here off the back of finishing fourth in the Group 2 Premio Oaks d'Italia Tattersalls at San Siro. She finished one place in front of Andrew Balding's Prizeland (rated 94) - which gives the form some familiarity.

Yann Barberot saddles the unbeaten gelding Mazzala, who won at Saint-Cloud on debut before following that up with a second success at Lyon next time out. This son of Frankel must warrant respect under the mercurial Maxime Guyon.

7.50 Windsor - Exciting Sunshine Star returns for the Gosdens

Sunshine Star - an exciting looking filly for the Gosdens and Lady Bamford - returns to the track tonight for the British Stallion Studs EBF Support The Big Bear Voyage Fillies' Handicap.

A half-sister to Oaks winner Soul Sister, she was entered in the Ribblesdale but was withdrawn - which could be an indicator of just how highly she is thought of at Clarehaven. This three-year-old was sent off an 8/11 favourite in a nice novice at Sandown in April, but was beaten by the talented Felicitas. Ed Walker's filly then franked the form, finishing a close second in the Musidora. Subsequently, Sunshine Star took a drop in grade and bolted up at Lingfield at the beginning of June. With another month run on her back, she should take all the beating here.

Capichera is the nearest threat, having bought up her first win at Pontefract last month. This horse showed a good level of form in behind So Regal at Newmarket on her first start of the year and could well progress further today.

Best of the rest

In Windsor's opening A1R Services Ltd Nursery Handicap (5.50pm), previous winners Arabica Queen and Theheatison look the key players having tasted success when last seen. El Lambo was not suited by an ease in the ground on Oaks day at Epsom but should fare better back on a sounder surface.

Later on the card, the Fitzdares Sprint Series Handicap (7.20pm) sees eight-time course scorer Lequinto look to contend with a 5lb rise in the weights following his upturn in form. Amazonian Dream has been knocking on the door of late and could finally hit the target having not been penalised by the handicapper for back-to-back runner-up efforts.

Sports.title: 'We were the better team' - Spain beat Argentina to win World Cup
Sports.content:
Spain won their second World Cup title after Ferran Torres' 106th-minute smashed finish earned a 1-0 win against defending champions Argentina in the 2026 final.

Spain were deserved winners. Torres scored with Spain's 20th shot while the game ended without Argentina registering a single shot on target.

Lionel Messi touched the ball just 54 times in a match that took three hours to complete and featured a 27-minute half-time break.

Spain's win had shades of their maiden victory in 2010 too, scoring in the second period of extra-time after a goalless 90 minutes. Then, it was Andres Iniesta against Netherlands - now another Barcelona player, Torres, adds his name to the history books.

Image: Spain's Rodri lifts the World Cup

A nod back from fellow substitute Nico Williams saw the former Manchester City forward storm on to the ball and fire past Aston Villa goalkeeper Emi Martinez. It came minutes after Williams had an initial strike ruled out for an alleged Mikel Merino foul on Nicolas Otamendi.

Argentina did keep their shape well as Spain applied consistent pressure - especially after Chelsea's Enzo Fernandez was sent off for a reckless second yellow at the end of normal time - and relied on Martinez to make a string of saves.

Image: Enzo Fernandez fouls Pau Cubarsi resulting in a red card for the Argentina midfielder

Image: Enzo Fernandez was sent off late in the second half as Argentina finished the game with 10 players

Their only threat emerged in added-on time at the end of extra-time, with Giuliano Simeone blazing over a shot that could have sent the game to penalties.

But there was no fairytale end to Messi's expected final World Cup appearance, with the Argentina skipper anonymous for much of the game. He was also beaten to his first World Cup Golden Boot by France's Kylian Mbappe, who won it by two goals.

Image: A tearful Lionel Messi reacts to Argentina's defeat in the World Cup final (AP Photo/Pamela Smith)

Spain remain undefeated under manager Luis de la Fuente in tournament matches and add a World Cup win to their Euros title from 2024. It has been quite the tournament from an opening draw to Cape Verde to making France and Argentina look like average teams and lifting the World Cup.

Image: Shot map comparison

Paredes and Molina involved in angry scenes after full-time

Image: Leandro Parades was sent off after the game after starting a brawl with some of Spain's players

There were unsavoury scenes at full-time in the World Cup final, with Argentina duo Leandro Paredes and Nahuel Molina striking out at the celebrating Spain players.

Molina threw out an elbow and caught Rodri as the Spain captain ran past him, while Paredes kicked Eric Garcia to the floor and pushed him back with a strong hand around his neck when the Spaniard got back to his feet to confront him.

Spain sub Gavi was then held back by another Argentina player before Paredes came in, ripped his bib and swung for him twice, catching him in the face.

Paredes, who came on at half-time, had been booked within minutes of entering the field and escaped picking up a second yellow for a string of subsequent fouls.

However, he was eventually sent off for his actions in the post-match hostilities.

Image: Spain's Ferran Torres celebrates scoring their winner (AP Photo/Julio Cortez)

5: SHOT! Lamine Yamal has the first shot on target.

39: SHOT! Oyarzabal strikes - but it goes straight at Emi Martinez.

77: CHANCE! Pedro and Pau Cubarsi draw saves from the Argentina goalkeeper as Spain keep pushing for a goal.

90+3: RED CARD! Fernandez sent off for second yellow card after reckless challenge on Cubarsi.

90+9: SAVE! Lamine Yamal forces a great save from Emi Martinez after a whipped effort.

96: NO GOAL! Williams has the ball in the net, but it is ruled out as Merino inadvertently catches Otamendi on the foot in the build-up.

106: GOAL! Torres fires home from Williams' cushioned effort.

114: OFFSIDE! Torres has the ball in the net again, but he is flagged offside.

120+2: OVER! Simeone has the chance to equalise, but sends an effort over the face of goal as Spain win the World Cup.

Image: Spain's Nico Williams reacts after seeing his strike on goal ruled out by VAR

Image: Momentum graphic

Analysis: Spain worthy World Cup winners

Sky Sports' Adam Bate: "Spain began this World Cup with a goalless draw against Cape Verde but they end it as worthy winners. They beat the favourites in the semi-final and the reigning champions tonight.

"One goal conceded in eight games, never behind in the tournament, they played all the football here. Passed Argentina off the park. The European champions are World Cup winners too. Thoroughly deserved."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Ferran Torres scores a crucial goal in added time for Spain to make it 1-0 in the World Cup final game against Argentina

Sky Sports' Gary Neville speaking on ITV: "Spain are not the best individual players, what they are is the best team, the best collective. And also the best system of play.

"I spent a very short time in Spain and what I found was that they were a different technical and tactical level to Premier League teams, their understanding of the game.

"That comes out most in international football when you are playing every four days in 35-degree heat. Technically and tactically, they are outstanding."

Three Spain players win World Cup awards Player of the tournament: Rodri

Golden Glove: Unai Simon

Young player: Pau Cubarsi

Image: Spain's Rodri poses with the award for the tournament's best player (AP Photo/Ashley Landis)

Image: Spain goalkeeper Unai Simon poses with the Golden Glove award (AP Photo/Ashley Landis)

Torres: Destiny was written for us to win

Spain forward Ferran Torres to FIFA: "I think in the end the goal came from 47 million people (approximately the population of Spain), not just those of us that are here.

"Today destiny was written, it was made for us to win. We're far from our people today, but we tried to be as close as possible to them.

Image: Ferran Torres celebrates his goal in extra-time to win the World Cup for Spain

"Finals are hard. When you have [Lionel] Messi on the opposing team, you do get worried, but we always backed ourselves and tried to show our football and I think we managed to do it once again.

"[It was] a huge relief [to score]. I've been criticised throughout the whole tournament but, as I said before, destiny was written.

"Thanks to God, he always gives me the strength to continue and in the end he grants things to those that most deserve them."

Merino: We knew we were a better footballing side than Argentina

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Spanish fans go wild as they claim their second World Cup trophy over Argentina

Spain's Mikel Merino speaking to ITV: "Unbelievable. It's the perfect moment for us.

"We are such a golden generation with these young players that give everything they have for this country, for these fans. Luckily, we got the trophy today.

"It was a game about concentration. We knew we were a better team in terms of football.

"The pitch was dry, it was a difficult game because they are a very, very competitive side and they know how to make the game difficult for you. I think the team was outstanding today and we deserve it.

"When you are facing a low block and you have a team that is defending in your own box, you have to attack the box with bodies on the line and then control the transitions.

"We have very good players that can cross the ball, big threats in the box and the old-school way of scoring goals and we did it."

Analysis: Messi conspicuous by his absence

Image: Argentina's Lionel Messi missed out on winning his first World Cup Golden Boot

Sky Sports' Charlotte Marsh: "The World Cup game perhaps epitomises the importance of Messi to Argentina in his anonymity.

"They have relied on the 39-year-old time and again in this tournament, and much like a few of his contemporaries, he did go missing in one of the biggest moments.

"However, that wasn't entirely his fault. Argentina had 34.9 per cent possession and were not able to work anything for their star man to use.

"In the final five minutes, Messi had a few glimpses but this time, he and Argentina ran out of time, with no shots registered on target.

"But by his absence and his team unable to provide for him, it shows even more just how much they rely on him for their goals."

Sports.title: Bellingham, kits and team names: What’s changed in The Hundred for 2026?
Sports.content:
As The Hundred returns for 2026 - live on Sky Sports from Tuesday July 21 to Sunday August 16 - we look at what has changed for the ECB's 100-ball competition…

New team trophy

An innovation this year is for a combined men's and women's trophy to be awarded to the Hundred team performing best across both competitions, in addition to the individual men's and women's titles that will be presented to the tournament winners.

Every match win - whether in the group stage, eliminator or final - is worth four points with a franchise's men's and women's totals added up for a combined score.

Image: Individual men's and women's titles will still be awarded around the combined silverware

Four bonus points each are up for grabs for the men's and women's sides that top the league table, avoid the eliminator and head straight to the competition final.

If two franchises finish level on points come the end of the tournament, the team with a squad that won a final will triumph. If both franchises won a final - or neither did - then most finalists and, if needed, combined net run-rate will determine a winner.

New owners and team names

All eight sides now have overseas investors, with deals for the Ambani family's Reliance Industries Limited to secure a 49 per cent stake in MI London - formerly Oval Invincibles - and Chelsea co-owner Todd Boehly's Cain International to acquire the same stake in Trent Rockets completed in late 2025.

Deals for the other six teams had previously been sealed but this is the first season where the new investors can really stamp their authority.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Real Madrid and England midfielder Jude Bellingham has announced his investment in Birmingham Phoenix earlier this year

England footballer Jude Bellingham now holds a 1.2 per cent stake in Birmingham Phoenix and will be involved in increasing participation in cricket in the community.

Knighthead Capital Management - who own Bellingham's former club Birmingham City and have NFL legend Tom Brady as a minority shareholder - own 48.4 per cent.

MI London are one of four teams to have Indian Premier League-affiliated investment, with the Ambani family also owning five-time IPL champions Mumbai Indians.

SunRisers Leeds - formerly Northern Superchargers - are entirely owned by the Sun Group that owns SunRisers Hyderabad, while RPSG Group - in charge of Lucknow Super Giants - hold a 70 per cent stake in Manchester Super Giants, previously Originals.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Jos Buttler will play for a Manchester Super Giants side that now features an elephant in their logo

Plus, GMR Group possesses a 49 per cent stake in Southern Brave, adding to a portfolio that includes IPL's Delhi Capitals and Hampshire.

Elsewhere, the American-based Tech Titans hold a 49 per cent share of the Lord's-based London Spirit, while Indian-American businessman Sanjay Goval, who owns Major League Cricket outfit Washington Freedom, has a 50 per cent stake in Welsh Fire.

New kits

This heavy overseas investment had also led to kits being tweaked, with the IPL-backed clubs now playing in the same colours as their Indian counterparts.

MI London performed in green under their Oval Invincibles moniker but will now wear blue with gold trim like Mumbai Indians, while SunRisers Leeds switch from purple to orange to match SunRisers Hyderabad.

Image: Here are the fresh threads the players will be sporting in 2026

Southern Brave's green get-up has been ditched as they alter to blue and red, the same as Delhi Capitals, and Manchester Super Giants swap from black and grey to the red and blue stripes of Lucknow Super Giants.

Birmingham Phoenix will don a black strip this term - they previously turned out in orange and yellow - with London Spirit remaining in blue but now also having an MCC 'egg and bacon' yellow and red stripe down their jersey.

Welsh Fire stay in red and Trent Rockets are still yellow and orange.

New money

New owners pumped over £500m into The Hundred when they purchased all or part of their clubs but the money continued to be splashed in the tournament's first auction earlier this year.

Sussex all-rounder James Coles - recently part of England's white-ball squads against India - was bought for £390k by London Spirit in the men's competition, with Welsh Fire forking out £200k on Jordan Cox after his player-of-the-tournament performances for Oval Invincibles, as they were then, in 2025.

Image: England all-rounder Dani Gibson was signed for £190k by SunRisers Leeds in the first Hundred auction

The women's auction was notable for England all-rounder Dani Gibson earning £190k as SunRisers Leeds came calling and legends of the game Beth Mooney (Australia) and Sophie Devine (New Zealand) securing £210k paydays from Trent Rockets and Welsh Fire respectively.

Plus, to further emphasise how The Hundred can now change a player's life, 18-year-old England spinner Tilly Corteen-Coleman went to Southern Brave for £105k. Being part of this competition is highly profitable gig for some.

Watch every match from The Hundred live on Sky Sports between Tuesday July 21 and Sunday August 16, with every day seeing a double-header of a women's fixture followed by a men's match at the same venue.

Reigning women's champions SunRisers Leeds kick of their defence against MI London at The Oval on opening day (2.45pm first ball), before MI London start their pursuit of a fourth consecutive men's title versus SunRisers Leeds from 6.30pm.

Sports.title: 'My hands were all over the place!' - Fox savours dramatic Open win
Sports.content:
Ryan Fox admitted it was a "dream come true" as he defied the nerves to clinch a dramatic victory in The Open at Royal Birkdale.

The 39-year-old New Zealander produced a superb finish to the final round to overtake clubhouse leader Cameron Young and snatch a one-shot win.

Fox, who had carded a 62 on Saturday to put himself in contention to claim a maiden major success, looked to be slipping out of it after making his second bogey of the day at the 11th.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Highlights of the final round of the 154th Open as Fox claimed the victory

Back-to-back birdies at the 13th and 14th put him back in the hunt and he then did well to escape with only a bogey at the 15th after a nightmare lie in a greenside bunker.

He hit back by birdieing the 16th following a brilliant approach and then, after missing a chance at the 17th, nailed two superb shots down the 18th before boldly draining a 12-foot putt to claim the Claret Jug.

"To play that last hole how I did, I stood on the tee and said to my caddie Dean (Smith), we're going to try to win this," said Fox.

"I hit two perfect shots. I'm not sure how I hit the putt. My hands were all over the place. I was just trying to get it towards the hole somewhere. It's surreal that it went in.

"My focus with the putter all day was just take a really deep breath before I hit it and just try to hit a line, and I did that.

Image: Fox celebrates after holing the winning putt

"I don't know how I managed to keep the putter face square enough for that to go on line, but I'll take it.

"Champion Golfer of the Year has got a pretty good ring to it. It is a dream come true.

"You do dream of this moment. I don't know whether I ever thought it was going to become a reality. Now it is, and to have my name etched in the history of the game is pretty awesome. I think it's pretty awesome for New Zealand as well. It's going to be big down there."

Fox, the first New Zealander to win The Open since Bob Charles in 1963, is the son of former All Blacks fly-half Grant Fox and the grandson of former New Zealand Test captain Merv Wallace.

"We've got a great history in our family," he said. "I was lucky enough to carve my own path there. I don't know if this tops their achievements, but it's certainly right up there.

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player Fox equalled the lowest round in Open history with a third-round 62 at Royal Birkdale

"I spoke to my kids last night, and they said bring back a trophy. I think this is a pretty cool one to bring back for them.

"I don't know if my dad would be able to contain himself when I was coming down the stretch. He's never been one who has been very good if he doesn't have control over things.

"I think when he was playing and in control of the output, under pressure he was fine. But when he doesn't have control, I think he's a nervous wreck. I'm sure he was."

Please use Chrome browser for a more accessible video player How Fox clinched victory in The Open at Royal Birkdale

'He stayed aggressive'

Sky Sports Golf duo Dame Laura Davies and Andrew Coltart were both full of praise for Fox and the aggressive approach he adopted on the back nine.

Davies said: "He was the most impressive player all day. He stayed aggressive; I don't think he was scared of losing it. If he lost it because he hit a shot that just didn't work out he was prepared to stay aggressive and I firmly believe that's why he did it.

"He hit irons when he had to, but when there was a chance, a sniff of a birdie, the driver was out, full commitment.

"And the way he played 18 I don't think you could have drawn that up any better. Two of the best shots he will ever hit in his life just to hit that green to give himself a chance."

Image: Fox proudly holds the Claret Jug

Coltart added: "I've never seen somebody push through the tape as hard as that right at the end of the tournament to win a major championship.

"At a place like this, too. It was just superb. The 62 on Saturday I think, helped cement his belief in his ability out there.

"While they all struggled with the pressure, he stood tall."

What's next?

The next PGA Tour event is the 3M Open at TPC Twin Cities in Minnesota, beginning Thursday, with early coverage on Sky Sports+ before switching to Sky Sports Golf at 7pm.

The 3M Open is part of a triple-header of live golf on Sky Sports, with the ISPS Handa Senior Open and ISPS Handa Women's Scottish Open also live. The women's major season then concludes with the AIG Women's Open from July 30-August 2, also live on Sky Sports Golf. Get Sky Sports or stream with no contract.

Sports.title: Hungarian GP: UK schedule and how to watch on Sky Sports
Sports.content:
Formula 1 hits the track for the final time before its summer break at one of the most popular venues on the calendar as the world championship fight rolls on to the Hungarian Grand Prix, live on Sky Sports.

The season's 11th round in Budapest is the last race for four weeks and therefore a key chance for the contenders to sign off on a high before they head on their holidays.

Kimi Antonelli will be full of confidence after a superb victory last time out in Belgium while his Mercedes team-mate George Russell retired after tangling with Lewis Hamilton on the opening lap.

Antonelli is 45 points ahead of Hamilton and 50 points in front of Russell in the Drivers' Championship and is likely to be the driver to beat at the Hungaroring.

But, the track characteristics should suit Ferrari as there are lots of corners so don't rule out Hamilton and Charles Leclerc having a shot at victory.

McLaren have claimed 1-2s in each of the past two years and the world champions will be hoping their major upgrade package can vault them into the fight at the front.

Hungarian GP track - Hungaroring

The Hungarian Grand Prix has been on the F1 calendar since 1986 and is one of the most popular events for fans.

It is renowned for its tight, twisty nature and was dubbed as 'Monaco without the barriers' due to the difficulty of overtaking.

However, it has thrown up some classic races over the years, including Michael Schumacher's incredible strategic win in 1998, Jenson Button's maiden victory in 2006, mixed conditions causing chaos in 2011 and 2014, plus Esteban Ocon's incredible triumph for Alpine in 2021.

Turn One is the prime overtaking spot, although battles often rage on down to Turn 2 and up the hill towards Turn Four. The middle sector is all about mechanical grip and keeping the tyres alive for the last few slow corners.

Hungarian GP weather in Budapest

In keeping with much of the European summer so far, dry conditions are expected throughout the Budapest weekend, although temperatures, while warm, are not forecast to be quite as sweltering as at some other events recently.

14m ago 03.44 EDT To return to the Spanish defence, though, Pau Cubarsi – what a player. I wonder whether, at some point, his relative lack of physicality costs him, but his nous, composure and ability on the ball are exceptional. Generally speaking, centre-backs break through later than players in any other position, so for him to be starting for champion sides, Barcelona and Spain, at 19 having debuted at 16, is extraordinary. Share

26m ago 03.31 EDT “One goal conceded was it?” asks Gary Naylor. “The best defences tend to win trophies.” Previous Spain trophy-winners had great defensive records too, but those, I’d argue, were the consequence of the greatest midfield ever – Busquets, Xavi, Iniesta – with Xabi Alonso added to it and sometimes Cesc Fàbregas as well – denying the opposition possession, especially in dangerous areas. And of course that’s still the principal aim, it’s just that the players aren’t quite as good in this era; the defensive record is as it is as much because Porro-Cubarsi-Laporte-Cucurella is a terrific back four in its own right. Share

35m ago 03.22 EDT Tell you what, bet there’s some regret among that England squad having watched that final. A tiny soupçon of courage – which sounds like a oxymoron but in this case is not, so minute is the amount about which we’re talking – was all it took to stop them losing to a side they ought really to have beaten with something to spare, and they were incapable of finding it. The players will, I imagine, be feeling extremely poorly with it and rightly so – but is the manager still blaming them, or will he have gone under the duvet when the night got dark and accepted his role, first in creating the environment, then making the changes largely responsibly for the subsidence? Share

53m ago 03.05 EDT Thanks Jo and, for the last time – sniff, snivel – greetings greetings one and all. “Dizguzting” – emphasis mine – is exactly the word I used to describe this abomination to my wife, with particular reference to Argentina spending the first 117 minutes of the final taking a grand total of zero shots at goal – far fewer than the cheap shots they took at the Spanish players. The trophy has gone to the correct place, so I guess we can sort of celebrate that – and, of course, a tournament which, though it phutted at the end, was a ridiculous amount of fun, love and joy. Please feel free to send in your analysis, reflections, best, worst and all of that. It’s over, but it’s in us. Share

1h ago 02.44 EDT World Cup Daily I’ll leave you with the latest episode from the team at World Cup Daily. Daniel Harris will be here take you through the rest of the news from the final. And “it was a disgusting final,” according to Jonathan Wilson. double quotation mark I think it would have been hilarious if Argentina had equalised and then won it on penalties. I think Argentina’s performance today was a consequence of the indulgence they’ve been shown throughout the tournament. Spain are world champions - World Cup Daily Read more Share

1h ago 02.35 EDT As Nick Ames writes, after a “tournament that has wrenched, tweaked and torn at the sport’s very fabric, the football itself appeared to be a sideshow for much of the afternoon”. double quotation mark It concluded with a disorientating fever dream beneath a bright blue American sky … Through it all Infantino and Trump sat abreast, absorbing the spectacle behind reinforced glass. Trump show offers fitting fever-dream end to a World Cup of excess and damage Read more View image in fullscreen Melania Trump, Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino watch from their position in the stands. Photograph: Alex Livesey/Danehouse/Getty Images Share

2h ago 02.20 EDT “I think I heard a match commentator say that the last team that beat Spain was Scotland. Does that mean Scotland have won the World Cup?!” asks Peter Oh. I don’t think that’s how it (unofficially) works sadly. The Knowledge took a look at the old winner-stays-on format earlier in the tournament, when Australia were unofficial world champions. But then the USA beat Australia, and then Turkey beat the USA … so I think it’s Turkey. But I could definitely be wrong. Share Updated at 02.36 EDT

2h ago 01.59 EDT De la Fuente on the victory Speaking after the match, Spain’s manager, who is a deeply religious person, said: “It was written, and we deserve it.” double quotation mark This team and this wonderful fanbase deserve everything. We had a date with destiny and we wanted to make it count. The players have asked me what we have left to win. Together we’ve figured out that it’s the next match in September [against England in the Nations League] because this team is tireless. ‘We had a date with destiny’: De la Fuente lauds Spain players after World Cup victory Read more View image in fullscreen Luis de la Fuente celebrates at New York New Jersey Stadium. Photograph: Hannah Peters/FIFA/Getty Images Share

2h ago 01.35 EDT The post-match altercation was a sad reflection of Argentina’s foiled attempt to use their physicality against a very patient Spain. And that patience ultimately paid off, Jacob Steinberg writes, with Argentina just become more frustrated as Spain refused to take the bait. Sports.title: Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino booed before US president attempts to crash Spain celebrations
Sports.content:
Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino were booed as they took to the field for the presentation ceremony before the US president attempted to gatecrash Spain’s victory party.

Trump arrived at the stadium on Marine One, with the president’s helicopter first flying over the stadium about 45 minutes before kick-off. He sat in a glassed-in section of luxury seats for the match, along with Infantino. Other dignitaries and former players sat nearby, including Spain’s king, Felipe VI, Canada’s prime minister, Mark Carney, and Mexico’s president, Claudia Sheinbaum.

Trump was briefly shown on the video screens at the stadium after the US national anthem was played. There were scattered boos from some in the crowd but nothing like the hostile reception he has received at other sporting events during his presidency. However, when the US president and Infantino came on to the field for the presentation after Spain clinched victory, boos rang out around the stadium. The White House pool report said that ambient crowd noise, which had been sitting at approximately 78 decibels before their introduction, rose to 84 decibels when Trump entered the field.

Then, after Trump presented Spain with the World Cup trophy, he attempted to stand with the team at the side of the podium as they celebrated before Infantino quietly ushered him away.

It was a repeat of last summer’s Club World Cup at the same stadium after Trump presented the trophy to champions Chelsea and tried to crash the celebrations to the bemusement of the players.

Trump has made several appearances at sporting events since his re-election. Last year, he attended the Super Bowl, tennis’s US Open, the Daytona 500 and golf’s Ryder Cup. This year, he has attended several golf events, college football’s national championship game and Game 3 of the NBA finals, where he was met with boos from the New York Knicks home crowd.

View image in fullscreen Lionel Messi receives his runner-up medal from Donald Trump. Photograph: Alex Pantling/FIFA/Getty Images

Trump’s appearance was the first time he has attended a match at this summer’s World Cup, which the have US co-hosted along with Canada and Mexico.

At the 2022 World Cup final, the emir of Qatar, Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani, joined Infantino to award the trophy to Lionel Messi and his Argentina teammates. Vladimir Putin awarded it to Kylian Mbappé and France after their win at the 2018 World Cup in Russia.

View image in fullscreen Rodri lifts the World Cup Trophy alongside Donald Trump and Gianni Infantino. Photograph: Carl Recine/Getty Images

Trump is the first sitting US president to attend a World Cup final on home soil. When the US hosted the tournament in 1994, Trump’s predecessor Bill Clinton did not attend the game. The trophy was instead presented by Clinton’s vice-president, Al Gore.

Trump has a close relationship with Infantino, and called the Fifa president to lobby for a review of USA star Folarin Balogun’s controversial red-card suspension before their last-16 match. Fifa did reverse Balogun’s ban, but the political circus cast a pall over the US team, who exited a promising World Cup with defeat to Belgium.

Sports.title: Hits, misses and Muppets: the star-studded World Cup half-time show nobody asked for
Sports.content:
Like hydration breaks and Donald Trump’s ability to get refereeing decisions overturned by simply phoning up the president of Fifa and complaining, the final half-time show is an innovation of the 2026 World Cup that comes with a degree of controversy attached. For one thing, its existence automatically means the World Cup final breaks the International Football Association’s 15-minute half-time mandate.

For another, its obvious antecedent lies in the NFL’s Super Bowl, where the half-time entertainment has mushroomed over the decades from a few marching bands to one of the big pop events of the year. To its detractors, it smacks of America not so much embracing the World Cup as imposing itself upon it.

View image in fullscreen Shakira performs during the World Cup final. Photograph: MB Media/Getty Images

But before you even got to the main event, there was more musical entertainment at the final to wade through, most notably the pre-match closing ceremony, a damp squib that neither the BBC nor ITV elected to broadcast live.

Anyone who hastened to iPlayer was rewarded not merely with Post Malone debuting what’s presumably the first single from his forthcoming album the Eternal Buzz, Chrome Heartbreaker (a pivot back to hip-hop-influenced pop after his recent diversion into country, should you be eagerly tracking the artistic vacillations of Post Malone’s career) and duetting with Swae Lee on their US chart-topper Sunflower, but also an online influencer-cum-professional wrestler called IShowSpeed performing Champions, a track that gained so much traction online that Fifa felt obliged to include it on the official Fifa World Cup album.

A frightful cocktail of thunderous drums and autotuned vocals, it featured lyrics that make your average football song sound as erudite and profound as the oeuvre of Leonard Cohen: “I take a breath and wait for the ref / This is the World Cup, put your hands in the air.” Alas, news of its social media virality clearly hadn’t reached the audience in the New York New Jersey Stadium. The deathly silence at its conclusion made you wonder if perhaps the TV broadcast couldn’t pick up the sound of the crowd, but no: some fireworks subsequently went off and they went audibly mental.

View image in fullscreen Three members of the Muppets’ house band the Electric Mayhem performed the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army. Photograph: James Lang/IMAGN IMAGES/Reuters

There was, it turned out, more to come. Jennifer Hudson sang the Star-Spangled Banner. Dutifully flogging a dead horse with all the professionalism he could muster, Robbie Williams performed the Fifa anthem, Desire, in the company of Laura Pausini and Nicole Scherzinger. The ballad debuted at the draw ceremony in December and – like all the musical entertainment at said event – it was overshadowed by the news that Fifa had apparently started making up awards in order to give them to Donald Trump. It vanished into obscurity thereafter, failing to chart anywhere in the world. Listening to it exhumed for another airing, you were forced to concede that the world had a point.

After all that, the actual half-time show felt like a comparative triumph. You could argue that the bar had been set pretty low without much dissent, but nonetheless, it zipped along, cramming a lot into its 11 minutes by the simple expedient of paring songs down to their bare essentials and swiftly cutting between artists. Madonna performed a version of her 2000 hit Music – reworked over a backing track immediately recognisable as derived from the Trammps’ Disco Inferno – on a vaguely Mad Max-ish vehicle piloted by Ronaldo and Ronaldinho.

Then the strains of the White Stripes’ Seven Nation Army rang out, ostensibly performed by three members of the Muppets’ house band the Electric Mayhem. There was no sign of their leader, Dr Teeth, but perhaps he was indisposed, being treated backstage after being exposed to Champions by IShowSpeed. BTS rattled through Dynamite, Shakira and Burna Boy played a truncated version of Dai Dai – the solitary World Cup song in recent memory to actually impact on the British charts – and Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love accompanied by a children’s choir: the latter looks horrendous on paper, but was far less sugary in reality, undercut by the farty blast of a crowd of vuvuzela players.

View image in fullscreen Coldplay performed a song called Believe in Love accompanied by a children’s choir that was far less sugary than it could have been. Photograph: Tullio Puglia/FIFA/Getty Images

The solitary misstep might have involved allowing Justin Bieber to perform a downcast acoustic ballad, Everything Hallelujah – viral hit following his performance at Coachella or not, this perhaps wasn’t the moment for introspection – but no matter: if the half-time show wasn’t sufficiently head-spinning to convince the viewer it should be a regular occurrence at every World Cup final, it worked well enough to justify its existence at least this time. Although clearly not everyone felt the same way: “I thought it was crap,” offered Wayne Rooney, when pressed for his opinions by BBC presenter Gabby Logan.

Sports.title: Lionel Messi’s World Cup fairytale ends with pitiful Argentina as final villains | Pablo Iglesias Maurer
Sports.content:
Playing on the grandest stage in sport for the last time, Lionel Messi seemed almost certain to provide one last memorable moment in this World Cup final.

Yet as the sun ducked behind the west stand of New York New Jersey Stadium on Sunday, it became clearer and clearer that Argentina had lost the magic they had carried through this tournament. And as Spain gradually wrested control, one was left to confront reality: Messi, and Argentina, had finally run out of time, having long since given in to their worst instincts in a 1-0 defeat.

This final presented a stark contrast to the Argentina – and Messi – we observed in every other match of the tournament. Almost without exception, La Albiceleste have been the tournament’s most entertaining team, not so much for how they’ve scored their goals but for when they’ve scored them, offering a masterclass in dramatic timing. Twice they were nearly eliminated by badly outmatched opponents, results that only galvanized them.

Finals are frequently forgettable matches that fail to entertain but even by that lowly standard the pacing of things felt dreadful. Spain were suffocating defensively and – after a forgettable first half – finally worked their way into things in the second 45, eventually breaking through in extra time, quite expectedly. Argentina? They became the first team in the near century-long history of the tournament to fail to record a shot in regular time of a World Cup final. Even when handed an additional half an hour, they never threatened.

And Messi? Until this final, he had presented observers with one of the rarest opportunities in professional sport: a chance to witness greatness free of stakes, entirely devoid of any real pressure to perform. At 39, Messi has done his time and nobody could criticize his collection of hardware – as an individual or as part of a club or country. This defeat does nothing to sully a spotless legacy; a win would have only strengthened his claim as the greatest player in the history of the sport. To some Argentinians, the victory against England in their semi-final likely carries nearly as much weight as a victory in the final would have.

Yet it has to be said: Messi was rarely involved in this match, a far cry from the player who has sometimes carried his team this summer. Much of this, of course, is down to a Spain masterclass in defending. That alone is not always enough to contain the diminutive Argentina captain. But give Spain their due: they badly outclassed Argentina in every way, neutralizing even Messi. By the end Argentina had become what so many observers pegged them to be in the first place, sometimes unfairly: underhanded, dirty and desperate.

Time has almost always been irrelevant to Messi on the field, because he so frequently bends it to his liking to elude those who defend him. The manner in which he performs at age 39 has a similar effect, tearing open a rift in time itself and transporting observers back to his glory days at Barcelona and elsewhere. Time itself has not passed him by as much as he’s marched alongside it, occasionally trailing behind a step or two but always eventually pulling even with it again.

View image in fullscreen Spain kept close tabs on Lionel Messi, who had little impact on the final. Photograph: Timothy A Clary/AFP/Getty Images

Yet now we are left to face the unmistakable reality that Messi is done, with the World Cup at least – this is, it’s worth noting, what was said after he led Argentina to their first World Cup in nearly four decades in 2022 and what was assumed in 2016, when Messi briefly retired from the national team after Argentina’s defeat in the Copa América final. Back then, the dialogue surrounding this player was that he would never play for Argentina the way he did for Barcelona, or even rumblings that Messi himself wasn’t sufficiently Argentinian, having spent so much of his life in Spain. Both arguments feel laughable 10 years later.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

It remains to be seen how Argentina’s performance will be perceived back home, where expectations were understandably high. The head coach, Lionel Scaloni, and even Messi had spoken at length before the final about how much they had already achieved. This final result, they implied, would do little to sully that sense of accomplishment.

This was, of course, before they took the field and more or less destroyed the game. Scaloni’s legacy, like Messi’s, was secure before this final, the coach having brought Argentina a third World Cup and a pair of Copa América titles, but this was a lost opportunity to solidify it. Two things can coexist: Scaloni is almost without question Argentina’s greatest coach, and this was one of his worst results and performances.

What feels much more real, though, is a sense of loss and disappointment after this pitiful final performance, which provided Argentina – and Messi – with a perfect opportunity to put the finishing touches on their fairytale. Instead, they turned from hero to villain – and needlessly so.

Sports.title: Top 30: from half a million World Cup photos, why I love these the best
Sports.content:
What makes a great World Cup photograph? Now there’s a question with myriad answers. Composition, newsworthiness, emotional resonance, expert timing and luck can all contribute to varying degrees. But one thing they all share is the power to capture attention.

On the Guardian sport picture desk, we have received more than 500,000 World Cup photographs over the past six weeks, with so many classics among them. Here, with much applause to the photographers who created them and a slight bias towards England, are my favourite images of the tournament.

1

Messi’s cathedral

View image in fullscreen Argentina’s Lionel Messi prepares to take a corner kick against Switzerland at Kansas City Stadium. Photograph: Julian Finney/Fifa/Getty Images

An absolute cracker to start with. In this picture, the cavernous Kansas City Stadium sweeps around a small corner of grass on which the world’s most famous footballer stands alone. You can’t really see it’s Lionel Messi, but somehow you can tell it’s him. It feels as though everybody’s eyes are pointed in his direction, as though they’re worshipping a deity in an epic footballing cathedral.

2

Goalline scramble

View image in fullscreen Brazil’s Endrick flings his boot at a loose ball as Japan’s players scramble to clear their lines. Photograph: Annegret Hilse/Reuters

Technological improvements have led to the creation of high-quality miniature remote-operated cameras which can be placed inside goalmouths. Seeing the game at such close quarters feels wonderfully dynamic. This frame in particular captures a mad scramble between Brazil and Japan; the wonky angle adds to the sense of chaos.

3

Tuchel’s close up

View image in fullscreen England’s manager, Thomas Tuchel, during the national anthem before the match with Croatia at Dallas Stadium. Photograph: Bradley Collyer/PA

A self-referential choice, but this was a big news story at the time: England played Croatia in their first game and the England manager, Thomas Tuchel, was so furious he couldn’t see the players during the national anthem that he asked Fifa to move the photographers for subsequent games. In fairness to him, you can see why. Four weeks later, Tuchel would garner headlines again after his substitutions in the semi-final against Argentina helped to trigger England’s collapse.

4

Balogun sees red

View image in fullscreen The USA’s Folarin Balogun fouls Tarik Muharemovic of Bosnia and Herzegovina, leading to a red card after a VAR check. Photograph: Michael Steele/Getty Images

At first glance it looks innocuous enough, then you notice Tarik Muharemovic’s right ankle buckling under the pressure applied by Folarin Balogun’s mistimed challenge. Replays of the incident suggested the foul was unintentional, though the Bosnian was lucky to escape injury. Balogun received a red card following a VAR review, but his one-game ban was suspended by Fifa after lobbying from Donald Trump. With Balogun back in the team, the USA were dumped out of their own tournament by Belgium in the next round.

5

Tartan trauma

View image in fullscreen Scotland’s Findlay Curtis (left) and Jack Hendry in the tunnel after their defeat by Brazil in Miami. Photograph: Carmen Mandato/Fifa/Getty Images

I’ve relished seeing so many photographs from inside the tunnels at this World Cup because the players seem to reveal a little more of themselves away from the public eye. This candid shot of Scotland players Findlay Curtis and Jack Hendry shows them in the wake of their 3-0 loss to Brazil – a defeat that was filled with calamity, and which ultimately led to Scotland’s early exit. They look like they’re outside a head teacher’s office waiting to be reprimanded.

6

Diving header

View image in fullscreen England’s midfielder Jude Bellingham scores his team’s first goal against Mexico at the Azteca. Photograph: Ulises Ruiz/AFP/Getty Images

I love a good diving header and this one by Jude Bellingham against Mexico was peachy. From a photographic point of view, you seldom get shots from tribune positions like this during a Premier League season, so they have a real novelty value during major tournaments. But it’s more than just novelty: the elevated vantage point helps to remove the surrounding clutter and give a proper fan’s eye view of the goal. I also love the verdant grass, the shocking pink goalkeeper’s jersey and the sense of anticipation because the ball has yet to cross the line. It reminds me of the signed photograph of Coventry’s Keith Houchen, from the 1987 FA Cup final, that hangs proudly on my dad’s office wall.

7

Bruno’s early bath

View image in fullscreen Brazil’s Bruno Guimarães cools down with a splash of water in the first half against Morocco in New Jersey. Photograph: Adam Hunger/AP

So many hydration breaks, so much Powerade, but only one player managed to look like a Portuguese water dog fresh from a dip in a lake. The Brazil midfielder Bruno Guimarães is pictured here dousing himself in H 2 O when his side faced Morocco in their opening game at New York New Jersey Stadium. Brazil ultimately went home for an early bath after losing to Norway in the last 16.

8

Viking row boat

View image in fullscreen Norway supporters gather to perform their rowing celebration on the iconic red steps in Times Square. Photograph: Anadolu/Getty Images

The mass rowing displays performed by Norway’s fans this summer have been a viral sensation. Seen everywhere from Times Square to Miami Beach, they also became a fixture of the team’s post-match partying, with Erling Haaland and Martin Ødegaard both banging a fan’s drum as the side progressed to the quarter-finals. The Vikings were stopped by England, but their journey was one of the feelgood stories of the tournament.

9

Light and shade

View image in fullscreen Kylian Mbappé of France dribbles the ball against Sweden at New York New Jersey Stadium. Photograph: Justin Setterfield/Getty Images

A gorgeous pool of afternoon sunlight spilling on to the pitch, surrounded by deep shadows. You couldn’t really create better low-key lighting conditions if you tried. The photographer just had to nail the exposure and wait for a subject to pass through. The fact that it’s Kylian Mbappé who’s skating across the turf in his rich blue France top adds a nice splash of colour and gravity to the scene.

10

Tunnel vision

View image in fullscreen Luka Modric of Croatia prepares in the tunnel before their match with Panama in Toronto. Photograph: Joosep Martinson/Fifa/Getty Images

Luka Modric has spoken in the past about not wanting to let his people down, and of carrying memories of his grandpa, Luka, with him. He appears to be deep in thought here before playing Panama. Perhaps it’s just a fleeting moment – a man simply massaging his temple or visualising the first tackle – or maybe he’s remembering his war-torn roots and the family member he was named after.

11

Loving Vozinha

View image in fullscreen Cape Verde’s Vozinha after the match against Spain in Atlanta. Photograph: Brett Davis/Imagn Images/Reuters

At the ripe age of 40 and with a club career that has taken him to Cyprus, Moldova, Portugal and Slovakia, the Cape Verde goalkeeper Vozinha became the breakout star at this year’s World Cup. His numerous saves against Spain in the group stage earned him global praise as well as 17 million followers on Instagram. Another stellar display against Argentina, in which he memorably denied a quick free-kick by Messi, further enhanced his reputation. I like his expression in this photograph as he soaks up the adulation from the crowd following the Blue Sharks’ remarkable goalless draw with Spain.

12

Gaza screening

View image in fullscreen Palestinian football fans gather among war-damaged buildings in Gaza City to watch the match between Argentina and Egypt on a giant outdoor screen. Photograph: Mohammed Skaik/TheNews2/Cover Images

This photograph shows the power of football while also putting the World Cup into perspective. These Palestinian residents in Gaza may have lost everything, but they gathered amid the ruins of their former homes to watch a screening of Egypt’s game against Argentina. A moment of normality amid the horror and heartache.

13

Power header

View image in fullscreen Erling Haaland of Norway scores against Brazil at New York New Jersey Stadium. Photograph: Image Photo Agency/Getty Images

Erling Haaland’s first goal against Brazil left his old Premier League rival, Gabriel Magalhães, in a heap. In this shot you can see water (or perhaps sweat) flying off the striker’s forehead, his neck fully strained after connecting with the ball. Haaland scored seven goals in five World Cup games: he netted from inside the box, outside the box, with his left foot, right foot and of course his head. Norway have still never been beaten by Brazil after five matches. No other nation can say that.

14

Lamine Yamal’s braces

View image in fullscreen Lamine Yamal bites the Spain badge during an official Fifa photocall prior to the tournament. Photograph: Karl Bridgeman/Fifa/Getty Images

This image was shot before the tournament, as part of Fifa’s official player portraits, but I’ve only recently seen it – and it’s well worth a mention. You don’t see many players with braces, but Lamine Yamal, who only turned 19 this month, wears his with pride. This frame was shot using a 24-70mm lens on a Canon R5 Mark II which has a whopping 45 megapixels, so I suspect it’s been cropped quite hard in post-production to achieve this composition.

15

Into orbit

View image in fullscreen Switzerland’s Manuel Akanji misses a penalty during the shootout against Colombia. Photograph: Agustín Marcarian/Reuters



Some penalty misses are worse than others. Germany’s Jonathan Tah and Manuel Akanji of Switzerland both had Chris Waddle moments as they blew their chances from 12 yards over the bar. Ordinarily I’d say you need to see the crossbar to illustrate that the shot went over, but the way the ball is rocketing skywards – almost as if it could escape the stadium roof – tells the story perfectly.

16

Neymar’s tears

View image in fullscreen Brazil’s Neymar is consoled by Raphinha after their side were eliminated from the World Cup by Norway. Photograph: James Lang/Imagn Images/Reuters

Even when your ego is as big as the sun, sometimes you just need a cuddle. This photograph captures Neymar Jr’s visible distress as he realises his international career is over and his childhood ambitions of lifting the World Cup will never be fulfilled. His teammate Raphina is there to support him. It lacks the humility of Freddie Flintoff consoling his opponent Brett Lee in the Ashes, or the stoicism of Derek Redmond being helped across the finish line by his father at the 1992 Olympics, but it still packs an emotional gut punch.

17

Upside down

View image in fullscreen Julián Alvarez with teammates after scoring Argentina’s second goal against Switzerland at Kansas City Stadium. Photograph: Ryan Pierse/Fifa/Getty Images

This photograph was flipped around by Getty Images before being transmitted to us. Manipulation of this ilk feels almost heretical in the world of photojournalism, and yet I’m inclined to say it’s compelling. It shows Julián Alvarez celebrating his late winner against Switzerland, and it makes me question my fundamental photographic principles. Would I print it in the newspaper like this? Absolutely not. Would I include it in an online gallery of images that caught my eye this summer? Evidently so.

18

Big screen

View image in fullscreen A giant video screen signals a goal for Spain against Saudi Arabia in Atlanta. Photograph: Colin Hubbard/AP

The stadums in the US have been mind-blowing in scale. Atlanta Stadium, home of the NFL’s Atlanta Falcons and the city’s MLS and NWSL teams, has a maximum capacity of 75,000 people, a climate-controlled environment and a 335-metre display known as the “halo”. This picture from up in the gods looks suitably epic. Initially I assumed the camera was remote-controlled, but it transpires some photographers were actually working up there on the gantry. What a view they had!

19

Motion blur

View image in fullscreen Sweden winger Anthony Elanga is challenged by two Japan defenders during their game at Dallas Stadium. Photograph: Lars Baron/Getty Images

This is a beautiful example of a photographer using a slow shutter speed while panning gently with the action. I especially like the details within: Anthony Elanga’s facial expression is crisp, and the pink boots leave a painterly trail.

20

Heroic Harry

View image in fullscreen Harry Kane and Jude Bellingham of England celebrate against DR Congo at Atlanta Stadium. Photograph: Ian MacNicol/Getty Images

Harry Kane’s late strikes against the Democratic Republic of Congo in the last 32 led to an outpouring of emotion from the England captain. I was torn over which frame to select – there are some lovely ones of him sprinting across the turf, flanked by Jude Bellingham and Anthony Gordon – but this one of him being embraced by Bellingham serves as a perfect reminder of their twin heroics at the tournament. It’s clean, nicely balanced and full of bromance.

21

Gómez goes berserk

View image in fullscreen Gustavo Gómez of Paraguay looks delighted after José Canale scored the winning penalty in a shootout against Germany in Boston. Photograph: Robert Cianflone/Getty Images

The guaranteed agony and ecstasy of penalty shootouts always makes for brilliant images. This year, Gustavo Gómez of Paraguay takes the crown for the wildest reaction. After beating Germany during sudden death, Gómez, who scored his own spot-kick, surges across the pitch like a heron taking flight, almost vaulting his teammates José Canale and Orlando Gill as he went to embrace them. He then careered through the photographers behind the goal in pursuit of a mobile phone so that he could document the moment himself.

22

Living statue

View image in fullscreen Michel Nkuka Mboladinga, also known as Lumumba Vea, holds firm in the stands during their match against Colombia. Photograph: Daniel Becerril/Reuters

Michel Nkuka Mboladinga, also known as Lumumba Vea, is dubbed a “living statue” because he doesn’t move during games. Instead, the DRC fan poses on a plinth for the entire match, raising his right arm to mimic the statue of Patrice Lumumba, the first prime minister of the First Congolese Republic, which stands in Kinshasa. Why anyone would go to a football match and not respond to the on-pitch action is beyond me, but Mboladinga insists it’s his patriotic duty.

23

Senegal swan dive

View image in fullscreen Youri Tielemans heads in Belgium’s second goal against Senegal at Seattle Stadium. Photograph: Jared C Tilton/Fifa/Getty Images

Youri Tielemans scored twice in Belgium’s stunning comeback against Senegal in the last 32. This 89th-minute header might have been a little trickier to control had the defender Moussa Niakhaté competed for the ball instead of diving theatrically to the ground at the first sign of contact. The virtue of modern cameras, many of which shoot 30 frames per second, is that the full sequence of this goal was captured, and we could choose the exact frame when Tielemans’s head connects with the ball.

24

Comeback king

View image in fullscreen Sasa Kalajdzic after scoring Austria’s third goal during a thrilling game against Algeria at Kansas City Stadium. Photograph: Alex Pantling/Fifa/Getty Images

Sasa Kalajdzic overcame three anterior cruciate ligament injuries in the years and months prior to the 2026 World Cup, but the Austrian enjoyed a moment to savour when he netted a 96th-minute equaliser against Algeria to keep his side in the tournament. The game ignited accusations of fixing, because a 3-3 draw ensured both sides went through, but a finale like that – and celebrations like this – cannot be scripted.

25

View image in fullscreen Connor Metcalfe of Australia shows the referee his bloodied forehead against Paraguay at San Francisco Bay Area Stadium. Photograph: Stu Forster/Getty Images

Australia’s Connor Metcalfe needed three stitches in his eyebrow after being clipped by a stray boot from Andrés Cubas during the Socceroos’ group match with Paraguay. Maybe it’s the slumped shoulders or the shirt pulled up around his neckline, but he looks like a forlorn child who needs a parent to clean him up.

26

Big Dan Burn

View image in fullscreen England’s Dan Burn blocks a bicycle kick from Raúl Jiménez during the last-16 match in Mexico City. Photograph: Jam Media/Getty Images

You could say this is just another “two men and a ball” photograph (an expression the Guardian’s photographer, Tom Jenkins, uses to describe generic images of sporting action). But I particularly like this one because of the contrast of sporting prowess – the acrobat versus the brick wall – and for the misshapen ball which appears ready to pop. Dan Burn has become a cult figure for England, in the mould of Peter Crouch. Many supporters call the 6ft 7in defender Big Dan Burn, but Bellingham apparently calls him Burninho. There’s no way Raúl Jiménez, the Mexico striker, was ever getting the ball past him.

27

Koné’s injury pain

View image in fullscreen Canada’s Ismaël Koné on the ground after sustaining a broken leg against Qatar. Photograph: Lee Smith/Reuters

Ismaël Koné’s eyes say it all. The Canada midfielder had just broken the tibia and fibula bones in his lower left leg after a challenge by Qatar’s midfielder Assim Madibo, who would receive a red card and a five-match ban. As a photo editor, when incidents like this occur you have to weigh up decency and news value before publishing (I still feel traumatised by the uncensored images I saw of Eduardo’s broken leg in 2008). I think this image conveys the severity of the incident without being unduly graphic. Koné left the pitch on a stretcher but waved to fans as he exited.

28

Crowd scene

View image in fullscreen Canada fans take in their game against Bosnia and Herzegovina at Toronto Stadium. Photograph: Joosep Martinson/Fifa/Getty Images

The composition of this photograph is simple but beautiful. The intersecting diagonals, the contrast between light and shade, and the depth within the scene … it all makes for rich viewing.

29

Emotional Messi

View image in fullscreen Argentina’s Lionel Messi after their 3-2 victory over Egypt at Atlanta Stadium. Photograph: Patrick Smith/Fifa/Getty Images

Let’s be honest, Lionel Messi is not very good at penalties. He’s missed four of eight in World Cup matches and 34 of 151 in his career, including shootouts. A botched effort against Egypt, in a match which the African side went on to lead 2-0, could have been a harrowing ending to his gilded international career. Instead, Messi did what Messi does: he scored the equaliser and drove his team to a remarkable 3-2 win in normal time. This picture, taken after the match, speaks to the weight he carries on his shoulders. Is he feeling relief or guilt? Either way, he looks tortured by expectation.

30

Cubarsi’s cartwheel

View image in fullscreen Argentina’s Enzo Fernández fouls Spain’s Pau Cubarsi and is later shown a second yellow card leading to a red. Photograph: Maddie Meyer/Fifa/Getty Images

Ordinarily I’d select a celebration photograph from the World Cup final among my favourites, but this ‘tackle’ by Enzo Fernández was so bad – and the image of Pau Cubarsi flying through the air so striking – that I couldn’t look beyond it. An absolutely dreadful final sparked into life at this moment. Cubarsi rose from the turf to claim the title of ‘best young player’ of the tournament and, more importantly, a World Cup winner’s medal.

Sports.title: At the World Cup of superstars, a team take home the trophy | Sid Lowe
Sports.content:
Release the pressure, let it out. All of it and all of them. Again and again they had come, again and again they had been halted but they would not be denied. A dozen different players had taken aim at Emi Martínez’s goal but somehow he was still standing and time was slipping away, yet Spain refused to do so, so they came some more.

And then, suddenly, only this wasn’t really sudden, the result instead of the purest logic, the clearest justice, Pedro Porro’s deep cross found Nico Williams at the far post and he headed back. The ball dropped deep inside the Argentina penalty area, bounced on the turf and just kind of sat there: waiting, willing someone take this moment.

So at 5.42pm eastern daylight time, 37 seconds into the second period of extra time, Ferran Torres did. And with Spain’s 20th shot of this final, with all his might and all his soul, he won the World Cup. The ball travelled at 102km/h, tearing into the net, and Torres turned and tore in the other direction, sprinting to the corner where he leapt into the air and volleyed that too. Not quite so hard as he had hit the shot, but hard. From the bench and the pitch his teammates raced towards him, liberated at last, the joy flooding out. Oh, the release.

Andrés Iniesta once said that the moment the ball sat up for him in the 116th minute of the final in South Africa in 2010, he heard the silence. Maybe Torres heard it too; maybe he heard history call. More often he has heard noise. Here there was an explosion, everyone at that end of New York New Jersey Stadium going absolutely mad. Torres stood there, doing a familiar gesture: jibber-jabber hands, ears “listening” wondering where the critics were now. Then he got the biggest hug Lamine Yamal has ever given.

Late in Spain’s victory over Saudi Arabia on the day that Luis de la Fuente celebrated his 65th birthday, Torres had come on as a substitute and scored the final goal – or thought he had – only for the video assistant referee to take it from him. As they reviewed the footage, Ferran had stood with his hands in front of his mouth in a praying position, muttering to himself: por favor, be a goal; por favor, be a goal. This seemed like a portrait of the pressure, of what players put up with sometimes, a picture perhaps of desperation too. Spain were four goals up already, but here he was pleading for it to count.

In the previous game against Cape Verde, he had hit the bar. In the next game, against Uruguay, he did it again. There was something that his critics took as confirmation, something cruel in how close it was. Too often he had felt that fate somehow was conspiring against him. Turned out, it was saving something for him: the greatest goal, the greatest moment in any player’s career. Justice had been done, not just in the game, which Spain had dominated Spain’s way – at that point Argentina had not had a shot – but to this team. This family, as De la Fuente calls them, all in it together.

It felt right almost that it should be Torres, a symbol of all of them – like this was another moment shared, the collective expressed in one man who hasn’t always felt it but will now be for ever beloved. Torres became the seventh different Spain player to score in the US. At the World Cup of the stars, a team took the trophy. The European champions were the best team here, lifting that trophy having conceded just one goal, and this was a victory for a system, an ideal, a commitment to an identity. In that, it can feel almost inevitable but it is not. This was also a victory for vindication, for the belief their manager has in them and they have in each other, even if others do not. “People have been very unfair with him but he has a spectacular mentality, he keeps going, keeps working, and today life has paid him back,” Pedro Porro said of Torres. “This is for all 26 of us.”

Coming into the tournament, Rodri, the captain, had not completed his rehabilitation yet. Lamine Yamal, the star, was returning from injury too, everyone waiting for him until they realised that maybe they didn’t have to. Williams, who had provided the assist, thought he wouldn’t get there: injured for much of the season, he fought back then feared Uruguay had kicked him out of the World Cup.

Fabián Ruiz had missed most the season injured. Aymeric Laporte, imperious again, suffered with Athletic. Behind him, the debate around Unai Simón wouldn’t relent. Eric García and Martín Zubimendi came on here to win it: neither had had a minute yet, meaning Spain finished the competition with only two outfielders who have not played. Who had Pedro Porro and Marc Cucurella down as the world’s best full-backs before the tournament? Plenty do now. Mikel Merino, the superest of super subs, had played only 28 minutes since March, but appeared to rescue them. Not once, but twice.

skip past newsletter promotion Free newsletter | Every weekday Sign up to Football Daily Kick off your evenings with the Guardian's take on the world of football Preview latest Enter your email Sign up after newsletter promotion

And then, at the biggest moment of all, there was Torres.

De la Fuente said that Spain had been “stung” by the doubts in those early games, the lack of recognition. “They are the best players in the world,” he kept saying, and it turned out he was right. Spain’s coach is a man of faith: faith in his footballers, his “family”; and faith, faith. Every day over the last month he has exchanged messages with a friend Antonio, who is like a son to him, expressing the conviction they both felt. “It is written,” the messages say, and now it is.

Sports.title: Fifa gives fraud ‘an open door’ with betting, says Council of Europe chief
Sports.content:
Fifa has been accused of providing an “open door to fraud” and allowing political influence to cast doubt on the integrity of the World Cup in a stinging rebuke by the Council of Europe’s secretary general.

In an open letter published to coincide with Sunday’s final, Alain Berset also called for a new integrity framework to be built before the 2030 tournament, which is mainly being staged in Europe, and warned that Fifa was embroiled in a crisis involving money and power.

Berset referenced the scandal surrounding Fifa’s decision to shelve the suspension of the USA striker Folarin Balogun and made apparent allusions to comments made by the Paraguayan senator Celeste Amarilla about Kylian Mbappé and by the former Spanish prime minister Mariano Rajoy about the France team.

“The Fifa World Cup 2026 has raised question after question,” Berset wrote. “A sanction suspended under pressure, within days, with no reasons given. The authority of referees called into question. Racist abuse of players, some of it from elected officials. Betting on every pass, every card, every corner. The celebration will end tonight. The questions will not.”

It is a significant intervention given Fifa and the Council of Europe signed a memorandum of understanding in 2018, which remains valid. The agreement was struck to strengthen their work together on a number of topics, including “human rights, integrity and good governance in sport”. Open criticism of one partner by another is extremely rare.

Berset took aim at Fifa’s deal with ADI Predictstreet, which became the World Cup’s official prediction market partner in April. “Betting has moved from the result of a match to moments a single player can produce without changing the score,” he said. “A bet is won by making others lose. It is an open door to fraud. And this World Cup has opened the door wider.”

In further reference to the lifting of Balogun’s ban by Fifa, which occurred after a phone call to its president, Gianni Infantino, by his US counterpart, Donald Trump, Berset said: “When the rules bend under pressure, every result is open to doubt.”

View image in fullscreen Gianni Infantino with Donald Trump at the World Cup final reception at Trump Tower on Friday 17 July in New York. Photograph: Ira L Black/Fifa/Getty Images

Infantino has said the decision to revoke Balogun’s ban was taken independently by Fifa’s disciplinary committee “based on the applicable regulations and the specific facts”.

Berset, who is Swiss, proposed a “working dialogue that starts tonight” to begin the “urgent work of strengthening the integrity of sport” before future World Cups. He referenced work by the Council of Europe – which is the continent’s intergovernmental human rights organisation – in creating a binding treaty to keep fans safe three months after the Heysel Stadium disaster in 1985, as well as further legislation set up to tackle doping in athletics and match-fixing.

The letter comes a week and a half after 72 members of the European parliament wrote to the 27 EU-based football associations asking for an investigation into Infantino’s involvement in the Balogun case. It pointed to alleged breaches of political neutrality and suggested Fifa had contravened its own code of ethics.

It does not appear likely that Uefa, European football’s governing body, will formally take the matter further. In June, 50 members of the European parliament wrote to Infantino and the Fifa council requesting an investigation into the awarding of the Fifa peace prize to Trump.

Fifa was contacted for comment.

This past week it was revealed that more that 200 of Fifa’s member associations have formally backed Infantino’s attempt to be re-elected for a fourth term in March.

Sports.title: Kane says Tuchel will ‘learn a lot’ from England pressures after exit to Argentina
Sports.content:
Harry Kane has backed Thomas Tuchel to learn from England’s World Cup semi-final defeat against Argentina and believes they must use the forthcoming Nations League campaign to gain experience of playing against the top teams.

Kane was an unused substitute as England sealed third place with an entertaining 6-4 victory against France on Saturday – their best finish at a World Cup on foreign soil.
