World.title: Georgia and Turkmenistan agree to deepen cooperation
World.content:
Prime Minister Irakli Kobakhidze has summed up the state visit of Turkmen President Serdar Berdimuhamedow to Georgia, saying the two sides signed a joint statement, cooperation agreements across a range of sectors, and memorandums of understanding.

Serdar Berdimuhamedow arrived in Tbilisi on 16 July with members of his delegation. It was his second state visit to Georgia. Kobakhidze himself visited Turkmenistan three times last year.

According to the prime minister, the agreements reached during the visit will further strengthen the existing ties between the two countries.

Kobakhidze said that during his one-on-one meeting with Serdar Berdimuhamedow, they discussed the main areas of Georgian-Turkmen relations, as well as regional and international issues.

“Central Asia as a whole is a region of particular interest to Georgia. In this context, we view Turkmenistan as a reliable partner and a friendly country,” he said.

Kobakhidze said relations between the two countries are based on a long-standing friendship and mutual respect, which he argued provides a solid foundation for further expanding cooperation.

The prime minister also highlighted Turkmenistan’s economic development, the expansion of its transport and logistics capabilities, and its infrastructure projects.

During the expanded-format talks, the two sides discussed prospects for strengthening trade ties, promoting exports, and developing transport links. Particular attention was paid to the development of the Middle Corridor — the transport route connecting Asia and Europe — and opportunities to attract additional cargo.

The talks also covered closer cooperation in tourism, culture, and education. According to Kobakhidze, there is scope for further strengthening people-to-people ties between the two countries.

The prime minister thanked the Turkmen authorities for supporting Georgia’s sovereignty and territorial integrity within its internationally recognised borders.

“We attach particular importance to deepening relations with Turkmenistan across political, economic, educational, cultural and other areas. I am confident that the president’s visit will give fresh momentum to our bilateral relations,” Irakli Kobakhidze said.

Georgia and Turkmenistan deepen cooperation

World.title: ‘Smear campaign’ in Russian media and Azerbaijani foreign minister’s Moscow visit: What’s changing?
World.content:
Russia’s smear campaign against Azerbaijan

A new wave of anti-Azerbaijani content has emerged across Russia’s information space. State television channels, online media outlets and Telegram channels have been publishing material with strikingly similar messaging. Azerbaijan’s pro-government news agency Report describes it as a “coordinated smear campaign” and links it to President Ilham Aliyev’s speech at the Fourth Shusha Global Media Forum.

The agency’s rhetoric is particularly notable. Its coverage uses terms such as “war hawks”, “a racist, chauvinistic ideology with fascist tendencies”, “Ruscism”, and “nationalist and fascist circles”. This highly charged language targets specific groups within Russia, particularly supporters of the war in Ukraine and those promoting ideas of Russian superiority over other nations.

In recent years, the term “Ruscism” has become widely used in Ukrainian and broader Western discourse to describe what is characterised as a form of Russian fascism. By adopting this terminology, the agency frames the dispute not simply as a diplomatic disagreement but as an ideological confrontation.

At the same time, its assertion that the “previous methodology is completely outdated” suggests that some actors have failed to adapt to the region’s changing realities. Such uncompromising rhetoric could provoke an equally sharp response from Moscow and further deepen tensions between the two countries.

Foreign minister’s visit to Moscow

Against the backdrop of this media campaign, Azerbaijani Foreign Minister Jeyhun Bayramov’s visit to Moscow on 16–17 July has taken on added significance. On 15 July, Russian Foreign Ministry spokeswoman Maria Zakharova announced that Bayramov would hold talks with his Russian counterpart, Sergei Lavrov.

Baku’s decision to go ahead with the visit has been widely seen as a signal that it wants to keep dialogue alive. In other words, despite the increasingly sharp rhetoric on both sides, official channels of communication remain open.

On 17 July, Bayramov laid flowers at the Tomb of the Unknown Soldier in Moscow before holding one-on-one talks with Lavrov. According to a post on Zakharova’s official Telegram channel, the meeting took place behind closed doors.

Azerbaijani media reported that the ministers discussed a broad range of bilateral issues, including political, economic, trade, transport and humanitarian cooperation, as well as regional and international security.

The two sides also focused on the work of the intergovernmental commission on economic cooperation, the role of the Russian-Azerbaijani Business Council, the development of the International North–South Transport Corridor, and environmental issues affecting the Caspian Sea. They also discussed expanding cooperation in culture, education, humanitarian affairs and youth exchanges.

Addressing developments in the South Caucasus, Bayramov said the region’s new realities were based on the principles of international law, including sovereignty, territorial integrity and the inviolability of internationally recognised borders. At the end of the meeting, the two countries signed a consultation plan between their foreign ministries for 2026–2027.

Statements at the Shusha Global Media Forum

Much of the attention has focused on the Shusha Global Media Forum, held on 13–14 July. Responding to a question from a Ukrainian journalist, President Ilham Aliyev said Azerbaijan firmly supports Ukraine’s territorial integrity, considers occupation unacceptable, and calls for an immediate end to the war. While this position is consistent with Baku’s long-standing policy, it was voiced at a particularly sensitive moment for Russia.

Aliyev struck a different tone when responding to a Russian journalist at the same forum. He said bilateral relations were improving, describing the trend as positive and noting that contacts between governments, ministries and presidential administrations had resumed. By saying that “the difficulties are behind us”, Aliyev signalled that he viewed the previous period of tensions as over.

His assertion that “the previous approaches to understanding and perceiving the South Caucasus are completely outdated” has been interpreted as a broader political message. It reflects the new balance of power that has emerged in the region since 2020, following Azerbaijan’s restoration of control over its internationally recognised territory, its growing role in regional transport and energy corridors, and the changing dynamics of its relations with Armenia. The underlying message is that the old approach to treating the South Caucasus as a sphere of influence no longer works.

The context behind the “smear campaign”

From an analytical perspective, Azerbaijan’s position on Ukraine is not the only factor behind the reported smear campaign. Some circles in Russia are increasingly concerned about Moscow’s declining influence in the South Caucasus. Media commentary suggests that Baku’s multi-vector foreign policy—maintaining ties with the West, Turkey, Central Asia and Russia simultaneously—conflicts with Moscow’s desire to preserve its dominant role in the region. In this context, coordinated media campaigns can serve as a tool of diplomatic pressure.

By combining a firm stance on Ukraine with a pragmatic approach towards Russia—reflected in Bayramov’s visit to Moscow and Aliyev’s remarks about improving bilateral ties—Baku is pursuing a classic balancing strategy. The message is aimed both at a domestic audience, by reaffirming support for sovereignty and international law, and at foreign partners, by signalling a willingness to maintain relations with Russia. Such a dual-track approach, however, carries risks, as both sides could begin to view Azerbaijan as an unreliable partner.

Aliyev’s remarks in Shusha can also be seen as a call to recognise the new realities across the post-Soviet space. The regional order that shaped the 1990s—and, to a large extent, even the 2010s—has changed. Azerbaijan increasingly presents itself as a middle regional power and expects that status to be acknowledged. If Russia fails to adapt to these changes, periodic crises in bilateral relations are likely to continue.

The outlook for relations between the two countries remains mixed. Official dialogue continues, but the information confrontation is intensifying. Bayramov’s visit may help ease tensions in the short term, yet the underlying structural issues—including competition for influence, ideological differences and the changing regional balance of power—remain unresolved. In these circumstances, both sides may achieve more by moving away from emotionally charged rhetoric and focusing instead on dialogue based on practical interests.

The limits of Azerbaijan’s balancing policy

Another development is worth noting in this context. Just days before President Ilham Aliyev’s remarks at the Shusha Global Media Forum, the city hosted an international conference on 6 July titled Cultural and Ethnic Diversity: Lessons from History, Contemporary Challenges.

Participants criticised the discrimination faced by ethnic minorities in Russia, including Azerbaijanis, as well as the reported forced mobilisation of minorities for the war in Ukraine and manifestations of chauvinism. They also called for the recognition of the Circassian genocide. The conference’s messaging appears to foreshadow Aliyev’s subsequent remarks: only a few days later, he reaffirmed support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity while simultaneously stressing the normalisation of relations with Russia.

At the same time, Ukrainian media have periodically published critical reports and investigations into Azerbaijan’s position on the war. Taken together, the Shusha conference on discrimination and criticism from Ukrainian commentators help illuminate another dimension of Baku’s foreign policy. In his speech, Aliyev sought to reconcile continued engagement with Russia and support for Ukraine’s territorial integrity, avoiding a complete break with either side while keeping relations with both within carefully managed limits.

Balancing, however, rarely produces perfect equilibrium. At certain moments, closer alignment with one side inevitably becomes more visible than with the other. Despite tensions with Moscow, Azerbaijan continues to maintain relations with Russia while also demonstrating friendly ties with Ukraine. In practice, this has made the country one of the arenas for indirect competition between Moscow and Kyiv.

Baku is trying to keep its relationships with both sides within carefully defined boundaries without crossing either’s red lines. Both Russia and Ukraine appear to recognise this approach and have responded with their own warning signals. The information campaign of recent days, and the reactions that followed, may be another consequence of Azerbaijan’s balancing strategy.

Russia’s smear campaign against Azerbaijan

World.title: Pottery emerges as popular form of art therapy in Armenia
World.content:
Pottery as a form of art therapy

Pottery is one of the world’s oldest crafts. In recent years, it has also become a popular form of art therapy. In Armenia in particular, pottery-based art therapy has gained widespread popularity.

Psychologists say that touching clay and shaping it with the fingers, which contain numerous nerve endings, stimulates people’s senses and emotions. This, in turn, helps strengthen the connection between the body and emotions.

A pottery wheel. Photo: JAMnews

How a hobby became a life’s work

In Mariam Gevorgyan’s hands, clay is more than just a material. Every piece she creates has its own story, character and mood. Malleable clay transforms thoughts, unspoken words and memories into works of art. It also inspires her students to express themselves in the same way.

Mariam Gevorgyan looks over her students’ work. Photo: JAMnews

However, the story did not begin with a childhood dream or a carefully planned career choice. It all started with a mug she made for a colleague.

“One day, a colleague was telling me about a moustache mug. He couldn’t find one anywhere. Feeling rather pleased with myself, I said I could make one. We made a bet over whether I could. I came to the Terracotta art studio and made the mug. The moustache turned out well, but the mug itself wasn’t very practical. I gave it to him anyway and won the bet. I don’t remember what happened next. But after that, I made many more pieces and carried on working with ceramics,” she says.

The hobby might never have become her profession had it not been for Mariam’s curiosity. During her very first lesson, she even tasted the clay. Later, she tried the glaze used to give pottery its glossy finish.

“I was fascinated by the material I was working with. I wanted to know what it tasted like. The next step was tasting the glaze, which I would never recommend to anyone because it’s essentially glass. It comes as a powder, but you definitely shouldn’t eat it. Of course, I tried it anyway. It didn’t taste good,” she recalls.

Mariam says pottery helps build resilience. It teaches patience, encourages people not to rush, and helps them overcome the fear of making mistakes.

She says those skills now help her in her other job in the service industry as well.

“Working on the potter’s wheel is the hardest part of the process. First, you have to centre the clay on the wheel. For beginners, that’s extremely difficult, and many people give up at that stage. Over time, your hands learn to feel the clay and the movement of the wheel so well that lifting and shaping the clay becomes smooth. The clay mustn’t bend or become too thin, otherwise it will collapse. I’ve broken many pieces that I didn’t like, and I’ve ruined many others because of my own mistakes. But there’s no other way to learn. You need patience and you have to keep trying again and again until you succeed,” Mariam says.

Mariam and her colleagues. Photo: JAMnews

Several years after she first learned to work with clay, the studio where she trained noticed her progress and invited her to become an instructor.

Mariam says she enjoys teaching both children and adults. She has also noticed that many people now come to the studio not because they want to learn ceramics, but because they are looking for a form of therapy.

“We live in a constant state of pressure, stress and rushing from one thing to the next. People are looking for a place where they can switch off from everyday worries and their phones, spend some time alone and gather their thoughts. This is one of the best places to do that. Couples come here to grow closer and get to know each other better. As they work with clay, people try to ease their anxiety and manage their emotions. That’s what most of them come here for.”

Mariam at work. Photo: JAMnews

She believes pottery goes beyond art and enters the realm of deeper emotions when qualified psychologists become part of the process.

Art therapy is not about creating beautiful works of art

Psychologist and art therapist Karina Khachatryan explains how art therapy differs from traditional psychotherapy. She says it provides a safe space where people can express pain, anxiety and fear not through words, but through colours, shapes, materials and symbols.

“Unlike traditional psychotherapy, which relies solely on conversation, art therapy introduces a third element. That element is the artwork itself, which becomes a kind of mediator between the therapist and the client. People often struggle to put their pain or anxiety into words. Sometimes those feelings lie so deep within the psyche that words simply are not enough. This is where artistic materials such as paper, paint, clay and sand come in. They become a bridge that allows people to bring their inner experiences into the outside world, giving them a safe way to engage with even their most difficult emotions.”

The Terracotta art studio. Photo: JAMnews

According to the art therapist, these are not ordinary painting or pottery classes. Participants do not need any artistic skills.

No one teaches painting or sculpting techniques, or how to use a brush or a carving tool. The aim of art therapy is not to create beautiful works of art, but to express emotions and personal struggles through the creative process.

“The creative process becomes therapeutic when it takes place in a professional art therapy setting and focuses on a clearly defined psychological issue that the client and the art therapist work through together. The art therapist creates a sense of emotional safety, guides the client through the process, and later helps them put into words and make sense of what they have created.

The art therapist closely observes the entire process. Do they approach the paper or clay with confidence, or with anxiety and hesitation? Every detail matters: how they choose colours, how tightly they hold a pencil, how they touch the clay, whether their movements are abrupt or gentle. Even their reaction to ‘mistakes’, such as torn paper or spilled paint, can reveal a great deal. The finished piece is the result of that process. It offers a safe representation of the client’s inner world. Together, we examine it and try to understand how it connects to their life,” Karina Khachatryan explains.

However, she says the creative process alone cannot restore mental well-being. Working with clay can become one way for people to listen to themselves and better understand who they are. But in most cases, recovering mental health also requires support from a psychologist or psychiatrist.

“People need to recognise they have a problem and want to work through it with a psychologist”

Psychologist Armen Hovhannisyan says he has encountered many different cases in his practice. He believes the best starting point is when people themselves realise they need help. According to him, unexpected life events often prompt people to seek psychological support because they overwhelm their ability to cope. At such moments, many feel they are facing insurmountable problems.

“Sometimes people don’t realise they need a psychologist. Their parents or friends recognise it and encourage them to seek therapy. But if they don’t trust the process, resist it or remain sceptical about our work, there won’t be any results. People need to recognise they have a problem and genuinely want to work through it with a psychologist. Usually, they first try to solve the problem on their own. They seek professional help only when they realise they can’t cope by themselves,” he says.

Hovhannisyan explains that psychologists study mental processes, behaviour, emotions and the way people perceive the world. Psychiatrists, meanwhile, diagnose and treat mental disorders and prescribe medication when necessary.

He says psychologists and psychiatrists sometimes work with the same patient at the same time. In such cases, they consult each other and share information with the patient’s consent.

When someone is experiencing severe depression or other serious mental health conditions, psychological counselling alone is not enough, he says. A psychiatrist then decides whether medication is needed. Hovhannisyan adds that cooperation between psychologists and psychiatrists often produces better outcomes.

He also notes that psychology and psychotherapy have become increasingly popular, yet many people still struggle to understand how they differ from simply talking to a neighbour or a close friend.

“People close to us cannot always remain impartial. They tend to see events from our perspective. A psychologist, by contrast, maintains professional neutrality and helps people view a situation from different angles.

Looking after mental health is a difficult but important part of life. One art therapy session or one conversation with a psychologist will not solve every problem. It requires daily self-care. Making pottery or seeking professional help are simply different paths towards the same goal: living a more mindful and balanced life.”

Pottery as a form of art therapy

World.title: Abkhazia debates whether MPs should be required to speak Abkhaz as president struggles to win support
World.content:
Abkhazia‘s parliament has rejected a proposal by President Badra Gunba to exempt some parliamentary candidates from the requirement to speak the Abkhaz language.

For now, Gunba’s proposal to introduce different implementation dates for the language requirement has failed to secure the backing of the parliamentary committee on state and legal policy. The final decision, however, will be made by the full parliament.

The language issue has proved so sensitive that the parliamentary committee meeting was held behind closed doors, despite parliamentary rules requiring it to be open to the media. After the meeting, parliament’s press service issued only a brief statement saying the committee had declined to recommend the bill for approval at its first reading.

President Badra Gunba has proposed delaying the implementation of the law requiring parliamentary candidates to speak Abkhaz for candidates who are not ethnic Abkhaz.

The requirement for parliamentary candidates to be proficient in Abkhaz was adopted in 2021 and is due to come into force on 1 January 2027. Gunba, however, wants to postpone its application for candidates of other ethnic backgrounds until 2032.

With the next parliamentary elections approaching, the issue is becoming increasingly pressing.

The proposal to introduce different language requirements has triggered strong criticism in Abkhazia.

“Attempts to amend, reinterpret or postpone the deadlines, let alone divide the citizens of the Republic of Abkhazia along ethnic lines in the application of a constitutional law, are not only unfounded and unjustified but also unconstitutional,” the public organisation People’s Force said in a statement.

Former parliament speaker Valery Kvarchia has also appealed directly to President Badra Gunba, urging him to withdraw the bill.

“We must not remain captive to the degrading part of our society that wraps anti-Abkhaz and unconstitutional initiatives in attractive packaging. Among them are people who hope to run for president, parliament or ministerial posts, believing that, as ‘internationalists’, they will gain the support of the non-Abkhaz section of the population,” Kvarchia said.

Toponyms, terminology, views and opinions expressed by the author are theirs alone and do not necessarily reflect the views and opinions of JAMnews or any employees thereof. JAMnews reserves the right to delete comments it considers to be offensive, inflammatory, threatening or otherwise unacceptable.

Should Abkhazia’s MPs be required to speak Abkhaz?

World.title: India's 'cockroach' movement supporters caned by police
World.content:
Supporters of India's youth-led "cockroach" movement have been caned by police as they sought to march on the nation's parliament, despite authorities denying permission for the protest.

Thousands of protesters gathered in New Delhi on Monday to march ‌and demand the resignation of the country's education minister as part of the Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) movement.

Protesters ran for cover as police in blue riot gear charged at them near the Jantar Mantar protest site, an AFP journalist reported.

The two-month-old CJP movement and the planned protest is seen as the biggest public challenge to Prime Minister Narendra Modi in his third term in office, garnering millions of supporters on social media and mobilising support on the ground as well.

The movement has been galvanised since police forcibly moved hunger-striking activist Sonam Wangchuk to hospital on Saturday, with thousands of supporters arriving at the protest site through the night for a march on the opening day of parliament's monsoon ⁠session.

Scores of police and paramilitary security personnel were deployed at the heavily-barricaded site, threatening a stand-off a few kilometres from parliament if the protesters sought to go ahead with their march.

"Quit, quit," the protesters chanted.

People move barricades from a protest site ahead of Monday's march by supporters of India's Cockroach Janta Party. (Reuters: Anushree Fadnavis)

"Dharmendra Pradhan quit", "Narendra Modi quit" they chanted in Hindi, referring to the education minister as well as the prime minister.

Two members of the CJP were on their way to meet a senior minister in the prime minister's cabinet, chief party spokesperson Saurav Das said in a post on X on Monday.

"The government had reached out for talks in the morning. Our demands are clear. The youth has gathered in huge numbers," Mr Das said.

The movement began after national medical school entrance test papers were leaked in May, affecting more than 2 million students as it forced them to sit the test a second time.

"All these leaders in power are illiterate and I am here to protest because we do not want question papers to leak," said Adi Nathan, a 21-year-old student from Meerut city.

Mohammed Tabrez, a 22-year-old student preparing for competitive examinations that allow student admissions into professional courses or jobs, said he had come from Amroha in Uttar Pradesh.

"We want this corruption to end," he said.

"We want all the fraud in paper leaks, in competitive examinations, to end, and this is the reason I have come here."

Activist sets terms to end his fast

The CJP initially drew support largely online, amassing 22 million followers on Instagram within days before broadening its appeal and drawing the support of some opposition parties.

CJP founder Abhijeet Dipke and his supporters began a sit-in last month seeking the resignation of Mr Pradhan.

Supporters of the CJP chant slogans and wave their mobile phones with their flashlights. (Reuters: Anushree Fadnavis )

On June 28 they were joined by Mr Wangchuk, ⁠who launched an indefinite hunger strike at the site.

In a handwritten note from hospital posted on his X account on Monday, Mr Wangchuk said he would end his fast if the government takes accountability for the paper leaks and recent failures in the education system, or if CJP protesters are allowed to reach parliament and lawmakers assure them that ⁠the issues would be taken up in the chambers.

He said he would also end the fast if lawmakers and leaders of various parties meet him in hospital and give him the same assurances since his health does not allow him to march on parliament.

The rise of the CJP reflects frustration among young ⁠Indians over issues like high youth unemployment and frequent examination paper leaks, analysts say.

Reuters/AFP

World.title: Former soldier avoids jail for trafficking cocaine in Australian Army
World.content:
A former army rifleman who purchased 45 grams of cocaine to traffic to fellow Australian Defence Force (ADF) soldiers has been spared jail.

Brett McMaster, 24, appeared in the Supreme Court of Queensland in Townsville on Monday and pleaded guilty to trafficking cocaine in 2024.

McMaster served in the Australian Army's Townsville-based armoured infantry battalion, 3RAR, as a rifleman and field medic.

The court heard that during his service he purchased 45 grams of cocaine over six weeks from fellow soldier Jack Alex Cullen.

Jack Alex Cullen, 25, was jailed for trafficking cocaine in May. (ABC News: Baz Ruddick)

Cullen was jailed in May after pleading guilty to trafficking large quantities of cocaine whilst serving as an army infantry soldier.

The Supreme Court heard McMaster paid Cullen in cash, and at times placed the payments in Cullen's army backpack at Lavarack Barracks in Townsville.

Justice Christopher Johnstone KC, who has been deployed in active service for the Royal Australian Air Force, called McMaster's conduct "offensive".

"You offended whilst you had the honour and the privilege of being a member of the Australian Defence Force," he said.

" An honour, a privilege and a trust which you abused grossly. "

Justice Christopher Johnstone KC called the conduct by McMaster "offensive". (ABC News: Lily Nothling)

The court heard that McMaster was discharged from the army due to his failure of a drug test in 2024, which coincided with him being charged.

McMaster's barrister, Ross Malcomson, provided a psychiatrist report which stated the former soldier self-medicated mental health challenges with cocaine.

Justice Johnstone questioned why the former rifleman texted supplier Cullen stating he was "slowly getting more blokes onto my stuff".

"That statement is a little at odds with the submissions that have been made about your psychological wellbeing," he said.

Justice Johnstone accepted submissions from prosecutors that McMaster had ambitions to grow his business before he was caught.

After pleading guilty to a total of two charges, McMaster was sentenced to a four-year prison term that will be suspended for five years so long as he does not reoffend.

He was ordered to pay a $10,000 fine over 12 months for possessing a phone used for drug trafficking.

He must repay the Commonwealth $36,000 from a $50,000 retention bonus he received from the ADF.

He will continue to receive payments from the Department of Veterans Affairs due to injuries sustained in the army.

World.title: LGBT club's lease at old Sydney church terminated due to 'offensive trade'
World.content:
The owners of a deconsecrated church in Sydney's CBD have terminated the lease of an LGBTQIA+ pop-up club, claiming the venue had been used for "offensive trade".

Organisers of Divine Playhouse were served with a breach notice earlier this month, in the wake of complaints from some members of the Christian community.

On Monday, organisers confirmed they had been told to vacate the premises on Kent Street within three days.

In a statement, Divine Playhouse and Heaps Gay founder Kat Dopper said she was "devastated".

"Divine Playhouse was created as a critical new cultural home for diverse artists and communities from all over Sydney and New South Wales," she said.

"It's sitting empty — no artists, no audiences, the joy and community we built in that room, silenced."

Ms Dopper says she is devastated by the decision. (Supplied: Anna Hay)

Protests at opening night

The 158-year-old church building was deconsecrated in 1932 and has operated as a theatre for the past 70 years.

The venue was then leased by developer Revelop to Heaps Gay, a nightlife group that hosts parties and other events for Sydney's LGBTQIA+ community and allies.

But its new tenants faced backlash from some Christian groups, who claimed their choice of venue "mocks religious faith".

Earlier this month, about 70 protesters gathered outside Divine Playhouse to rally against its opening night.

Lawyers for the building's owners then issued a breach notice to Heaps Gay Events, which holds the lease for the venue.

The notice, seen by the ABC, said the tenants had carried on an "offensive" trade that had caused "grievance and disturbance to owners of adjoining properties and to the general public".

The church was deconsecrated in 1932. (ABC News: Floss Adams)

The lawyers also noted the "significant protest and public criticism" directed at the venue.

It prompted Divine Playhouse to close and all events at the venue to be cancelled.

The ABC has contacted Revelop for comment.

Heaps Gay said it had now been officially asked to leave.

"The termination came with no conversation and no good-faith engagement — just legal letters and a deadline to strip out months of work," the statement read.

The ABC understands Heaps Gay is considering a legal challenge against the owners.

"We believe this termination was unlawful and unjust," Ms Dopper said.

"If a landlord's personal beliefs can shut down an arts venue, no stage in this country is safe. Who decides what art is acceptable? Right now, the answer is whoever owns the building.

"If we walk away, they'll believe that intimidation works, and they'll come back, again and again, for every other group they don't agree with."

Divine Playhouse will hold a sing-in rally in Sydney's CBD this weekend, follwing the termination.

A fundraiser is also being organised, featuring artists whose performances or events at the location had been cancelled.

Divine Playhouse said it was calling on developers, landowners and private space owners with "something unique" to come forward, as it searches for a new location.

World.title: Man found guilty of murdering 2yo boy found with brain injury
World.content:
A 40-year-old man has been found guilty of murdering a two-year-old boy on the New South Wales Mid North Coast in 2022.

Warning: This story contains details of child abuse that some readers might find distressing.

The 40-year-old, who cannot be named for legal reasons, was standing trial in the New South Wales Supreme Court accused of murdering the child at a home in Coffs Harbour.

After hearing four weeks of evidence, the jury returned a guilty verdict on Monday after deliberating for four days.

The offender, who had been out on bail, was taken into custody.

During the trial, the jury heard that on May 23, 2022, the toddler's mother tried to wake him at the home, but he did not respond.

He was flown to John Hunter Hospital in Newcastle, where he died of a catastrophic brain injury two days later.

The two-year-old was found to have a fractured pelvis, rib and bruising on his body, including his penis.

The trial heard the man was in a relationship and living with the child's mother at the time of the baby's death.

During the trial, the jury heard evidence that the accused would discipline the child by locking him in a dark garage with the lights off, putting him in the bath and by taking away his mattress and pillow.

The perpetrator spent 10 months in prison, and was given bail on August 28, 2025.

During the trial, the jury heard from a number of experts who detailed the chances of the baby sustaining the injuries from a head banging episode or a fall down the stairs the afternoon before.

Paediatric endocrinologist Margaret Zacharin gave evidence earlier this month stating her professional opinion was that the injuries were inflicted.

Defence barrister David Price said no-one had ever admitted to inflicting an assault on the young boy as it was a circumstantial case.

Justice Philip Boulten told the court the defence requested the offender remain on bail so that he could do a few things around the house before he was put into custody.

"Mr Price says it'd be good to have a day or so to get his house in order," Judge Boulten said.

Judge Boulten told the court the defence also requested he remain on bail due to his medical conditions.

"He has issues that relate to episodic changes of consciousness or fits. This has been pointed out by his counsel," Judge Boulten said.

"Effectively the corrective services are going to have to find a way to deal with him."

Justice Boulten told the court the risk of the offender not appearing in court on the next occasion was high.

" In the wake of a guilty verdict to murder, the prospects of not appearing are heightened. The risk of flight even overnight are real. "

"I do not find this an exceptional or special case or that there are special circumstances that justify the granting of bail," Judge Boulten said.

The man has been refused bail and will be sentenced on October 30.

World.title: Live: Crows, Darcy Fogarty challenge three-match striking ban at tribunal
World.content:
The Crows challenge Darcy Fogarty's three-match striking ban at the AFL Tribunal, as they try to avoid losing a key forward for vital games in the lead-up to finals.

Fogarty was charged after his high hit on Sydney's Harry Cunningham in the second quarter of Adelaide's game with the Swans at the SCG.

Cunningham was ruled out of the game with concussion and will miss this week's match against cross-town rivals GWS.

Follow all the proceedings in our live blog.

World.title: SA's largest electorate to be renamed in honour of Aboriginal leader
World.content:
WARNING: Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander readers are warned that this story includes the name and image of an Indigenous person who has died.

South Australia's largest federal electorate will be renamed in honour of Aboriginal leader Dr Lowitja O'Donoghue, despite opposition from the local Liberal MP.

The Australian Electoral Commission (AEC) confirmed on Monday that the regional seat of Grey, named after former SA governor Sir George Grey, would now be called O'Donoghue.

The electorate covers more than 92 per cent of the state and has been named Grey since it was created in 1903. It is currently held by Liberal MP Tom Venning.

Dr Lowitja O'Donoghue in a photograph commemorating her 90th birthday. (Supplied: Lowitja Institute)

Dr O'Donoghue was the first Aboriginal person to train as a nurse at the Royal Adelaide Hospital and had a celebrated career in the public service, which included being a senior member of the team that negotiated Australia's historic Native Title legislation in 1993.

She passed away in February 2024, aged 91.

Sir Grey was a Portuguese-born colonial explorer, soldier and administrator who governed the near-bankrupt colony of South Australia into prosperity from 1841 to 1845 before moving to govern the British colony in New Zealand.

Sir George Grey governed the state for four years. (Supplied: National Library of New Zealand)

The AEC said Dr O'Donoghue's connection to the APY Lands and her achievements provided "strong reasoning" to rename the seat in her honour.

The O'Donoghue family this morning welcomed the name change.

"Dr Lowitja O'Donoghue was born, raised, worked, and lived within the electorate for much of her life, and over many decades made substantial contributions to the region across health, education, and social justice rights," the family said in a statement released by the Lowitja O'Donoghue Foundation.

"She always considered it to be her home, no matter where her career path took her."

'We can honour her in other ways', Liberal MP says

The renaming of Grey was the most controversial element of the AEC's redistribution of South Australian federal electorates.

After floating it in March, the AEC said it received 310 submissions about the renaming: 75 in support and 235 against.

Push to rename SA electorate Sir George Grey was the former governor of South Australia and is remembered as a "bundle of contradictions" in both Australia and New Zealand.

The AEC said it considered the arguments in support of renaming the electorate to be "well detailed, informative, convincing and ultimately persuasive".

"This contrasted with most of the submissions objecting to the renaming of the electorate," the AEC said.

"Amongst other things, the arguments for renaming the electorate O'Donoghue noted Dr O'Donoghue's significant contribution to communities, including within the electoral boundaries of Grey, the State of South Australia, and Australia as a whole.

" They provided strong and convincing reasons to rename the electorate in her honour. "

Tom Venning says the AEC has not necessarily listened to the people of Grey. (ABC News: Olivia Mason)

Liberal MP Tom Venning said a majority of his constituents wanted Grey's name to remain.

He accused the AEC of "not necessarily listening to the people of Grey".

"He's a founding father of this state and country people are used to that name," he said.

"The submission from the AEC this morning said that a majority of submitters did not want the name changed, and I think it's disappointing that that has occurred," he said.

"I have great respect for Dr Lowitja O'Donoghue. She's a fantastic Indigenous woman who did fantastic things, and I think we can honour her in other ways".

Rebranding is costly

Mr Venning said renaming a state electorate — or a future new SA federal seat — were among the other ways to honour Dr O'Donoghue.

He said rebranding his electorate office and other materials would now cost "tens of thousands" of dollars.

Tom Venning says a majority of his constituents wanted Grey's name to remain.

"Only at the start of this year was my third electorate office rebadged with the 'Grey, Tom Venning' branding, so that will all need to be changed as well," he said, adding that the cost of rebranding one of his four electorate offices was around $3,500.

" All the letterheads, all of the online components of our websites where Grey is mentioned — there will be significant cost. "

Election analyst Ben Raue, founder of elections blog The Tally Room, said the Grey renaming was part of a broader shift from the AEC.

"The AEC for a while now has been undergoing a bit of a practice of reconsidering the names of people who don't have much of a connection to Australia," he said.

"This is a bit of a continuation of more seats named after women, seats named after Indigenous people and getting rid of some of these names of people in the early 19th century who didn't stick around long in Australia."

Ben Raue says O'Donoghue is "probably" the most likely SA seat to fall to One Nation. (Supplied)

Mr Raue highlighted a similar AEC proposal to rename the Tasmanian seat of Franklin to Tongerlongeter, after an Aboriginal resistance warrior.

Only minor changes to SA electoral map

The Grey name change was part of the AEC's redistribution of South Australian seats ahead of the next federal election, which has only resulted in minor changes to the electoral map.

Just 24,000 people are shifting electorates, according to the AEC: less than 2 per cent of the enrolled population.

The boundaries of O'Donoghue are unchanged, with a proposal to shift the new Riverlea housing development from the Labor seat of Spence into O'Donoghue abandoned.

The Federal Electorate of Grey as at August 30, 2017. (Supplied: Australian Electoral Commission.)

Mr Raue said O'Donoghue was "probably" the most likely SA seat to fall to One Nation.

He highlighted that it was the SA seat where One Nation did best at the 2025 federal election.

The 2026 state election also saw One Nation win two seats that overlap with O'Donoghue: the Yorke Peninsula electorate of Narungga and Mid North seat of Ngadjuri.

Independent MP Rebekha Sharkie's seat of Mayo has lost the City of Mitcham to neighbouring Boothby, held by Labor MP Louise Miller-Frost, and Callington and Kanmantoo to Barker, held by Liberal MP Tony Pasin.

"There's no seats that have been abolished, there's no seats where the MP isn't going to be in a position to hold the seat after the next election, and the changes in the margin are all pretty minor," Mr Raue said.

In the northern suburbs, Labor MP Tony Zappia's seat of Makin will gain part of the City of Salisbury from neighbouring Spence, held by fellow Labor MP Matt Burnell.

Spence and Makin are considered Labor's two most vulnerable seats to One Nation in SA, after the right-wing party recorded significant swings in the northern suburbs at the March state election.

One senior Labor source suggested the Makin-Spence redistribution could consolidate One Nation's challenge in Spence, but overall it had a "minimal effect".

World.title: 'Like The Castle': Restaurant owners launch petition against land grab
World.content:
An Adelaide Hills restaurant owner has launched a petition against the state government's plan to build a $61.1 million school at the site — and has likened his experience over the past week to the Australian film The Castle.

The South Australian government last week announced a preschool and primary school would be built on a 5.5-hectare parcel of land in Mount Barker's south-east, including on the site of the Thai restaurant.

The decision shocked Aston Hills Mount Barker developers Lanser, who said they had been working on a master plan for more than 16 years — and that the acquisition would mean the loss of up to 150 new homes, trees, a new reserve and the Thai restaurant, Wok the Duck.

The Thai restaurant owners took to social media to express their dismay, explaining they had sold their family home to open the business and were just one year into a nine-year lease.

Their video has since been viewed more than 400,000 times on Facebook and co-owner David Keir said they had received support from around the world.

Wok the Duck owner David Keir says they sold their family home to make the investment. (ABC News: Brant Cumming)

"The success and the support is measured in people coming in the shop," Mr Keir told 891 ABC Adelaide.

"We have had thousands, and I mean thousands, come in over the weekend — all sorts of people from everywhere.

"We're actually getting phone calls from people in the UK wanting petitions so it's not only just people in the community in the Adelaide Hills, it's people everywhere.

" The word has spread and people don't like seeing what's happening. "

On Saturday, the restaurant owners launched a petition imploring the SA government to pause the proposed acquisition and to consider an alternative location.

"They said they've looked at 16 sites … I'd like them to let us know the 16 sites," Mr Keir said.

"It's actually like the Castle. To me, something doesn't smell right."

Mr Keir said he would meet with the government tomorrow.

Calls for government to consider other options

Independent MP Matt Schultz told 891 ABC Adelaide he had signed the petition and had requested a meeting with the education minister.

"I've written to the minister seeking a meeting so I can get a better understanding of what other sites had been looked at and why this one was preferred over those," he said.

" I would hope that we could find a way to get a win-win solution by having the school built but also seeing a much-loved family-owned community business be able to stay where it is. "

Independent MP Matt Schultz told ABC 891 he has signed the petition. (Facebook: Matt Schultz - Member for Kavel)

Mr Schultz said Mr Keir had prepared meals for the community during the 2019 bushfires, "helped out with meals during COVID" and supported the Uniting Church with Hungry No More.

"This isn't just a cafe or a restaurant sitting on a plot of land, they’ve done a great job of supporting community over the years," Mr Schultz said.

" These are people that are contributing back to our community and they need to be supported. "

Minister for Housing and Urban Development Nick Champion told 891 ABC Adelaide the issues surrounding planning in Mount Barker were well known.

"We’ll obviously work with this much-loved local restaurant," he said.

"As I understand it, the education department are going to meet with the restaurant, have a full-time person dedicated to their relocation and to assist in that."

SA housing minister Nick Champion says the department will work with the restaurant to help them relocate. (ABC News: Briana Fiore)

Education Minister Lucy Hood said 16 other sites were evaluated but had not been chosen "for various reasons".

"This is about making decisions in the best long-term interest of the whole Mount Barker community," she said.

Ms Hood said the department would meet with Mr Keir to provide information about how the site was selected and the acquisition process.

Mr Keir said he did not plan to relocate.

"I'm more than happy to talk to them about relocating the school because it's an absolutely ridiculous space they've chosen," he said.

" They haven't come and spoken to us, they haven't consulted us, they have not comprehended that it's a much-loved restaurant in the Adelaide Hills. "

World.title: Telehealth ban still standing between dying patients and their doctors
World.content:
It's a crisp and bright Canberra autumn day. I am sitting outside at the Queen's Terrace Cafe in Parliament House with local family, Jason and Anthea Smith, and their adult children, Georgia and Brae.

They are here in support of the campaign of Go Gentle, an organisation I founded in 2016, to amend a federal law which threatens doctors with a $300,000 fine and a criminal record if they use electronic communications, such as the internet or phone, to discuss matters relating to voluntary assisted dying (VAD).

Even though Telehealth is now an established part of healthcare, and despite calls for change from state health ministers and attorneys-general (along with the Australian Medical Association), the federal government will not budge. The prohibition stands.

With it, the suffering of dying people, forced to travel hundreds, sometimes thousands, of painful kilometres to see a doctor face to face, not once, but multiple times, in order to access their legal right to VAD. Or, alternatively, endure an agonising and fearful wait, hoping a doctor can get to them.

Telehealth ban hits remote communities hardest

Jason is here as a living example of what this ban means. Only he doesn't live thousands, or even hundreds, of kilometres from Parliament House. He lives 20km away, a 25-minute drive at most. But to get here today, took him, and the family, and his full-time-carer, three hours.

Jason and Anthea Smith with their adult children, campaigning with Go Gentle Australia for VAD law reform. (Supplied: Go Gentle Australia/Paul Chapman)

Jason has Motor Neurone Disease. The "Beast", as it's known by some. It's the same disease which took down AFL footballer Neale Daniher and which NRL player Jai Arrow has recently being been diagnosed with. Like those two men, Jason was young — just 39 – fit and strong, when he was diagnosed in 2017.

Looking at photos from this time, I see a large man, bearded and smiling with his youngest, Georgia. Perhaps not surprising, her description of him is as "a big teddy bear".

But, today, sitting in the Canberra sunshine, that Jason is scarcely recognisable. MND attacks nerve cells and causes muscles to waste away. It has no known cure and most people do not survive its ravages beyond five years.

To the astonishment of his doctors, Jason has lived with his MND for eight years. He's still at home, and determined to keep going. But the cost is clear to see.

Still a big man, Jason is now difficult to distinguish from the electric wheelchair that carries him everywhere, and which holds his medical equipment, including his NIV (Non-Invasive Ventilation) mask, which helps him breathe.

Rugged up in blanket and beanie by his teenage sweetheart Anthea, he can do nothing for himself, other than communicate with difficulty through long bouts of racking coughs. Every minute requires monitoring and assistance.

If this is how hard it is for someone who lives 20km away,' I thought, 'what must it be like for someone forced to travel hundreds? Thousands?'

As Jason's muscles continue to die, and swallowing becomes more difficult, one of his greatest fears is he will choke to death.

Loading...

That's why, on the very morning VAD became legal in the ACT last year, he became the first person to apply for it.

He's not alone. It's a remarkable fact that one third of Australians who've died of MND over the last year have made the same choice.

That choice not to suffer is of such importance. It doesn't remove the harsh inevitability, or sadness, of dying. But, by offering people control, it removes the fear of being forced to go through — and forcing your family to witness — the very worst.

The choice the church would deny

There has been no stauncher, or more powerful, opponent of VAD in Australia than the Catholic Church, and its many representatives in the medical profession.

As the fight for its legalisation progressed around Australia (it is now legal everywhere but the NT) they argued that VAD wasn't necessary because doctors had powerful drugs they could deploy at the end of life so people would not die in pain.

It was both true, and a clever sleight of hand. First, because it left all the power in the hands of the treating doctor, and his or her personal beliefs. But also because pain is just one of many things which can degrade a dying person's capacity to endure — let alone enjoy — their life.

When your systems start to collapse, as they had with Jason; when your dignity is stripped away; when there is no hope of something better on the path ahead, only fear and distress (yours, and that of the people who love you), the word to describe this is not 'pain'. It's 'suffering'.

There is no drug, however powerful, that can take suffering away.

Darwin's Catholic Bishop Charles Gauci says the focus should be on care, not on ending life early. (ABC News: Dane Hirst)

Yet still the church argues, as it is now in the Northern Territory, its last frontier in the fight against VAD, that, rather than being given control of their own destiny, 'more must be done' to help people who are medically helpless. People like Jason.

"I'd like to see what we can do to help people in the dying process so they will not necessarily need to take their own life," says Darwin's Catholic Bishop, Charles Gauci.

What Bishop Gauci isn't saying is that the Vatican describes VAD as an "intrinsically evil act … that no end can justify". No matter your suffering, or how untreatable it may be, it is not up to you to take control. Only God will decide.

And if this means that you have no choice but to endure suffering you do not wish to endure? Well, there's virtue in that. As Sydney's Catholic Archbishop, the Reverend Anthony Fisher told the ABC in 2011:

"The thought is, for Christians, by uniting that suffering with the suffering of Christ, that it's part of building up their own virtue, their own contribution to the world. That it's not completely meaningless."

This is more than just a philosophical thought. Because the Catholic Church is also, by some margin, Australia's largest non-governmental healthcare provider.

Even when the hospitals it runs are funded by public money, it insists its values must prevail. In May, Queensland opened its first new public hospital since 2013, a 186-bed facility south-west of Brisbane, at a cost (including its first four years of operation) to the taxpayer of just over $1billion.

It will be run by Mater Health, part of Catholic Healthcare, which refuses to offer abortion, contraception, or VAD care at the hospital. As the chief executive explains: "We have always been a Catholic healthcare provider… There are alternative hospitals around where patients can access those services."

Jason Smith was the first person to apply for voluntary assisted dying the day it became legal in the ACT. (Compass: Mary Tran)

Had Jason no choice but to spend his last days in a faith-based hospital, he would either have been denied his right to VAD, or been forced to travel, at his most unwell and vulnerable, to another hospital which did support VAD, however far away that may be.

On his own terms

Fortunately, like many who choose VAD, Jason was able to die at home, surrounded by his family and immersed in love. It's a choice the Catholic Church would have denied him. He left on his own terms in June (even watching his favourite movie, 'Spaceballs', while waiting for the VAD team to arrive). He left behind a family, grieving, but also deeply grateful for the peaceful, dignified manner of Jason's passing.

Anthea used one word to describe it: "Beautiful."

It's a moment the NT Parliament should keep in mind when it votes on VAD later this year.

Watch Dying On My Own Terms now on iview.

World.title: Israel blasts Labor’s ‘one-sided’ policy platform as Palestinian advocates push further
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Israel blasts Labor’s ‘one-sided’ policy platform as Palestinian advocates push further Matthew Knott July 20, 2026 — 6:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Israel is seeking to water down criticism of the Jewish state in Labor’s policy platform, which is set to call out settler violence in the West Bank, condemn a controversial new death penalty law and back two international courts considering genocide and war crimes charges against Israel. As Palestinian advocates call for Labor to go further by banning defence exports to Israel and imposing sweeping sanctions, the Israeli embassy in Canberra argued Labor’s draft national platform is one-sided against Israel while going easy on Hamas and other Palestinian factions for failing to advance the peace process. Israel’s embassy, led by ambassador Hillel Newman, is pushing Labor to change its policy platform. Alex Ellinghausen With Prime Minister Anthony Albanese seeking to project party unity under his leadership, Labor’s three-day national conference in Adelaide is unlikely to feature lively debates on contentious issues such as AUKUS after senior ministers spent months settling arguments behind the scenes to avoid public brawls on the conference floor. But debate could flare up over the Middle East, with the draft policy platform going into more detail on the Israeli-Palestinian dispute than past manifestos and pro-Palestinian activists on the march after Albanese last year decided to recognise Palestinian statehood.



The draft platform does not contain accusations of genocide over the way Israel fought the war in Gaza or call for restrictions on arms sales to Israel, but party activists are pushing behind the scenes to make it tougher. Related Article Exclusive

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Troubling’: Top Australian Jewish groups denounce Israel’s new death penalty “Labor opposes the annexation of Palestinian territory and wants Israel to bring its illegal settlement activity and the occupation to an end, to see security for Palestine, for Israel and for the region,” the draft platform states. “Labor urges the government to prevent any support being given to illegal settlement activity or extremist settler violence, and to implement further action and sanctions as necessary.” It also condemns a law passed by the Israeli parliament in March which expands the use of the death penalty for terror offences in the occupied West Bank and “all other discriminatory laws which target Palestinians”.



The Israeli embassy issued a statement on Monday saying it “respectfully submits that several elements of the draft national platform risk placing responsibility for the conflict on one party while giving insufficient attention to the decisions, conduct and continuing obligations of the Palestinian leadership and terrorist organisations such as Hamas”. The embassy noted that the “policy motions are still in draft form, and will continue to engage constructively with the Australian Labor Party through the usual diplomatic channels”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in New York last year, when he officially recognised Palestine at the United Nations. Dominic Lorrimer The draft platform also states: “Labor believes in international law and will defend it. “Labor supports the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court and compliance with their binding decisions.”



The International Court of Justice is considering a genocide case brought against Israel over its conduct in the war in Gaza, while the International Criminal Court is considering war crimes allegations against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The draft platform also says Labor “unreservedly condemns terrorism and violent extremism, including as perpetrated by Hamas and other extremists”. The Israeli embassy said in its statement: “The reality is that the moment Palestinians recognise the existence of the State of Israel and undergo significant reform, the path to peace will be paved. “That outcome cannot be achieved by pressuring Israel.” The embassy claimed that settler violence, which has surged in the West Bank over recent years, is a “reprehensible but marginal phenomenon” that receives disproportionate international attention.



“The government of Israel and the settler movement itself condemns it, and security forces work to apprehend these forms of illegal behaviour,” the statement said. The United Nations said in June that there had been an average of six settler attacks a day this year on Palestinians causing casualties or property damage – the highest on record. Related Article Exclusive

Middle East at war ‘I’m under siege’: The families fighting for their homes on the West Bank The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network is urging Labor to end Australian defence exports and military co-operation with countries that risk contributing to war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. The group is also calling for an end to Australian trade and investment with Jewish settlements in the West Bank and for the Future Fund to scrap all investments linked to the settlement enterprise.



“Australia must reckon with the obligations that flow from its recognition of Palestine and the Conference must draw a red line on genocide and Australian complicity,” APAN president Nasser Mashni said. He said Australia must comply with a 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that found Israel’s presence in the occupied Palestinian territories was unlawful and Israeli settlements were illegal. “Recognition of Palestine cannot remain symbolic. Australia must impose wide-ranging and wholesale sanctions on the Israeli regime and anyone or any entity associated with the settlement enterprise,” he said. Albanese’s recognition of Palestinian statehood last September at the United Nations General Assembly fulfilled a pledge embedded in Labor’s policy platform in 2018. World.title: Harness racing bosses sue News Corp over drug scandal articles
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesDefamation Harness racing bosses sue News Corp over drug scandal articles Kishor Napier-Raman July 20, 2026 — 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two top harness racing officials say they were exposed to hatred, ridicule and contempt by a series of articles in News Corp mastheads accusing them of presiding over a doping crisis. Harness Racing NSW chief executive Peter Buckman and the sport’s chief integrity officer, Michael Prentice, commenced defamation proceedings in the Federal Court last month after articles accusing them of failing to warn trainers that a popular animal medication had become contaminated with levamisole, a deworming drug that is prohibited in equestrian sports because it acts as a powerful stimulant. Two top harness racing officials are suing News Corp over a series of articles about a drug scandal. None of those pictured are involved in the saga. Katherine Griffiths As a result of the contamination, several trainers were banned from participating in the sport, under its strict doping regime. Buckman and Prentice claim the articles published in The Daily Telegraph, The Australian and Code Sports by journalist Julian Linden defamed them by holding the pair responsible for HRNSW failing to warn participants about the potential contamination, and accused them of contributing to an emerging drug scandal in the sport.



The pair claim Linden’s reporting depicted them as “callously indifferent to the lives and livelihoods of harness racing trainers”, including former firefighter Scott Wade, who had been disqualified for life but maintains his innocence. Related Article Defamation ‘A fair degree of heat’: Peter V’landys claims early win in fiery defamation battle “Both applicants have been exposed to hatred, ridicule and contempt, and have been gravely injured in their personal and professional reputations, and have suffered and will continue to suffer hurt, distress and embarrassment,” a statement of claim filed by the pair said. Buckman and Prentice are seeking aggravated damages and an injunction restraining further publication of the articles. In response, News Corp’s lawyers say the articles are substantially true, and that they are protected by a public interest defence. Before Linden’s articles were published, 12 trainers had been suspended or disqualified from the sport after their samples were contaminated with levamisole, News Corp said in documents lodged with the court.



The media company’s lawyers submitted that in July 2025 HRNSW had detected quantities of the prohibited substance in Fenbender 100, a popular chemical used by farmers to treat livestock. However, no notification was provided to the industry for over two months, News Corp said, an act which showed “a callous indifference to the lives and livelihood of trainers in New South Wales”. News Corp’s lawyers submitted that the articles were in the public interest because they concerned HRNSW, the statutory body responsible for regulating the harness racing industry, and the considerable consequences of potential disqualification for trainers who had inadvertently used the banned substance. Linden, a Walkley-award winning sports reporter, had reasonably believed the stories to be in the public interest, and had spoken to dozens of industry figures including three anonymous sources during the reporting process, News Corp submitted. Looming over harness racing is the shadow of the 2011 Green Light scandal, in which corrupt stewards allegedly tipped off trainers about when their horses would be drug tested. The episode led to criminal changes for some stewards, and bans for several high-profile drivers.



News Corp’s lawyers, in their submission, wrote that there was “a perception in the industry that HRNSW had gone too far in seeking to address corruption in the sport ... by imposing draconian punishments for breaches of its rules”. Related Article Defamation Disgraced doctor Munjed Al Muderis launches Nine defamation appeal The public interest defence to defamation, introduced in 2021, allows a publisher to defeat a claim in cases where it held a reasonable belief that the publication was in the public interest. It was first successfully applied last year when Nine, owner of this masthead, defeated a defamation claim brought by orthopaedic surgeon Munjed Al Muderis over reports alleging negligent surgery. Last month, he launched an appeal against that decision. A first case-management hearing in the Buckman matter was held before Justice Michael Lee in the Federal Court last Friday. The parties have been ordered to enter into mediation before November. Both sides were contacted for comment. World.title: Labor recruits ex-Liberal premier to champion multiculturalism
World.content:
Exclusive NationalPolitical leadership Labor recruits ex-Liberal premier to champion multiculturalism Annika Smethurst July 20, 2026 — 6:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Tasmanian Liberal premier Peter Gutwein has been appointed, by Labor, as chair of Australia’s peak multicultural advisory council, warning that rhetoric from parts of the political right is fuelling hatred and vilification. Gutwein, himself a migrant, said One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s call for Australia to become a monocultural society should have been met with “appropriate disdain”, saying it was disappointing that Opposition Leader Angus Taylor didn’t immediately condemn the remarks when first asked about them. Former Tasmanian premier Peter Gutwein. Alex Ellinghausen On Monday, the Albanese government revealed Gutwein, who led Tasmania between 2020 and 2022, had been appointed chair of the Australian Multicultural Council, the independent body that provides advice to the government on multicultural affairs and social cohesion. His appointment comes amid fierce debate on the political right over multiculturalism, and a surge in support for Hanson who last month warned Australia must exist as a “monocultural society”, warning high migration had caused the country to lose its values and identity.



Former Liberal prime minister Tony Abbott has since claimed that multiculturalism has failed, prompting frontbench Liberal Andrew Bragg to reject his comments and say that it was not a view shared by elected Liberal members in parliament. Related Article Opinion

Political leadership On borrowed time? Why Liberals are starting to chatter about Angus Taylor James Massola Chief political commentator In his first interview as chair, Gutwein told this masthead that Australia had benefited from decades of bipartisan support for multiculturalism and that such an approach provided certainty and confidence in the system. “Quite obviously that’s not occurring at the moment,” Gutwein said. “Unfortunately, the leaning towards the right, especially some of the national narrative that we are seeing at the moment, is very unhelpful ... both for the country but also for the communities in which people live.



“There has been green-lighting of an opportunity for those that might seek to do others harm through inciting hatred or vilification, that green lighting’s been occurring by voices on the right at the moment. I don’t think that’s good enough, and it needs to be called out.” He said political leaders had a responsibility to reject rhetoric that risked dividing Australians rather than allowing multiculturalism to become another source of division. Gutwein said Australia’s success had always depended on leaders resisting attempts to turn multiculturalism into a partisan issue. “I believe that as a country, we need to govern from the centre,” he said. Gutwein said Australia remained one of the world’s strongest examples of a successful multicultural society.



“You have to work hard at it. You need to lean into it. You need to accept it and embrace it.” In 2024, Gutwein led a 330-kilometre walk to highlighted the contributions of Tasmania’s migrant and refugee communities to the state’s social and economic wellbeing. Loading The former premier said Australia had to spend more time highlighting the contribution migrants make to communities, businesses and public life. “One thing that I think we have to do, and be very loud about, is the need to celebrate the contributions more that people make.”



Born in England to a British mother and an Austrian-Yugoslav father, Gutwein migrated to Tasmania as a child in 1969. He said his own family experience had shaped his belief that immigration had made Australia stronger. “We are a multicultural country. We have been for a long period of time,” he said. Related Article Opinion

Diversity We’ve never been a monoculture: One group of Australians knows this Aunty Munya Andrews Indigenous elder “As a former migrant myself ... through my own lived experience, I know that if provided with opportunity, people can do wonderful things both for themselves and for the communities they live in.” He also pushed back against attempts to harness community frustration over housing affordability by blaming immigration, saying it had become a political scapegoat, pointing to Tasmania’s experience during the pandemic.



“We had negative net migration. We increased supply, we reduced migration and house prices still went up,” he said. “To have a strong, growing economy, especially at a time when you have low unemployment, we require immigration to fill those skill gaps.” Assistant Multicultural Affairs Minister Julian Hill said Gutwein brought “strong leadership” and would help guide the council as it worked to bridge communities and build a more cohesive Australia. “He brings a track record in strong leadership and a demonstrated commitment to speaking out

against racism and standing in support of the rights of all Australians to participate in our national life. Editor's pick Dementia Almost 50 per cent of dementia cases could be prevented. This new advice tells us how



“Shared values, mutual respect and a genuine sense of belonging is the foundation of success in modern, multicultural Australia.” Minister for Multicultural Affairs, Dr Anne Aly, said the council’s work helped ensure that people of all backgrounds felt valued, connected and able to contribute to Australia’s future.
