World.title: Putin is running out of time and money
World.content:
BusinessThe economyRussia-Ukraine war Opinion Putin is running out of time and money

Ambrose Evans-Pritchard July 20, 2026 — 6:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The four-year stalemate in Ukraine has suddenly broken. For the first time in modern memory, Russia is having to import fuel to keep its economy and society afloat. The speed of events is extraordinarily rapid and portends a tectonic shift in the global balance of power, dramatically improving the strategic fortunes of Europe. Russia’s energy crisis is bringing to a head a long-simmering economic crisis. AP Ukraine’s drone force of “Magyar’s Birds” has struck 30 oil and gas tankers in the Black Sea region since Wednesday. It claims to have hit 147 vessels linked to Russia in 10 days, effectively closing the Sea of Azov and tightening the blockade of the Crimean Peninsula. It is attacking refineries at will, continuously, from St Petersburg to Siberia, crippling Russia’s biggest plant some 2250 kilometres into the interior at Omsk. The range has jumped fivefold since early last year. “Russia no longer has a safe rear, and distance is no longer protection,” said Sergiy Makogon, from the Centre for European Policy Analysis.



Ukraine’s hi-tech counter-punch has echoes of the final months of the First World War when Allied armour smashed through the trenches, exploiting the breakdown on the German home front already well underway. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Russia hits Ukraine with most ballistic missiles in any attack since start of war, Kyiv says “The Ukrainians have figured out how to target the refraction facilities of the plants,” said Professor Alan Riley, an energy expert at the Atlantic Council and an adviser to the Ukrainian military. “Once you take out the most complex parts of the refinery, replacements have to come mostly from China. That can take a year or 18 months. “Russia’s air defences are around Moscow and St Petersburg, and they are designed to intercept missiles, not mass drone attacks. Refineries around the country are basically undefended,” he said. Private companies are desperately putting up wire mesh to defend their plants, sauve qui peut.



“The attacks on coastal terminals are aimed at cutting off Russia’s export revenues: the strikes on inland refineries are to bring the economy to a standstill and undermine Russia’s ability to wage war. Vladimir Putin is in very serious trouble,” said Riley. S&P Global Energy estimates that 60 per cent of Russia’s refining capacity may now be offline, cutting supply by four million barrels a day in the week ending June 10. The volumes are staggering, with immediate knock-on effects through the global economy. Russia’s military is under immense pressure, with recruitment falling. AP Russia was the world’s second-biggest exporter of refined fuel earlier this year. It has now imposed an export ban and is to import fuel from Kazakhstan and India in an extremely tight global market. Crude prices are not the relevant marker for stress in the international energy system today. The trouble has switched to the key distillates – gasoline, diesel and jet fuel – that people actually consume. The diesel “crack spread” in Rotterdam is hovering near record highs at $US70 a barrel. It is normally $US10 to $US20.



Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s outgoing defence minister, led this creative drone warfare before being sacked this week in another episode of wearisome cronyism by Volodymyr Zelensky’s venal circle. His exit will not derail the winning strategy. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Putin is losing the Ukraine war. But if he goes down, he could take us all with him Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author Russia’s energy crisis is bringing to a head a long-simmering economic crisis. Data from the finance ministry show that adjusted budget revenues from oil and gas were down 23 per cent during the January-to-June period from a year earlier despite the Iran war. They are now in free fall. The Kremlin has raised refining subsidies sixfold to hold down costs at the pump and head off popular anger – already smouldering as fuel queues reach 12 hours and the ration is cut to 20 litres in some cities. The Duma has torn up the legal budget code. Fiscal discipline is collapsing. The liquid reserves of the Kremlin’s rainy day fund are exhausted. The country cannot easily borrow on the capital markets. China has refused to allow the sale of sovereign rouble bonds on Chinese platforms. Russian banks are being pressured into funding the military-industrial apparatus and plugging the budget deficit via short-term loans.



Reuters reports that a leaked intelligence document entitled “On the probability of a banking crisis in Russia in 2026” warns that the banking system is buckling behind a veneer of illusory stability. Russia’s internet controls have failed to scotch rumours of a coming confiscation of bank savings, which is what happened to deposits at the Soviet Sberbank in 1990. It is perilous for a regime when such feverish suspicions take hold. S&P Global Energy estimates that 60 per cent of Russia’s refining capacity may now be offline, cutting supply by four million barrels a day in the week ending June 10. Bloomberg On the military front, Putin is running out of human drone fodder. He has deployed more troops than the entire British Army in a nine-month battle to capture the small town of Kostiantynivka in the Donbas, so far without clear success. The Centre for Strategic and International Studies estimates that Russia has suffered 1.4 million casualties. It is losing 30,000 to 35,000 a month in the kill zone. This, too, drains the budget. The family payout per death is £90,000 ($173,000). A lost leg costs £28,000.



A rush of recruits signed up last year to lock in the enlistment bonus – betting on easy barracks duty – when Donald Trump seemed eager to betray Ukraine. The online investigative journal Verstka, run by diaspora journalists with clandestine sources inside Russia, says recruitment since then has plummeted. “It’s as if we’ve run out of people. There are no more fools for money,” said one soldier, claiming units in his regiment were below 40 per cent strength. If the Russian invasion of Ukraine ends in a miserable whimper, it would be an undisguisable defeat for the Sino-Russian authoritarian axis, forcing opportunistic fence-sitters across the Global South to rethink their assumptions. Another told Verstka that the 2026 intake is “unfit to fight” and often press-ganged. “Some are taken from prison, others from the streets, literally homeless, already so old and ill that they can barely stand.” They are put through three days of “training” and sent straight into the kill zone. The mood is mutinous. “It’s already hatred, but not yet rage, and that’s where it’s all heading. Honestly, I’m scared for the country,” he said.



Putin faces the choice of military failure or rolling the dice on a general mobilisation, which would be politically explosive. Verstka reports that the army is already preparing camps to train tens of thousands at a time. “Everybody knows it’s a meat grinder. If Putin goes for mobilisation, there could be half a million people protesting on the streets,” said Riley. “You could see a situation like 1917, when Russian troops refused to go to the front.” The status quo is equally dangerous. Putin’s hopes of splitting European NATO or seducing Trump have come to nothing. The US Senate wants to impose ferocious secondary sanctions on buyers of Russian hydrocarbons. Trump is bored and no longer sniffs a winner in Putin. The “spirit of Anchorage” is today a sick joke in Moscow. These fast-moving events are pregnant with risk. Putin’s reflex is to escalate when his back is against the wall. Although if he tried to launch a hybrid attack on Lithuania’s 97-kilometre Suwalki Corridor – as some fear – he would run today into the teeth of Germany’s 45th Panzer Brigade.



Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war The gold walls are closing in on Putin Events are also pregnant with opportunity. If the Russian invasion of Ukraine ends in a miserable whimper, it would be an undisguisable defeat for the Sino-Russian authoritarian axis, forcing opportunistic fence-sitters across the Global South to rethink their assumptions. It would be a potent shot in the arm for a resurgent Europe, further devalue the coin of Trump’s bluster and restore the trans-Atlantic relationship to dignified balance. The West might live on yet. World.title: AFL legend Mick Malthouse says accused home invaders were ‘a bunch of cockatoos’
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts AFL legend Mick Malthouse says accused home invaders were ‘a bunch of cockatoos’ Lachlan Abbott July 20, 2026 — 6:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

AFL legend Mick Malthouse says a group of intruders who tried to force their way into his home behaved like “a bunch of cockatoos”. The former Collingwood, Carlton and West Coast coach told Melbourne Magistrates’ Court he couldn’t believe how much noise the trio made as they tried to break into the East Melbourne property in September last year. Mick Malthouse leaves Melbourne Magistrates’ Court after providing evidence on Monday. Jason South Malthouse told the court he got up in the middle of the night when he heard a noise, armed himself with a small, solid exercise bar and opened his apartment door to find three men. “I can’t believe they were that stupid and made that much noise trying to get in,” Malthouse said in his statement.



He described the ensuing confrontation as chaotic, as he swung the exercise bar “and they swung back”. Malthouse said he then chased the trio down the stairwell to a basement carpark, with one of the men claiming they’d “got the wrong building”. “Like a bunch of cockatoos, they all followed one bloke,” Malthouse said. Malthouse said he initially ordered the trio into a corner of the car park in the hope of keeping them there until police arrived, but soon decided it was too dangerous and decided to the open the garage door. “It was like trying to herd cats – they were all over the place,” Malthouse told the court.



The trio then moved past him toward the exit, Malthouse said, as he swung the exercise bar he had to keep them away. Malthouse told the court one of the men then stabbed him in the sternum with a screwdriver and said: “‘Now I’ve stabbed you, you bastard’ or something like that.” “That stays in my mind,” he added. Malthouse told the court that another man then raised a crowbar towards him, but he was able to wrestle it off him despite being dressed in his pyjamas. The men then fled. Joshua Di Cello, Aysar Mashu and Andrew Carroll have been charged with trying to invade Malthouse’s home, along with a raft of other offences. They have not yet been required to enter a plea.



Defence barrister John Desmond, for Mashu, cross-examined Malthouse during the preliminary hearing, accusing the esteemed coach of angrily turning on the men when he confronted them. “You cracked not one, but two of them?” Desmond asked, referring to Malthouse swinging at the men with the exercise bar. Lawyer John Desmond. Jason South Malthouse replied: “If I had my way, I would’ve had the three of them.” Desmond then suggested to Malthouse that he’d effectively controlled the door through which the men could escape whilst swinging his exercise bar.



Related Article Updated

Crime ‘I made a big mistake’: AFL legend Mick Malthouse describes fighting off home invaders “As absurd as it may sound, their liberty was deprived in those minutes or seconds by you,” Desmond said. “Yeah, well, if that’s the case, that’s the case,” Malthouse responded, agreeing he was angry. “It’s fight or flight – you don’t choose.” Desmond countered: “Well, you’ve never been known to take a backwards step on the footy field, have you?” After an objection from prosecutor Sam Jayasekara, Desmond said he was attempting to question Malthouse about an incident during his time at the West Coast Eagles in the 1990s to show that “in an angry state of mind, this man reacts angrily and violently”.



Earlier in the hearing, Malthouse defended the steps he took to fight off the intruders and inconsistencies between his first and second police statements. He frequently disagreed with the defence’s characterisations, such as a suggestion he might not remember the order of events due to the chaotic situation. “I thoroughly remember being stabbed first,” Malthouse said, later re-enacting the thrust towards him in the witness box. Malthouse said he didn’t receive any medical treatment, but said he misjudged the trauma of the incident, during which he worried about the safety of his wife and a family with a young daughter in his building. “I don’t read minds of these sorts of people. I’ve got no idea how they operate,” he said. The hearing continues. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter here.

World.title: Perth property developer sues politicians, journalists over ‘toxic soil’ articles
World.content:
NationalWACourts Perth property developer sues politicians, journalists over ‘toxic soil’ articles Holly Thompson July 20, 2026 — 6:09pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

A prominent Perth property developer has appeared in the Supreme Court for the first of an earmarked 13-day trial into allegations he was defamed after being accused of trying to secure a deal to dump millions of tonnes of toxic soil in the Peel region. Strzelecki Group chairman Greg Poland quit his role as deputy chairman of the Peel Development Commission in 2019, following questions from WAtoday to several government ministers regarding that allegation. Perth developer Greg Poland arrives at court on Monday for the first day of hearings in his defamation case against WAtoday. Colin Murty Poland alleges two articles published in 2019 following his resignation are defamatory, and is suing the masthead for damages, with his lawyer Martin Bennett on Monday outlining the detail of the case. The first article, regarding the dumping of the toxic sand, was written based on a recording obtained by journalists, which was also sent to Liberal MP Andrew Hastie. Hastie was in the public gallery on Monday to observe the proceedings.



Poland has brought defamation action against WAtoday, journalists Nathan Hondros and Kate Hedley, as well as several others including Hastie and former WA Liberal leader Zak Kirkup. Hastie and Kirkup were both added to the proceedings over their alleged roles in the dissemination of the recording, however it remains unclear how Kirkup was alleged to have been involved. In the recording, Poland can allegedly be heard telling a local business owner they could acquire a parcel of land in Myalup without going to tender, if they solved a headache for the state government – facilitating the dumping of “between two and eight tonnes” of toxic soil from the Forrestfield Airport Link to his land in Waroona. Bennett told the court on Monday that the soil mentioned in the story was never toxic, and that there was a public document available that would have confirmed this to be the case. That document, Preliminary site investigation and limited sampling – Perth Airport, was released by the engineering consultant AECOM, engaged to take soil samples around the airport, including in Forrestfield, over concerns with firefighting activities given that firefighting foam contains PFAS.



The findings of that report indicated the PFAS in all samples was less than the concentration needed to harm humans. WA Liberal frontbencher Andrew Hastie arrives at court on Monday. Colin Murty Bennett told the court that the soil should never have been categorised as toxic, and the journalists involved could have referred to this report but did not. He said the source of their knowledge on what made the soil toxic needed to be questioned. “If it is just because they were told it was toxic – that reasoning is fallacious,” Bennett said.



“Responsible reporting would have discovered this repo rt.” In an email from Transport Minister Rita Saffioti’s media advisor, who was sent questions over the alleged soil transfer, information provided on background also confirmed that the soil was not considered toxic. Another key complaint from Bennett was that his client was not directly contacted by journalists at this masthead. Instead, Poland and the Peel Development Commission were contacted for comment in the same email, and given one work day to respond. Poland was unavailable during that time due to being involved in meetings. Bennett told the court the first article was based on what Poland believed to have been a private conversation at the Subiaco Hotel that was recorded without Poland’s knowledge.



He argued that recording was also illegal, but was questioned by the judge because the meeting was about a public matter, on official business with the Peel Development Commission. “You can have a private conversation for a public purpose,” Bennett said. Poland has claimed that the first article infers he is “corrupt in that he arranges secret deals between the state government and private businesspeople without due process”, according to his statement of claim filed to the court, and that he “exerts improper political influence over members of the state government”. The second article included in the proceedings alleges that Poland claimed an attempt to increase WA’s lobster catch had been his plan, but that the minister for regional development – at the time Alannah MacTiernan – had botched it. The second article allegedly implies that Poland also “falsely exaggerates boasting about his political influence”.



The hearing continues. Start the day with a summary of the day’s most important and interesting stories, analysis and insights.

World.title: Israel blasts Labor’s ‘one-sided’ policy platform as Palestinian advocates push further
World.content:
PoliticsFederalIsraeli-Palestinian conflict Israel blasts Labor’s ‘one-sided’ policy platform as Palestinian advocates push further Matthew Knott July 20, 2026 — 6:28pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Israel is seeking to water down criticism of the Jewish state in Labor’s policy platform, which is set to call out settler violence in the West Bank, condemn a controversial new death penalty law and back two international courts considering genocide and war crimes charges against Israel. As Palestinian advocates call for Labor to go further by banning defence exports to Israel and imposing sweeping sanctions, the Israeli embassy in Canberra argued Labor’s draft national platform is one-sided against Israel while going easy on Hamas and other Palestinian factions for failing to advance the peace process. Israel’s embassy, led by ambassador Hillel Newman, is pushing Labor to change its policy platform. Alex Ellinghausen With Prime Minister Anthony Albanese seeking to project party unity under his leadership, Labor’s three-day national conference in Adelaide is unlikely to feature lively debates on contentious issues such as AUKUS after senior ministers spent months settling arguments behind the scenes to avoid public brawls on the conference floor. But debate could flare up over the Middle East, with the draft policy platform going into more detail on the Israeli-Palestinian dispute than past manifestos and pro-Palestinian activists on the march after Albanese last year decided to recognise Palestinian statehood.



The draft platform does not contain accusations of genocide over the way Israel fought the war in Gaza or call for restrictions on arms sales to Israel, but party activists are pushing behind the scenes to make it tougher. Related Article Exclusive

Israeli-Palestinian conflict ‘Troubling’: Top Australian Jewish groups denounce Israel’s new death penalty “Labor opposes the annexation of Palestinian territory and wants Israel to bring its illegal settlement activity and the occupation to an end, to see security for Palestine, for Israel and for the region,” the draft platform states. “Labor urges the government to prevent any support being given to illegal settlement activity or extremist settler violence, and to implement further action and sanctions as necessary.” It also condemns a law passed by the Israeli parliament in March which expands the use of the death penalty for terror offences in the occupied West Bank and “all other discriminatory laws which target Palestinians”.



The Israeli embassy issued a statement on Monday saying it “respectfully submits that several elements of the draft national platform risk placing responsibility for the conflict on one party while giving insufficient attention to the decisions, conduct and continuing obligations of the Palestinian leadership and terrorist organisations such as Hamas”. The embassy noted that the “policy motions are still in draft form, and will continue to engage constructively with the Australian Labor Party through the usual diplomatic channels”. Prime Minister Anthony Albanese in New York last year, when he officially recognised Palestine at the United Nations. Dominic Lorrimer The draft platform also states: “Labor believes in international law and will defend it. “Labor supports the International Court of Justice and the International Criminal Court and compliance with their binding decisions.”



The International Court of Justice is considering a genocide case brought against Israel over its conduct in the war in Gaza, while the International Criminal Court is considering war crimes allegations against Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu. The draft platform also says Labor “unreservedly condemns terrorism and violent extremism, including as perpetrated by Hamas and other extremists”. The Israeli embassy said in its statement: “The reality is that the moment Palestinians recognise the existence of the State of Israel and undergo significant reform, the path to peace will be paved. “That outcome cannot be achieved by pressuring Israel.” The embassy claimed that settler violence, which has surged in the West Bank over recent years, is a “reprehensible but marginal phenomenon” that receives disproportionate international attention.



“The government of Israel and the settler movement itself condemns it, and security forces work to apprehend these forms of illegal behaviour,” the statement said. The United Nations said in June that there had been an average of six settler attacks a day this year on Palestinians causing casualties or property damage – the highest on record. Related Article Exclusive

Middle East at war ‘I’m under siege’: The families fighting for their homes on the West Bank The Australia Palestine Advocacy Network is urging Labor to end Australian defence exports and military co-operation with countries that risk contributing to war crimes, crimes against humanity and genocide. The group is also calling for an end to Australian trade and investment with Jewish settlements in the West Bank and for the Future Fund to scrap all investments linked to the settlement enterprise.



“Australia must reckon with the obligations that flow from its recognition of Palestine and the Conference must draw a red line on genocide and Australian complicity,” APAN president Nasser Mashni said. He said Australia must comply with a 2024 International Court of Justice advisory opinion that found Israel’s presence in the occupied Palestinian territories was unlawful and Israeli settlements were illegal. “Recognition of Palestine cannot remain symbolic. Australia must impose wide-ranging and wholesale sanctions on the Israeli regime and anyone or any entity associated with the settlement enterprise,” he said. Albanese’s recognition of Palestinian statehood last September at the United Nations General Assembly fulfilled a pledge embedded in Labor’s policy platform in 2018. World.title: Harness racing bosses sue News Corp over drug scandal articles
World.content:
Exclusive BusinessCompaniesDefamation Harness racing bosses sue News Corp over drug scandal articles Kishor Napier-Raman July 20, 2026 — 6:27pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Two top harness racing officials say they were exposed to hatred, ridicule and contempt by a series of articles in News Corp mastheads accusing them of presiding over a doping crisis. Harness Racing NSW chief executive Peter Buckman and the sport’s chief integrity officer, Michael Prentice, commenced defamation proceedings in the Federal Court last month after articles accusing them of failing to warn trainers that a popular animal medication had become contaminated with levamisole, a deworming drug that is prohibited in equestrian sports because it acts as a powerful stimulant. Two top harness racing officials are suing News Corp over a series of articles about a drug scandal. None of those pictured are involved in the saga. Katherine Griffiths As a result of the contamination, several trainers were banned from participating in the sport, under its strict doping regime. Buckman and Prentice claim the articles published in The Daily Telegraph, The Australian and Code Sports by journalist Julian Linden defamed them by holding the pair responsible for HRNSW failing to warn participants about the potential contamination, and accused them of contributing to an emerging drug scandal in the sport.



The pair claim Linden’s reporting depicted them as “callously indifferent to the lives and livelihoods of harness racing trainers”, including former firefighter Scott Wade, who had been disqualified for life but maintains his innocence. Related Article Defamation ‘A fair degree of heat’: Peter V’landys claims early win in fiery defamation battle “Both applicants have been exposed to hatred, ridicule and contempt, and have been gravely injured in their personal and professional reputations, and have suffered and will continue to suffer hurt, distress and embarrassment,” a statement of claim filed by the pair said. Buckman and Prentice are seeking aggravated damages and an injunction restraining further publication of the articles. In response, News Corp’s lawyers say the articles are substantially true, and that they are protected by a public interest defence. Before Linden’s articles were published, 12 trainers had been suspended or disqualified from the sport after their samples were contaminated with levamisole, News Corp said in documents lodged with the court.



The media company’s lawyers submitted that in July 2025 HRNSW had detected quantities of the prohibited substance in Fenbender 100, a popular chemical used by farmers to treat livestock. However, no notification was provided to the industry for over two months, News Corp said, an act which showed “a callous indifference to the lives and livelihood of trainers in New South Wales”. News Corp’s lawyers submitted that the articles were in the public interest because they concerned HRNSW, the statutory body responsible for regulating the harness racing industry, and the considerable consequences of potential disqualification for trainers who had inadvertently used the banned substance. Linden, a Walkley-award winning sports reporter, had reasonably believed the stories to be in the public interest, and had spoken to dozens of industry figures including three anonymous sources during the reporting process, News Corp submitted. Looming over harness racing is the shadow of the 2011 Green Light scandal, in which corrupt stewards allegedly tipped off trainers about when their horses would be drug tested. The episode led to criminal changes for some stewards, and bans for several high-profile drivers.



News Corp’s lawyers, in their submission, wrote that there was “a perception in the industry that HRNSW had gone too far in seeking to address corruption in the sport ... by imposing draconian punishments for breaches of its rules”. Related Article Defamation Disgraced doctor Munjed Al Muderis launches Nine defamation appeal The public interest defence to defamation, introduced in 2021, allows a publisher to defeat a claim in cases where it held a reasonable belief that the publication was in the public interest. It was first successfully applied last year when Nine, owner of this masthead, defeated a defamation claim brought by orthopaedic surgeon Munjed Al Muderis over reports alleging negligent surgery. Last month, he launched an appeal against that decision. A first case-management hearing in the Buckman matter was held before Justice Michael Lee in the Federal Court last Friday. The parties have been ordered to enter into mediation before November. Both sides were contacted for comment. World.title: Labor recruits ex-Liberal premier to champion multiculturalism
World.content:
Exclusive NationalPolitical leadership Labor recruits ex-Liberal premier to champion multiculturalism Annika Smethurst July 20, 2026 — 6:21pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

Former Tasmanian Liberal premier Peter Gutwein has been appointed, by Labor, as chair of Australia’s peak multicultural advisory council, warning that rhetoric from parts of the political right is fuelling hatred and vilification. Gutwein, himself a migrant, said One Nation leader Pauline Hanson’s call for Australia to become a monocultural society should have been met with “appropriate disdain”, saying it was disappointing that Opposition Leader Angus Taylor didn’t immediately condemn the remarks when first asked about them. Former Tasmanian premier Peter Gutwein. Alex Ellinghausen On Monday, the Albanese government revealed Gutwein, who led Tasmania between 2020 and 2022, had been appointed chair of the Australian Multicultural Council, the independent body that provides advice to the government on multicultural affairs and social cohesion. His appointment comes amid fierce debate on the political right over multiculturalism, and a surge in support for Hanson who last month warned Australia must exist as a “monocultural society”, warning high migration had caused the country to lose its values and identity.



Former Liberal prime minister Tony Abbott has since claimed that multiculturalism has failed, prompting frontbench Liberal Andrew Bragg to reject his comments and say that it was not a view shared by elected Liberal members in parliament. Related Article Opinion

Political leadership On borrowed time? Why Liberals are starting to chatter about Angus Taylor James Massola Chief political commentator In his first interview as chair, Gutwein told this masthead that Australia had benefited from decades of bipartisan support for multiculturalism and that such an approach provided certainty and confidence in the system. “Quite obviously that’s not occurring at the moment,” Gutwein said. “Unfortunately, the leaning towards the right, especially some of the national narrative that we are seeing at the moment, is very unhelpful ... both for the country but also for the communities in which people live.



“There has been green-lighting of an opportunity for those that might seek to do others harm through inciting hatred or vilification, that green lighting’s been occurring by voices on the right at the moment. I don’t think that’s good enough, and it needs to be called out.” He said political leaders had a responsibility to reject rhetoric that risked dividing Australians rather than allowing multiculturalism to become another source of division. Gutwein said Australia’s success had always depended on leaders resisting attempts to turn multiculturalism into a partisan issue. “I believe that as a country, we need to govern from the centre,” he said. Gutwein said Australia remained one of the world’s strongest examples of a successful multicultural society.



“You have to work hard at it. You need to lean into it. You need to accept it and embrace it.” In 2024, Gutwein led a 330-kilometre walk to highlighted the contributions of Tasmania’s migrant and refugee communities to the state’s social and economic wellbeing. Loading The former premier said Australia had to spend more time highlighting the contribution migrants make to communities, businesses and public life. “One thing that I think we have to do, and be very loud about, is the need to celebrate the contributions more that people make.”



Born in England to a British mother and an Austrian-Yugoslav father, Gutwein migrated to Tasmania as a child in 1969. He said his own family experience had shaped his belief that immigration had made Australia stronger. “We are a multicultural country. We have been for a long period of time,” he said. Related Article Opinion

Diversity We’ve never been a monoculture: One group of Australians knows this Aunty Munya Andrews Indigenous elder “As a former migrant myself ... through my own lived experience, I know that if provided with opportunity, people can do wonderful things both for themselves and for the communities they live in.” He also pushed back against attempts to harness community frustration over housing affordability by blaming immigration, saying it had become a political scapegoat, pointing to Tasmania’s experience during the pandemic.



“We had negative net migration. We increased supply, we reduced migration and house prices still went up,” he said. “To have a strong, growing economy, especially at a time when you have low unemployment, we require immigration to fill those skill gaps.” Assistant Multicultural Affairs Minister Julian Hill said Gutwein brought “strong leadership” and would help guide the council as it worked to bridge communities and build a more cohesive Australia. “He brings a track record in strong leadership and a demonstrated commitment to speaking out

against racism and standing in support of the rights of all Australians to participate in our national life. Editor's pick Dementia Almost 50 per cent of dementia cases could be prevented. This new advice tells us how



“Shared values, mutual respect and a genuine sense of belonging is the foundation of success in modern, multicultural Australia.” Minister for Multicultural Affairs, Dr Anne Aly, said the council’s work helped ensure that people of all backgrounds felt valued, connected and able to contribute to Australia’s future. World.title: Putin is running out of time and money
World.content:
BusinessThe economyRussia-Ukraine war Opinion Putin is running out of time and money

Ambrose Evans-Pritchard July 20, 2026 — 6:20pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

The four-year stalemate in Ukraine has suddenly broken. For the first time in modern memory, Russia is having to import fuel to keep its economy and society afloat. The speed of events is extraordinarily rapid and portends a tectonic shift in the global balance of power, dramatically improving the strategic fortunes of Europe. Russia’s energy crisis is bringing to a head a long-simmering economic crisis. AP Ukraine’s drone force of “Magyar’s Birds” has struck 30 oil and gas tankers in the Black Sea region since Wednesday. It claims to have hit 147 vessels linked to Russia in 10 days, effectively closing the Sea of Azov and tightening the blockade of the Crimean Peninsula. It is attacking refineries at will, continuously, from St Petersburg to Siberia, crippling Russia’s biggest plant some 2250 kilometres into the interior at Omsk. The range has jumped fivefold since early last year. “Russia no longer has a safe rear, and distance is no longer protection,” said Sergiy Makogon, from the Centre for European Policy Analysis.



Ukraine’s hi-tech counter-punch has echoes of the final months of the First World War when Allied armour smashed through the trenches, exploiting the breakdown on the German home front already well underway. Related Article Russia-Ukraine war Russia hits Ukraine with most ballistic missiles in any attack since start of war, Kyiv says “The Ukrainians have figured out how to target the refraction facilities of the plants,” said Professor Alan Riley, an energy expert at the Atlantic Council and an adviser to the Ukrainian military. “Once you take out the most complex parts of the refinery, replacements have to come mostly from China. That can take a year or 18 months. “Russia’s air defences are around Moscow and St Petersburg, and they are designed to intercept missiles, not mass drone attacks. Refineries around the country are basically undefended,” he said. Private companies are desperately putting up wire mesh to defend their plants, sauve qui peut.



“The attacks on coastal terminals are aimed at cutting off Russia’s export revenues: the strikes on inland refineries are to bring the economy to a standstill and undermine Russia’s ability to wage war. Vladimir Putin is in very serious trouble,” said Riley. S&P Global Energy estimates that 60 per cent of Russia’s refining capacity may now be offline, cutting supply by four million barrels a day in the week ending June 10. The volumes are staggering, with immediate knock-on effects through the global economy. Russia’s military is under immense pressure, with recruitment falling. AP Russia was the world’s second-biggest exporter of refined fuel earlier this year. It has now imposed an export ban and is to import fuel from Kazakhstan and India in an extremely tight global market. Crude prices are not the relevant marker for stress in the international energy system today. The trouble has switched to the key distillates – gasoline, diesel and jet fuel – that people actually consume. The diesel “crack spread” in Rotterdam is hovering near record highs at $US70 a barrel. It is normally $US10 to $US20.



Mykhailo Fedorov, Ukraine’s outgoing defence minister, led this creative drone warfare before being sacked this week in another episode of wearisome cronyism by Volodymyr Zelensky’s venal circle. His exit will not derail the winning strategy. Related Article Opinion

Five Minutes with Fitz Putin is losing the Ukraine war. But if he goes down, he could take us all with him Peter FitzSimons Columnist and author Russia’s energy crisis is bringing to a head a long-simmering economic crisis. Data from the finance ministry show that adjusted budget revenues from oil and gas were down 23 per cent during the January-to-June period from a year earlier despite the Iran war. They are now in free fall. The Kremlin has raised refining subsidies sixfold to hold down costs at the pump and head off popular anger – already smouldering as fuel queues reach 12 hours and the ration is cut to 20 litres in some cities. The Duma has torn up the legal budget code. Fiscal discipline is collapsing. The liquid reserves of the Kremlin’s rainy day fund are exhausted. The country cannot easily borrow on the capital markets. China has refused to allow the sale of sovereign rouble bonds on Chinese platforms. Russian banks are being pressured into funding the military-industrial apparatus and plugging the budget deficit via short-term loans.



Reuters reports that a leaked intelligence document entitled “On the probability of a banking crisis in Russia in 2026” warns that the banking system is buckling behind a veneer of illusory stability. Russia’s internet controls have failed to scotch rumours of a coming confiscation of bank savings, which is what happened to deposits at the Soviet Sberbank in 1990. It is perilous for a regime when such feverish suspicions take hold. S&P Global Energy estimates that 60 per cent of Russia’s refining capacity may now be offline, cutting supply by four million barrels a day in the week ending June 10. Bloomberg On the military front, Putin is running out of human drone fodder. He has deployed more troops than the entire British Army in a nine-month battle to capture the small town of Kostiantynivka in the Donbas, so far without clear success. The Centre for Strategic and International Studies estimates that Russia has suffered 1.4 million casualties. It is losing 30,000 to 35,000 a month in the kill zone. This, too, drains the budget. The family payout per death is £90,000 ($173,000). A lost leg costs £28,000.



A rush of recruits signed up last year to lock in the enlistment bonus – betting on easy barracks duty – when Donald Trump seemed eager to betray Ukraine. The online investigative journal Verstka, run by diaspora journalists with clandestine sources inside Russia, says recruitment since then has plummeted. “It’s as if we’ve run out of people. There are no more fools for money,” said one soldier, claiming units in his regiment were below 40 per cent strength. If the Russian invasion of Ukraine ends in a miserable whimper, it would be an undisguisable defeat for the Sino-Russian authoritarian axis, forcing opportunistic fence-sitters across the Global South to rethink their assumptions. Another told Verstka that the 2026 intake is “unfit to fight” and often press-ganged. “Some are taken from prison, others from the streets, literally homeless, already so old and ill that they can barely stand.” They are put through three days of “training” and sent straight into the kill zone. The mood is mutinous. “It’s already hatred, but not yet rage, and that’s where it’s all heading. Honestly, I’m scared for the country,” he said.



Putin faces the choice of military failure or rolling the dice on a general mobilisation, which would be politically explosive. Verstka reports that the army is already preparing camps to train tens of thousands at a time. “Everybody knows it’s a meat grinder. If Putin goes for mobilisation, there could be half a million people protesting on the streets,” said Riley. “You could see a situation like 1917, when Russian troops refused to go to the front.” The status quo is equally dangerous. Putin’s hopes of splitting European NATO or seducing Trump have come to nothing. The US Senate wants to impose ferocious secondary sanctions on buyers of Russian hydrocarbons. Trump is bored and no longer sniffs a winner in Putin. The “spirit of Anchorage” is today a sick joke in Moscow. These fast-moving events are pregnant with risk. Putin’s reflex is to escalate when his back is against the wall. Although if he tried to launch a hybrid attack on Lithuania’s 97-kilometre Suwalki Corridor – as some fear – he would run today into the teeth of Germany’s 45th Panzer Brigade.



Related Article Opinion

Russia-Ukraine war The gold walls are closing in on Putin Events are also pregnant with opportunity. If the Russian invasion of Ukraine ends in a miserable whimper, it would be an undisguisable defeat for the Sino-Russian authoritarian axis, forcing opportunistic fence-sitters across the Global South to rethink their assumptions. It would be a potent shot in the arm for a resurgent Europe, further devalue the coin of Trump’s bluster and restore the trans-Atlantic relationship to dignified balance. The West might live on yet. World.title: AFL legend Mick Malthouse says accused home invaders were ‘a bunch of cockatoos’
World.content:
NationalVictoriaCourts AFL legend Mick Malthouse says accused home invaders were ‘a bunch of cockatoos’ Lachlan Abbott July 20, 2026 — 6:19pm Save You have reached your maximum number of saved items. Remove items from your saved list to add more. Share A A A

AFL legend Mick Malthouse says a group of intruders who tried to force their way into his home behaved like “a bunch of cockatoos”. The former Collingwood, Carlton and West Coast coach told Melbourne Magistrates’ Court he couldn’t believe how much noise the trio made as they tried to break into the East Melbourne property in September last year. Mick Malthouse leaves Melbourne Magistrates’ Court after providing evidence on Monday. Jason South Malthouse told the court he got up in the middle of the night when he heard a noise, armed himself with a small, solid exercise bar and opened his apartment door to find three men. “I can’t believe they were that stupid and made that much noise trying to get in,” Malthouse said in his statement.



He described the ensuing confrontation as chaotic, as he swung the exercise bar “and they swung back”. Malthouse said he then chased the trio down the stairwell to a basement carpark, with one of the men claiming they’d “got the wrong building”. “Like a bunch of cockatoos, they all followed one bloke,” Malthouse said. Malthouse said he initially ordered the trio into a corner of the car park in the hope of keeping them there until police arrived, but soon decided it was too dangerous and decided to the open the garage door. “It was like trying to herd cats – they were all over the place,” Malthouse told the court.



The trio then moved past him toward the exit, Malthouse said, as he swung the exercise bar he had to keep them away. Malthouse told the court one of the men then stabbed him in the sternum with a screwdriver and said: “‘Now I’ve stabbed you, you bastard’ or something like that.” “That stays in my mind,” he added. Malthouse told the court that another man then raised a crowbar towards him, but he was able to wrestle it off him despite being dressed in his pyjamas. The men then fled. Joshua Di Cello, Aysar Mashu and Andrew Carroll have been charged with trying to invade Malthouse’s home, along with a raft of other offences. They have not yet been required to enter a plea.



Defence barrister John Desmond, for Mashu, cross-examined Malthouse during the preliminary hearing, accusing the esteemed coach of angrily turning on the men when he confronted them. “You cracked not one, but two of them?” Desmond asked, referring to Malthouse swinging at the men with the exercise bar. Lawyer John Desmond. Jason South Malthouse replied: “If I had my way, I would’ve had the three of them.” Desmond then suggested to Malthouse that he’d effectively controlled the door through which the men could escape whilst swinging his exercise bar.



Related Article Updated

Crime ‘I made a big mistake’: AFL legend Mick Malthouse describes fighting off home invaders “As absurd as it may sound, their liberty was deprived in those minutes or seconds by you,” Desmond said. “Yeah, well, if that’s the case, that’s the case,” Malthouse responded, agreeing he was angry. “It’s fight or flight – you don’t choose.” Desmond countered: “Well, you’ve never been known to take a backwards step on the footy field, have you?” After an objection from prosecutor Sam Jayasekara, Desmond said he was attempting to question Malthouse about an incident during his time at the West Coast Eagles in the 1990s to show that “in an angry state of mind, this man reacts angrily and violently”.



Earlier in the hearing, Malthouse defended the steps he took to fight off the intruders and inconsistencies between his first and second police statements. He frequently disagreed with the defence’s characterisations, such as a suggestion he might not remember the order of events due to the chaotic situation. “I thoroughly remember being stabbed first,” Malthouse said, later re-enacting the thrust towards him in the witness box. Malthouse said he didn’t receive any medical treatment, but said he misjudged the trauma of the incident, during which he worried about the safety of his wife and a family with a young daughter in his building. “I don’t read minds of these sorts of people. I’ve got no idea how they operate,” he said. The hearing continues. Get the day’s breaking news, entertainment ideas and a long read to enjoy. Sign up to receive our Evening Edition newsletter here.
